items.q: Your pre-ISB work was mostly journalism and policy research. Talk me through your quantitative skills.
p: Opens with a direct claim, not a defence of the background
Cites hard evidence: test quant score, ISB finance and accounting courses
Gives one work example where numbers drove the output
Names a model built on own: three-statement or DCF
items.a: Structure: claim, evidence from three places, link to the job. Skeleton: 'My quant skills are stronger than my job titles suggest. At [your research role], I built [a dataset or analysis, e.g. a district-level dataset of N rows] and ran [the analysis] that became the core of [the report]. At ISB I took [FADM, corporate finance, valuation] and did [your result, where disclosable]. On my own I built [a three-statement model and DCF for a listed company] and can walk you through it. So the analytical base is there, and on top of it I write clearly, which matters in pitch books and information memoranda.'
items.t: Getting defensive or listing soft skills instead of offering verifiable numbers and a model you can actually discuss.

items.q: In your wealth management role you reviewed client portfolios and recommended investments. How did you analyse the returns of a client's portfolio?
p: Uses XIRR for client returns, time-weighted return for manager skill
Compares each sleeve to the right benchmark, e.g. Nifty 500 TRI
Adjusts for risk: volatility, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown
Attributes returns to allocation versus selection, then fees and tax
items.a: I work in four steps. First, measure correctly: with SIPs and withdrawals, I use XIRR for the client's own return and time-weighted return to judge the fund manager. Second, benchmark: equity against Nifty 50 or Nifty 500 TRI, debt against a relevant bond index, and the whole portfolio against a blended benchmark. Third, risk: volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown, because 14% with half the drawdown can beat 15%. Fourth, attribution: was outperformance from asset allocation or stock selection, and what did fees and taxes cost? Finally I map it to the client's goals and risk profile, which drives the recommendation. At [your firm], this showed [your finding, e.g. regular plans with high expense ratios dragging returns].
items.t: Quoting a simple absolute return that ignores cash flow timing, the benchmark, risk, and post-fee, post-tax outcome.
items.in: SEBI requires mutual funds to benchmark against Total Return Indices, and equity versus debt fund taxation differs, so compare post-tax returns.

items.q: Before ISB you were an engineer at a real estate developer. Walk me through how you analysed space requirements for the projects you worked on.
p: Gives a clear step-by-step process, not a narrative
Names inputs, assumptions and constraints, e.g. users, norms, FSI
States a number and the decision it drove
Links the method to building a financial model
items.a: Structure: objective, inputs, method, check, outcome, link. Skeleton: 'The question was how much [built-up area] a [office / hospital / residential] project needed. I started from demand drivers: [headcount or users], growth over [N] years and per-user norms from [the code or client brief]. Then I applied constraints: plot area, permissible FSI, setbacks and the carpet-to-built-up efficiency ratio. I built it in Excel with scenarios for [growth], sanity-checked it against [comparable buildings], and landed on [a number, e.g. 15% less area than the brief, saving Rs. X crore]. It is the same discipline as a financial model: drivers, assumptions, scenarios and a check against comparables.'
items.t: Drowning the interviewer in engineering detail instead of showing a structured process that transfers to modelling.

items.q: You've practised corporate law for three years. What have you done on your own initiative to learn finance?
p: Lists concrete self-driven steps taken before ISB, with dates
Mentions a credential or course, e.g. CFA Level I, modelling course
Shows applied output: a model, stock pitch or deal analysis
Connects legal deal work to finance, e.g. SPA pricing clauses
items.a: Structure: trigger, actions, proof, bridge. Skeleton: 'On deals at [your firm], I drafted [SPAs and shareholders agreements] and kept meeting valuation and price adjustment clauses I could not fully evaluate, so I started learning finance deliberately. I [cleared CFA Level I / completed a modelling course] in [year], built [a DCF on a listed company] and tracked [deals in your sector]. At ISB I chose [finance electives] and in the Finance Club I [specific contribution]. My legal background is now an asset: I read term sheets, locked-box and earn-out mechanics and diligence findings faster than most finance candidates.'
items.t: Claiming interest without evidence; saying you read the business papers daily is not initiative.

items.q: Your undergraduate degree is in English literature. How do you know you can handle the quantitative rigour of investment banking?
p: Accepts the concern calmly, then answers with evidence
Cites quant proof: test score, ISB core finance and accounting results
Notes banking maths is mostly accounting, Excel accuracy and logic
Offers to take a technical question on the spot
items.a: Structure: reframe, evidence, offer. Skeleton: 'Fair question. Banking quant is less about advanced maths and more about accounting, Excel accuracy and logical modelling, and I have tested myself on exactly that. My [GMAT or GRE quant score] and ISB core courses such as [FADM and corporate finance], where I [result], are the formal proof. At work, at [previous role], I [handled budgets, data or financial reports: specific example]. I have also built [a three-statement model or comps sheet] on my own. Happy to take any technical question you would like.'
items.t: Apologising for the degree, or calling yourself a numbers person with no score, course or model to back it.

items.q: Tell me about a time you sent out a report or deliverable that had typos or errors in it.
p: Admits a real, specific error without minimising it
States the impact and how quickly it was fixed
Describes a lasting checking process adopted afterwards
Links to accuracy standards in pitch books and models
items.a: Structure: STAR, weighted toward the fix. Skeleton: 'At [your firm], I sent [a client deck or report] where [the client's name was misspelt / a table did not tie to the appendix]. [My manager or the client] caught it. I owned it, sent a corrected version within [time] and explained the change. The root cause was rushing the final read after late edits. Since then I run a fixed final check: numbers tie to source, names and logos, consistent formatting, then one read on a fresh screen or in print. On [a later deliverable] that check caught [an error]. In banking, one wrong number in a pitch book costs credibility, so I treat it as non-negotiable.'
items.t: Saying it never happens, or picking a trivial typo with no process change; both signal low self-awareness.

items.q: What is the heaviest academic or exam load you have carried at one time, and how did you perform across all of it?
p: Gives a specific number of courses or papers
States results honestly, including the weakest subject
Explains how time was prioritised across subjects
Links to handling several live deals at once
items.a: Structure: load, method, result, link. Skeleton: 'The heaviest was [an ISB term with N courses alongside Finance Club work and placement prep / both CA Final groups while working at [firm]]. I planned week by week, front-loaded [the quant-heavy subjects] and used [a study group or fixed daily blocks]. Results: [your outcomes, e.g. cleared both groups in one attempt / top quartile in X and Y]. My weakest was [subject], because [honest reason], and I fixed that by [action]. Banking teams juggle three or four live mandates, and that period was good rehearsal for it.'
items.t: Exaggerating the load, or hiding a weak result the interviewer can easily check later.

items.q: How well do you handle several tasks at the same time? Give me evidence.
p: Answers with a concrete example, not adjectives
Shows a prioritisation method: deadline, importance, dependencies
Mentions flagging trade-offs to seniors early
Quantifies parallel workstreams and the outcome
items.a: Structure: claim, example, method. Skeleton: 'Well, and I can show it. At [your firm], I ran [three client workstreams / a month-end close, an audit query and a new proposal] in the same [two weeks]. I listed every deliverable with its deadline and who depended on it, cleared the blocking items first, and told [my manager] early that [the lower-priority item] would slip a day, which they agreed to. All [three] went out on time and [outcome]. In banking I expect several live deals at once, so I prioritise by deadline and client impact and keep seniors informed before something slips, not after.'
items.t: Calling yourself an excellent multi-tasker with no example, or implying you never need to prioritise.

items.q: Have you worked on a report or deliverable that reached a large or very senior audience? What was your part?
p: Names the audience and its scale or seniority
Separates own contribution from the team's
Mentions the quality control applied given the visibility
States the outcome or decision it influenced
items.a: Structure: context, your part, quality step, impact. Skeleton: 'Yes. At [your firm], I [built the analysis for / wrote section X of] [a board presentation / a sector report / an investor update] that went to [the client's board / N clients / the CXO team]. My part was [the market sizing model and three exhibits]. Because of the visibility, I [tied every number to source and had a second reviewer check it]. It led to [the decision, e.g. approval of a Rs. X crore capex plan]. That is close to banking work, where pitch books and offer documents are read line by line by senior clients and investors.'
items.t: Claiming the whole deliverable as your own; interviewers probe, and over-claiming collapses under follow-up.

items.q: Walk me through your CV.
p: Two minutes maximum, chronological, with one clear thread
Explains why each move happened, not just what
Highlights one or two quantified achievements
Ends with why banking now and why this firm
items.a: Structure: start, transitions, ISB, why banking. Skeleton: 'I am [name], [degree] from [college]. I started at [first firm] as [role], where I [one quantified achievement]. I moved to [second role] because [reason tied to a growing interest in finance or deals], and there I [deal or analysis example]. That exposure to [transactions, valuation or fundraising] made me want to sit on the advisory side, so I came to ISB to build the finance toolkit through [courses] and [Finance Club or competition work]. Now I am targeting [M&A or ECM] roles, and [the firm] fits because [specific reason].'
items.t: Reading the CV line by line for five minutes; the interviewer wants the narrative and the logic of each move.

items.q: Why did you choose ISB? You presumably had other options.
p: Gives two or three specific reasons, not rankings alone
Mentions the one-year format relative to work experience
Names a concrete ISB resource used: course, club, competition
Links the choice to the banking goal
items.a: Structure: two reasons plus proof. Skeleton: 'Two reasons. First, with [N] years of experience, a one-year programme let me retool without stepping out of the market for two years. Second, ISB's finance faculty and its recruiter network in [Indian banking and advisory] matched my goal of moving into deals. Since joining I have [taken specific electives, worked on X through the Finance Club, competed in Y], which confirmed the choice. [If relevant: I also had an admit from [school], but ISB fitted my timeline and goal better.]'
items.t: Saying it is the best school in India or citing rankings only; that shows no thought about fit.

items.q: I see you spent time abroad in [location], on an exchange or an overseas posting. Tell me about it and why you went.
p: States a deliberate reason for going
Gives one concrete adaptation or learning example
Shows a cross-border or client skill useful in banking
Keeps it to about one minute
items.a: Structure: why, what, so what. Skeleton: 'I went to [location] for [an exchange term / an N-month client posting] because [deliberate reason, e.g. the client's project needed someone on site / I wanted exposure to a deeper capital market]. The biggest adjustment was [working style or client expectations], which I handled by [action]. A concrete result was [outcome]. It is relevant here because Indian deals increasingly involve foreign strategics, PE funds and global investors, and I am comfortable working across those teams and time zones.'
items.t: Turning it into a travel story with no learning and no link to the job.

items.q: Why did you choose [your undergraduate subject, e.g. mechanical engineering or B.Com]?
p: Gives an honest reason, including exam or family context
Names what the degree taught that is genuinely useful
Bridges the degree to the move into finance
Does not disown the subject
items.a: Structure: honest reason, what you gained, bridge. Skeleton: 'Honestly, [I was strong in maths and physics and engineering was the natural option / I wanted a commerce base for CA]. What it gave me was [structured problem solving / accounting fundamentals]. During [a course or project], I found I enjoyed [the costing or economics side] more than [core design], which pushed me toward [your next role] and eventually finance. So the degree was not a detour; it is where [the analytical habit] came from.'
items.t: Dismissing the degree as a mistake or as parental pressure without showing what you took from it.

items.q: Which other business schools did you apply to, and where did you get in?
p: Answers honestly and briefly
Names options without boasting or hedging
Explains why ISB won on specific criteria
Stays consistent with the why ISB answer
items.a: Structure: honest list, decision logic. Skeleton: 'I applied to [ISB, IIM X and an international school Y] and got into [list honestly]. I chose ISB because [the one-year format suited my experience / its finance placement record / the network in Indian banking], and for my goal of [IB in India] that mattered more than [the other school's advantage].' If ISB was your only admit: 'ISB was my first choice and I applied with that focus; I was fortunate it worked out.' Keep it to three sentences.
items.t: Inflating admits or criticising other schools; both are easy to spot and look petty.

items.q: Your CV says you are fluent in [language]. Tell me about the last time you used it at work.
p: Gives a specific professional use, not just classroom study
Is honest about level: fluent, professional or conversational
Is ready if the interviewer switches to that language
Links the language to clients or markets the firm covers
items.a: Structure: context, task, level, relevance. Skeleton: 'At [your firm], I used [language] [daily with the client's team in X / to review documents for a client based in Y]. For example, I [specific task, e.g. ran calls with the client's finance team or summarised diligence findings]. I would describe my level as [professional / fluent]. It could help here on [cross-border deals with strategic buyers from that country / clients in a particular region].' If you are not genuinely fluent, correct the CV before the interview.
items.t: Overstating fluency; interviewers sometimes switch languages mid-answer to test it.
items.in: Regional languages such as Gujarati, Marathi or Tamil genuinely help with promoter-led mid-market clients; mention it if true.

items.q: What do you do outside work?
p: Names one or two genuine interests with specifics
Shows commitment or progress, e.g. a race time or rating
Can sustain a follow-up conversation on it
Under 45 seconds
items.a: Structure: interest, detail, what it says about you. Skeleton: 'I [run / play chess / play club cricket / cook regional food]. I have [completed N half marathons, best time X / reached a rating of Y]. What I enjoy is [the discipline of a training plan / the problem solving], and I have kept it going at ISB by [routine]. [Optional: I also follow deals and markets closely, but that is closer to work.]' Choose something real; the interviewer may share the interest and ask more.
items.t: Naming only reading financial news, or an interest you cannot discuss beyond one line.

items.q: What was your favourite course, at ISB or in undergrad, and why?
p: Names a specific course and one specific idea from it
Explains why it engaged you
Shows application, e.g. a project, model or deal view
Can handle a technical follow-up on it
items.a: Structure: course, idea, application. Skeleton: 'At ISB it was [corporate finance / valuation / an M&A elective]. The idea that stuck was [e.g. that value comes from returns above the cost of capital, not growth by itself]. In our group project we [valued X / analysed the Y acquisition] and found [insight]. It also changed how I read deals: when [a recent Indian deal] was announced, I looked first at [the premium paid and whether the synergy case justified it].'
items.t: Picking a course and then being unable to answer a basic technical question on it.

items.q: What are some of your favourite books or films?
p: Names one or two titles you know well
Says what you took from each in a sentence
Avoids choosing titles only to impress
Brief and conversational
items.a: Structure: title, why, light link. Skeleton: 'Recently I enjoyed [book or film]. What stayed with me was [one specific idea or scene], because [personal reason]. On the business side, I liked [a business book you have actually read, e.g. on an Indian company or founder], especially [one point it made].' Keep the link to work light; the interviewer is trying to see who you are, and an honest, specific answer starts a real conversation.
items.t: Naming a famous finance book you have not read; one follow-up question exposes it.

items.q: Tell me something interesting about yourself that isn't on your CV.
p: One specific, memorable fact, not a personality trait
A short story with a detail that invites follow-up
Indirectly reveals a work-relevant quality
Under 45 seconds
items.a: Structure: fact, quick story, what it reveals. Skeleton: 'I [help run my family's business on weekends / taught myself X / trekked to Y / organised Z for N people]. For example, [one concrete detail with a number]. It taught me [one quality, e.g. negotiating with suppliers or persistence], which my CV does not show.' Pick something that makes you easy to remember for an interviewer who sees ten candidates that day.
items.t: Restating CV content, or giving a generic trait such as being very hardworking.

items.q: You've spent several years as an engineer at IT services and product companies. Why move into investment banking now?
p: Gives a specific trigger, not a general liking for finance
Explains what banking offers that tech roles do not
Shows concrete steps already taken toward finance
Positions tech background as an edge on tech mandates
items.a: Structure: trigger, why IB specifically, proof, edge. Skeleton: 'At [your company], I worked on [product or client], and I kept seeing that the decisions that mattered were driven by [funding rounds, acquisitions or capital allocation], not the code. I want to work on those transactions. IB specifically, because it gives deal exposure across many companies quickly and builds valuation and execution skills. I have tested the interest through [ISB courses, a model, a Finance Club project]. And I bring an edge on [tech or SaaS] mandates: I can assess product, tech stack and unit economics in diligence faster than most.'
items.t: Sounding like you are escaping engineering, or naming pay and prestige as the main driver.

items.q: You've been in Big 4 audit or transaction services for a few years. Why choose a role with far more stress and nearly double the hours?
p: Acknowledges the hours directly, without bravado
Motivation is owning the transaction outcome, not reviewing it
Cites proof of handling peak load, e.g. year-end or diligence
Shows realistic knowledge of the associate role
items.a: Structure: acknowledge, motivation, proof. Skeleton: 'I know the hours are long, and I have spoken to [associates at banks] about what that really means. What draws me is the role: in [audit or transaction services], I worked on deals after the fact or in pieces, [e.g. a quality of earnings review for a PE buyer]; in banking I would help shape the transaction and see it close. I have handled [year-end close or a two-week diligence] with long stretches, and I did my best work then. So the hours are a cost I have priced in, for work I actually want to do.'
items.t: Claiming the hours will not bother you at all; it sounds naive. Show you have priced them in.

items.q: You've spent four years in the M&A practice of a top Indian law firm and are on track for senior roles. Why give that up to restart as an Associate in banking?
p: Explains a clear pull toward commercial rather than legal questions
Accepts the step back in seniority and pay calmly
Highlights transferable skills: SPAs, diligence, negotiation
Shows long-term logic, not an escape from law
items.a: Structure: pull, trade-off, edge. Skeleton: 'On deals like [the transaction you worked on], I drafted the SPA, but the questions I found most interesting were commercial: what the business was worth, how the price was structured, why the buyer could pay for [synergy]. Bankers own those questions. I accept that I restart as an Associate and the pay resets for a while; I see that as an investment in a long advisory career. And I am not starting from zero: I know diligence, SPAs, conditions precedent and how negotiations move, which shortens my learning curve on execution.'
items.t: Criticising the legal profession, or seeming unaware that the switch is a real step back.

items.q: You spent a year at a strategy consulting firm and then a year at an advisory boutique before ISB. How do I know you're sure about banking?
p: Frames both moves as deliberate exploration with a conclusion
States what consulting lacked that banking offered
Gives concrete evidence from the banking stint
Shows clear commitment without dismissing consulting
items.a: Structure: tried both, chose one, why. Skeleton: 'I am sure precisely because I tried both. Consulting at [firm] taught me [structured problem solving], but I missed [financial depth and a tangible outcome]; recommendations often ended with the deck. At [the boutique], I worked on [deal], built [the model] and saw it through to [signing or closing]. That combination of financial work and a concrete result is what I want. Since then I have [taken specific electives and spoken to bankers], and I am interviewing only for [IB or M&A] roles.'
items.t: Badmouthing consulting, or hedging by saying you are still keeping options open.

items.q: You built and sold a D2C startup for about Rs. 8 crore within two years and run a profitable property portfolio. Why work for someone else in banking?
p: Shows humility; does not sound like a temporary stop
Names specific skills banking adds that founders usually lack
Shows comfort with a junior role in a hierarchy
Gives a credible reason for long-term commitment
items.a: Structure: what the sale taught you, what you lack, commitment. Skeleton: 'Selling [the company] was the most educational part of the journey. I saw how much [our adviser / the buyer's bankers] shaped value through the process, the buyer list and the negotiation, and I realised I had learned how to build, not how to value or transact at scale. Banking gives me exposure to dozens of businesses and deals in a few years, which I could not get alone. I am comfortable in a team structure: [example of working under someone]. And as a former founder, I understand how promoter clients think, because I have sat on their side of the table.'
items.t: Signalling you will leave to start another venture soon, or that junior work is beneath you.

items.q: You've worked on a prop trading desk and in institutional equities dealing. Traders are well paid and keep market hours. Why switch to investment banking?
p: Distinguishes trading horizons from multi-year corporate horizons
Gives a positive pull toward banking, not an escape
Positions market knowledge as an asset for ECM
Acknowledges the longer hours realistically
items.a: Structure: what you learned, what you want, edge. Skeleton: 'Trading taught me [speed, discipline and reading flows], and I enjoyed it. But my horizon was [minutes to days], and I became more interested in what drives a company's value over years: strategy, capital structure and transactions. I noticed this when [e.g. trading around a QIP or block deal made me want to understand it from the issuer's side]. Banking puts me on that side. I know the hours are longer. And I bring a market lens on how investors price an IPO or block, which is useful in ECM and in pitches.'
items.t: Implying you left trading because of losses, or that you think banking is easier work.

items.q: Where else are you interviewing? Only banking, or also consulting and corporate roles?
p: Honest, with banking clearly the priority
Describes the banking set broadly without listing every firm
Any non-banking option fits the same deal story
Brief; does not volunteer doubts
items.a: Structure: priority, honest range, consistency. Skeleton: 'My focus is investment banking. I am interviewing with [a few Indian banks and advisory boutiques], mainly for [M&A or ECM] roles. [If true: I am also in process for [corporate development or transaction advisory] roles, which use the same deal skills, but banking is my first choice because [reason].] I have not applied for [unrelated paths such as general consulting or product], because they do not fit what I want to do.'
items.t: Claiming you are interviewing nowhere else (not credible), or listing unrelated roles that undercut commitment.

items.q: Are you mainly interviewing at large banks like ours? Which parts of banking are you considering?
p: Shows awareness of the landscape: Indian banks, boutiques, global banks
Gives a reason for preferring this type of firm
Names a product or sector focus, e.g. M&A, ECM
Consistent with what this firm actually does
items.a: Structure: landscape, focus, preference. Skeleton: 'Mostly full-service firms with strong [M&A and ECM] franchises like yours, plus [one or two boutiques]. Within banking I am focused on [M&A, ECM or a sector such as X], because [reason tied to your background]. I prefer a platform like yours because [deal flow across sizes / ECM leadership / strong corporate relationships], which means more live execution early. If I am staffed in [ECM or a coverage team] instead, I would still be glad, because [reason].'
items.t: Not knowing what the firm is strong in, or saying you will take any banking job anywhere.
items.in: Domestic firms (Kotak, Axis Capital, JM Financial, ICICI Securities) rank high in Indian ECM; global banks win many large deals; Avendus is strong in PE-backed and tech M&A.

items.q: Before ISB you changed jobs roughly once a year. Why should I believe you'll stay with us for the long term?
p: Explains the moves briefly with one coherent thread
Owns any move that was a mistake
Presents ISB and banking as the end of exploration
Gives evidence of sticking with something hard
items.a: Structure: thread, ownership, commitment. Skeleton: 'Fair concern. The moves had a common thread: [from engineering toward business, then toward finance]. [Move 1] was for [reason]; [move 2] was because [reason]. In hindsight, [one move] was hasty, and I learned to [lesson]. ISB was the deliberate step to stop exploring and commit; this is the career I have been moving toward. On staying power: [a long commitment, e.g. three years leading a volunteer group, clearing CA, responsibility in the family business].'
items.t: Blaming previous employers or managers for every move; that is a bigger red flag than the moves.

items.q: Several of our analysts and associates have left early for private equity funds and family offices. If you got such an offer, why would you stay?
p: Does not pretend buy-side interest does not exist
Gives a reason to stay: breadth of deals, skill-building
Shows understanding of associate to VP progression
Cites this firm's specific advantages
items.a: Structure: honest, reason to stay, specific. Skeleton: 'I would stay because of what I want to build. Advisory gives me breadth: [sector] clients, sell-side, buy-side and capital raising. The step from associate to VP is where you start owning client relationships, which is my long-term goal; a buy-side seat is narrower. Here specifically, [the firm's mid-market depth / sector strength / early client access] is why I see a career, not a two-year stint. I would rather be the associate who gets promoted than one who treats the firm as a stepping stone.'
items.t: Claiming you would never look at PE (not credible), or admitting banking is a stepping stone.

items.q: Tell me about a time you failed to keep a commitment.
p: Picks a real, moderate failure, neither trivial nor disastrous
Says when and how the problem was flagged
Explains how the damage was repaired
States the changed habit and proof it works
items.a: Structure: STAR plus lesson. Skeleton: 'At [your firm], I committed to deliver [the analysis] to [client or manager] by [date]. I underestimated [the data cleaning / a dependency on another team], and I flagged the delay only [the day before]. I apologised, sent a partial version on time and the full one [two days] later. The lesson was that the real failure was the late warning, not the delay. Now I flag deadline risk as soon as I see it, with a revised plan; on [a later example], that let us still meet the client date.'
items.t: Choosing a story where someone else was at fault, or one with no change in behaviour afterwards.

items.q: If I made you an offer right now, would you accept on the spot?
p: Shows clear enthusiasm for the firm
Answer is consistent with placement rules and other processes
Not hesitant or visibly calculating
Under 30 seconds
items.a: Structure: enthusiasm first, a genuine condition only if real. Skeleton if this is your first choice: 'Yes. [The firm] is my first choice because [one specific reason], and I would accept.' If it is a strong choice but you have a genuine constraint: 'I would be delighted, and very likely yes. I would want to [speak to my family / follow the campus process], but this is where I want to be because [reason].' The interviewer is testing enthusiasm, so lead with it and keep any condition short.
items.t: Saying you would need to compare offers first; it tells them they are your backup.
items.in: On campus, ISB placement rules govern offer acceptance and further participation. Know them beforehand and never imply you would renege on an accepted offer.

items.q: Suppose we gave you an offer. How long would you need to decide?
p: Gives a short, specific timeframe
Justifies it with a real reason, not offer shopping
Stays within campus placement rules
Reaffirms interest in the firm
items.a: Structure: short answer, reason, enthusiasm. Skeleton: 'Not long. [On campus: I would respond within the timeline the ISB placement process sets.] [Off campus: a few days, mainly to discuss with my family and understand the team and location.] I am not looking to use an offer as leverage; [the firm] is high on my list because [specific reason], so I would expect to come back quickly.'
items.t: Asking for weeks, or hinting you will use the offer to negotiate elsewhere.
items.in: Campus offers follow the ISB placement committee's response rules; off-campus Indian firms usually expect a decision within days.

items.q: You worked in a global bank's India IB team before ISB. You'd be crazy not to go back. Why join our boutique's M&A team instead?
p: Does not criticise the previous bank
Gives specific reasons: deal responsibility, exposure, sector
References this firm's recent deals
Explains why the bigger brand is not the deciding factor
items.a: Structure: respect, trade-off, specific pull. Skeleton: 'I valued my time at [the global bank]; the brand and process discipline were excellent. But my role was mostly [one slice of large deals / pitch support, with execution led from a regional hub]. At [your firm], the deals are [mid-market, India-led, in sector X], and associates get [direct client time and full model ownership]. Your work on [a specific recent deal] is exactly what I want to execute. At this stage, that responsibility is worth more to me than the brand.'
items.t: Giving a missing return offer as the real reason, or failing to name a single deal this firm has done.

items.q: Your pre-ISB role was at a large bank, so you could likely join several big firms. Why us specifically?
p: Names two firm-specific reasons, not generic praise
Cites a recent deal, league table position or sector strength
Mentions a conversation with someone at the firm
Links the reasons to own background
items.a: Structure: two specific reasons plus people. Skeleton: 'Two reasons. First, [the firm's strength, e.g. leadership in Indian IPOs and QIPs / depth in sector X], which matches my background in [sector or skill]; deals like [a specific recent transaction] are what I want to work on. Second, [team structure, e.g. associates working across ECM and M&A / lean deal teams]. When I spoke to [an associate or VP in your team], [what they said] confirmed it. Not every large bank offers that combination.'
items.t: Generic answers about great culture and brand that could apply to any bank on the list.

items.q: You enjoyed the small team and hands-on work at a boutique before ISB. Why not go back? Why a large bank now?
p: Values the boutique experience genuinely
Names what a large platform adds: deal size, products, reach
Shows realism about bigger-team structures
Ties the choice to a long-term goal
items.a: Structure: what the boutique gave, what was missing, what you want next. Skeleton: 'The boutique gave me [end-to-end execution on N deals], and I would not trade that. What it lacked was [larger deal sizes / ECM and debt capability / cross-border reach]; on [a deal], we lost the mandate partly because the client wanted [an IPO capability we did not have]. Now I want to learn how larger, multi-product transactions are run. I also think the hands-on habit I built will make me useful quickly on a larger team.'
items.t: Implying you want the bigger brand for its own sake, or criticising the boutique.

items.q: Why our M&A team rather than an industry coverage group? Our consumer, financial institutions and healthcare teams have had a strong year.
p: Explains coverage versus product group roles correctly
Gives a reason for M&A: execution depth across sectors
Acknowledges coverage strengths and stays open on staffing
Links the choice to own background
items.a: Structure: show the distinction, then your reason. Skeleton: 'Coverage teams own client relationships in a sector and originate deals across products; M&A is the product team that executes transactions and goes deep on valuation, process and negotiation. Early in my career I want [that execution depth across sectors], because it builds the technical base for everything later. That said, my background in [sector] means I could add value working with your [sector] team on its M&A mandates, and I am open to wherever I am most useful.'
items.t: Not knowing the difference between coverage and product groups, or dismissing the sector teams' success.
items.in: In many Indian firms the split is less rigid: lean teams often cover a sector and also execute M&A and ECM, so signal flexibility.

items.q: Why capital markets, when equity and debt issuance can go quiet for quarters at a time?
p: Recognises issuance is cyclical and windows reopen quickly
Describes slow-period work: pipeline, IPO readiness, drafting
Cites recent data: IPO, QIP or bond issuance volumes
Gives a personal reason for liking markets-facing work
items.a: Structure: cycle, what the job is in slow periods, why you. Skeleton: 'Issuance is cyclical, but the work is not. In slow periods, ECM and DCM teams build the pipeline: preparing companies for IPO readiness, drafting offer documents so they can launch when a window opens, and running blocks, QIPs and bond deals, which continue in most markets. Windows also reopen fast; [cite the recent pattern, e.g. Indian IPO volumes over the last year]. I like the role because it sits between issuers and investors, which fits my [markets or investor-facing] experience at [role].'
items.t: Agreeing the market is dead, or not knowing recent issuance volumes and the largest recent deals.
items.in: Indian ECM spans IPOs, QIPs and rights issues under SEBI ICDR, plus exchange-route OFS and block deals; corporate bonds are mostly privately placed. Quote current figures.

items.q: What do you think our firm's biggest weaknesses are?
p: Gives a researched, fact-based observation, not an insult
Frames it as a gap the firm may be addressing
Shows how you could help close it
Measured tone, brief answer
items.a: Structure: researched observation, context, your role. Skeleton: 'From the outside, one area that looks less developed is [e.g. your share of mid-market tech M&A relative to your ECM franchise / outbound cross-border deals], based on [league tables or recent mandates]. That may be a deliberate choice, and I noticed [recent hires or deals that show investment there]. If it is a growth area, my background in [relevant sector] is where I could add value.' Use public data only, and keep it to one weakness.
items.t: Claiming the firm has no weaknesses, or delivering harsh criticism with no facts behind it.

items.q: Which of our competitors do you admire most, and why?
p: Names a real competitor and a specific reason
Grounds it in a deal, franchise or practice
Does not imply the competitor is better overall
Brings the answer back to this firm
items.a: Structure: name, specific reason, return. Skeleton: 'I admire [competitor] for [a specific strength, e.g. its new-age tech IPO franchise / PE-backed M&A in sector X], which I saw on [specific deal]. What impresses me is how they built it: [sector specialists, early founder relationships]. That said, I am here because [your firm] combines [strength A] with [strength B], which I think matters more for the kind of deals I want to work on.'
items.t: Refusing to name anyone, or praising a competitor so much that you seem to prefer it.

items.q: I know it's early, but have you thought about your long-term plans? Do you see yourself staying in investment banking?
p: Says yes to banking clearly
Describes progression: associate, VP, client ownership
Shows understanding of what senior bankers do
Does not mention an exit plan
items.a: Structure: commitment, progression, motivation. Skeleton: 'Yes. My plan is to build execution skill as an associate, then move into the VP role where you run deals day to day and start owning client relationships. Long term, I want to be the banker [promoters or CFOs in sector X] call first when they are considering a transaction. That takes ten or more years to build, and it is why I chose advisory over [the alternative you considered].'
items.t: Mentioning PE, a startup or a corporate role as the real long-term plan.

items.q: Your pre-ISB experience is quite varied. After the MBA, where do you see your career going over the long term?
p: Connects the varied past into one direction
Presents banking as the destination, not a stop
Explains how past roles add value in banking
Concise and specific
items.a: Structure: thread, destination, how the past helps. Skeleton: 'The common thread across [role 1, role 2 and role 3] was [moving steadily closer to financial decisions]. Long term, I see myself in advisory, building toward leading transactions for [sector] clients. The varied background helps: [engineering] lets me understand how the business works, and [consulting or audit] lets me build the numbers and run diligence. ISB is where I converted those into the finance toolkit for this path.'
items.t: Listing more options, which confirms the interviewer's worry that you are still exploring.

items.q: What is your career goal?
p: States the goal in one specific sentence
Gives a short-term and a long-term version
Short-term goal is the role on offer
Explains why this firm accelerates it
items.a: Structure: one-line goal, short term, long term. Skeleton: 'My goal is to become a trusted adviser to [companies or promoters in sector X] on their biggest financial decisions. Over the next three to four years, that means mastering execution as an associate here: models, diligence, documentation and running a process. After that, it means moving into a role where I originate and lead deals. [The firm] fits because [specific reason, e.g. its depth in that sector].'
items.t: Vague goals such as growing and learning, or a goal that clearly sits outside banking.

items.q: Looking ten years ahead, do you think you'll still be an investment banker?
p: Answers yes, clearly and early
Describes what the role looks like in ten years
Acknowledges uncertainty without hedging
Ties back to what motivates you
items.a: Structure: yes, picture, reason. Skeleton: 'Yes, that is my plan. In ten years I would like to be [a director or MD-level banker] leading [sector] mandates, with client relationships I have built myself. Nobody can be certain about a decade, but the things I enjoy, [understanding businesses, high-stakes transactions, client work], become more central as you get senior in banking, so I do not see a reason to leave.'
items.t: Saying probably not, or hinting at PE; firms hire with retention in mind.

items.q: In your last role before ISB, what feedback did you get from your manager or team?
p: Quotes specific positive feedback with an example
Includes one development point honestly
Shows what was done about the development point
References a formal rating or appraisal if strong
items.a: Structure: strength, development point, action. Skeleton: 'My [last appraisal / manager's feedback] at [firm] highlighted [a strength, e.g. accuracy and ownership of the model]; for example, on [project], I [specific action]. I was rated [rating, if good]. The development point was [e.g. being more concise in client updates / pushing back on scope earlier]. Since then I have [action], and at ISB [example of improvement]. I expect banking feedback to be blunt and frequent, and I find that useful.'
items.t: Reporting only praise; it suggests you cannot take criticism or are hiding something.
items.in: ISB's one-year PGP has no summer internship, so interviewers probe pre-MBA appraisals, ELP or live projects; prepare feedback from those.

items.q: What are a couple of areas your team said you should work on?
p: Names one or two real, non-fatal development areas
Avoids disguised strengths such as working too hard
Shows concrete steps taken and evidence of progress
Avoids core banking skills as the weakness
items.a: Structure: area, example, fix, progress. Skeleton: 'Two came up. First, [delegating or asking for help early]: on [project], I tried to do everything myself and it slowed the team down. I now [specific habit]. Second, [being more concise]: my updates had too much detail. At ISB I have worked on it by [leading presentations with the answer first], and [group or faculty] feedback has improved. Neither is fully solved, but both are clearly better.'
items.t: Choosing a core IB skill such as attention to detail or Excel, or offering a fake weakness.

items.q: Would your previous employer take you back? Did they try to keep you when you left for ISB?
p: Answers directly, yes or no
Gives evidence: retention offer, promotion, standing invitation
If no, explains calmly and briefly
Pivots to why banking is still the choice
items.a: Structure: direct answer, evidence, pivot. If yes: 'Yes. When I resigned, [my manager offered a role in X / a promotion / to keep the role open], and I left on good terms. I declined because [my goal was moving into deals], which is why I am here.' If not: 'They did not have [a role to return to / a rehiring practice], but [my manager] said [specific], and I am happy to share references.' Keep it factual and short.
items.t: Lying or getting defensive; a reference check will expose it.
items.in: With no summer internship at ISB, this tests pre-MBA standing; sponsored candidates should mention any return obligation honestly.

items.q: After a year in Big 4 audit, what did your year-end review say?
p: States the actual rating or band if strong
Gives a strength with an engagement example
Names one development area and the fix
Links audit skills to banking work
items.a: Structure: rating, strength, development, link. Skeleton: 'I was rated [rating or band] in my [year] review. The strengths highlighted were [e.g. handling complex revenue recognition and client communication]; on [engagement], I [specific example]. The development area was [e.g. clearing review notes faster / delegating to article assistants], and I worked on it by [action]. The audit training carries straight into banking: I read financial statements and notes quickly and spot quality-of-earnings issues early.'
items.t: Being vague about the rating; interviewers assume the worst when you avoid the number.
items.in: Ind AS audit exposure is a real edge; name areas like Ind AS 115 revenue or Ind AS 116 leases that matter in diligence.

items.q: If your closest friend described you in three words, which would they pick and why?
p: Three specific words, not cliches like hardworking
Each word backed by a one-line example
At least one word maps to a banking need
Under 60 seconds
items.a: Structure: word plus one-line proof, three times. Skeleton: 'They would say [reliable]: when [friend] needed [help with X], I [did Y]. [Curious]: I [dig into how things work, e.g. read the annual reports of companies I use]. And [calm]: during [a family emergency or tight deadline], I [specific action]. Those are also what a deal team needs: someone they can rely on late at night who stays composed under pressure.'
items.t: Listing three adjectives with no stories, or picking words a friend would never actually use.

items.q: If I spoke to someone you haven't got along with, what would they say about you?
p: Names a real conflict with specific context
States the other person's fair criticism honestly
Shows understanding of their perspective
Explains how behaviour or the relationship changed
items.a: Structure: who, their honest view, your learning. Skeleton: 'At [firm], [a peer or senior in another team] and I clashed over [priorities or approach on a project]. They would say I was [too insistent on my approach / impatient with their timelines], and that is fair. They would probably also say I was [reliable and well prepared]. Later I understood [their constraint]. I [changed behaviour, e.g. started agreeing timelines upfront], and we worked well together on [a later project].'
items.t: Claiming you get along with everyone, or describing the other person as the whole problem.

items.q: Why might we decide not to give you an offer today?
p: Names a plausible, non-fatal concern, e.g. a background gap
Addresses it immediately with evidence
Does not volunteer a genuine disqualifier
Ends on a confident close
items.a: Structure: name the likely concern, rebut, close. Skeleton: 'The most likely reason would be [my lack of direct banking experience / a non-finance undergraduate degree]. I would argue against it: I have [built models, done X at ISB, handled Y in my previous role], and on [a deal-like project] I did [analysis]. That makes me [ready to contribute early / a faster learner than my CV suggests]. So I hope that concern does not decide it.'
items.t: Offering a real red flag, or refusing to answer and saying there is no reason.

items.q: In three sentences, tell me why we should hire you.
p: Exactly three crisp sentences
Covers skills, evidence and fit with this firm
Includes at least one number or concrete proof
No hedging words
items.a: Structure: what you bring, proof, why here. Skeleton: 'I bring [technical depth in X plus Y years of client or deal work in sector Z]. At [firm], I [quantified achievement, e.g. built the model for a Rs. 500 crore acquisition / led diligence on N transactions], and at ISB I [one relevant achievement]. I want to build my career in [the firm's area], and I will work as hard as anyone on your team.' Rehearse it until it takes under 30 seconds.
items.t: Running past three sentences, or using generic claims like hardworking team player.

items.q: What has been your biggest failure?
p: A real failure with real stakes, not a disguised success
Takes clear ownership without blaming others
States a specific lesson and changed behaviour
Shows evidence the lesson worked later
items.a: Structure: setup, failure, ownership, lesson, proof. Skeleton: 'At [firm or venture], I [led or owned] [project], aiming for [goal]. It failed: [outcome, e.g. the client did not renew / the product got no traction] because I [your own mistake, e.g. did not test assumptions with users / overcommitted on timelines]. I owned that with [manager or team]. The lesson was [specific], and on [the next project] I [applied it], which led to [result].' Pick a failure that is meaningful but clearly recovered from.
items.t: Picking a failure caused by others, or one so trivial it shows no real self-reflection.

items.q: Tell me about a team project or group effort you were part of, at work, at ISB or outside. What was your role?
p: Sets context and the team goal in one or two lines
Names their specific role, not just what 'we' did
Gives a measurable outcome or result
Shares one lesson relevant to deal teams
items.a: Use a tight STAR structure and keep the spotlight on your contribution. For example: 'At [your firm], I was one of [four] people on [a due diligence or client implementation project] for [the client], with [a three-week deadline]. My role was [building the financial model and coordinating the data requests]. Midway, [a key input changed], so I [reworked the plan and took on the reconciliation myself]. We delivered [on time], and the client [used it to close the deal or cut costs by X percent]. What I took away is that small teams under deadline need one clear owner per workstream, which is exactly how deal teams run.'
items.t: Saying 'we' throughout so the interviewer cannot tell what you personally did.

items.q: Describe a time a team you were on did not work the way it should have. Whose fault was it?
p: Diagnoses the root cause: roles, incentives, communication or process
Takes a share of responsibility without blaming one person
Explains what they did to fix it
States what they now do differently
items.a: This tests ownership, so answer with diagnosis, not blame. Structure: what went wrong, why, what you did, what changed. For example: 'In [an ISB group assignment or a client project], we [missed an internal deadline] because [roles were never split clearly and two of us duplicated work]. Part of that was on me: I [assumed someone else was coordinating]. I [set up a simple tracker with one owner per section and a ten-minute daily check-in], and we [submitted on time with a strong result]. Since then, I agree owners and deadlines in the first meeting of any team effort.' If pressed on fault, say it was shared and name your part first.
items.t: Blaming a teammate by name, or claiming nobody was at fault; both signal poor ownership.

items.q: Tell me about an ethical dilemma you faced at work or in school. How did you handle it?
p: A real dilemma with genuine pressure, not a trivial choice
Explains how they weighed the options
Acted with integrity or escalated, despite a cost
Links to confidentiality and judgement in banking
items.a: Pick a real situation with some pressure attached, and show your process, not just a righteous ending. For example: 'At [your Big 4 or consulting firm], a [senior or client] asked me to [adjust a number, backdate a document or share another client's data] to [meet a deadline]. I did not want to damage the relationship, but it was clearly wrong. I [asked clarifying questions, explained the issue calmly and escalated to my manager with the facts]. We [corrected it], and although it [delayed the deliverable by a day], the client [accepted it]. In banking you handle price-sensitive information daily, so I treat confidentiality and accuracy as non-negotiable.'
items.t: Choosing a trivial example, or one where you went along with the wrong thing and never corrected it.
items.in: Showing awareness of SEBI insider trading rules and wall-crossing helps; Indian banks run strict controls on unpublished price-sensitive information.

items.q: What is the hardest situation you have handled as a leader, and how did you respond?
p: Stakes and difficulty are clear: conflict, failure or crisis
Specific actions taken, including a hard conversation
A concrete or quantified outcome
Reflects on what they would repeat or change
items.a: Choose a situation where leading was genuinely hard, such as a conflict, an underperformer or a crisis, and show judgement under pressure. For example: 'As [team lead] at [your firm], I had [six people] on [a client go-live] when [a key member resigned two weeks before the deadline]. Morale dropped and the client was nervous. I [reset the plan with the team, took over the most critical module myself and gave the client a transparent revised timeline]. I also [had a direct conversation with a teammate who had disengaged]. We [went live four days late with no data errors], and the client [renewed]. I learnt that in a crisis people need a clear plan and visible ownership from the leader.'
items.t: Describing a leadership title rather than a hard decision, or an example where everything went smoothly.

items.q: Tell me about a time you gave up personal time to get a team project over the line.
p: A real cost: weekend, festival or personal plan
Explains why it mattered to the team
Done willingly, without martyrdom or resentment
Connects to deal-time crunches in banking
items.a: Banks ask this to see whether you will show up when a deal needs it. For example: 'During [an audit close or an ISB case competition], our [model or deck] broke [two days before submission]. I had [planned to travel home for Diwali]. I [postponed by two days], rebuilt [the cash flow module with a teammate overnight], and we [submitted on time and finished in the top three]. It was a real cost, but the team was relying on me, and I would make the same call again. I know deal timelines work the same way, and I am comfortable with that.'
items.t: Sounding resentful, or picking an example where the sacrifice was trivial or self-serving.

items.q: Are you more effective as a leader or as a follower?
p: Avoids a one-word answer; shows both roles are needed
Recognises a junior banker mainly executes and supports
One short example of each role
Shows humility about starting as an associate
items.a: Give a balanced answer that shows you understand the job. 'I can do both, and the context decides. At [previous firm], I led [a team of three on X], so I am comfortable taking ownership. I have also been a strong team member, for example [building the model on a project led by a senior manager], where my job was to deliver accurate work fast and flag issues early. As an associate, much of my time will be execution supporting the VP and MD, while guiding analysts on specific workstreams. I am comfortable with that, and being a reliable follower is how you earn the right to lead.'
items.t: Insisting you are a natural leader; it suggests you may resist execution work as a new associate.

items.q: How would you describe your leadership style?
p: Names the style in one line
Backs it with one specific example
Shows adaptability to different people or situations
Mentions one area they are working on
items.a: Give a one-line label, prove it with an example and show you adapt. 'I would call my style [hands-on with clear ownership]. I set the goal and deadline, split the work so everyone owns a piece, and stay close enough to review quality. For example, at [your firm] I led [four people on a pricing analysis]; I [paired a newer analyst with me for the first week], then gave her full ownership of [the competitor model]. We [delivered two days early]. With experienced people I step back more. Something I am working on is [delegating earlier instead of fixing things myself].'
items.t: Listing adjectives like 'collaborative and empathetic' with no example to back them up.

items.q: Do you think the leader makes the team, or the team makes the leader?
p: Takes a clear position, then adds nuance
Explains what leaders control: direction, standards, people
Acknowledges team capability and trust also matter
Uses one brief example
items.a: Take a view rather than sitting on the fence. 'Largely, the leader shapes the team, but not alone. A leader sets direction, standards and who gets hired, and those decide how a team performs under pressure. I saw this at [your firm]: when [a new manager] took over [a struggling team], [turnaround time improved and attrition fell] within [six months] with mostly the same people. But a leader cannot make up for a team that lacks basic skills or trust, so the best leaders build the team rather than carry it. On a deal, the MD sets the tone, but the deal still depends on the numbers being right.'
items.t: Giving a vague 'it is both' answer with no position or example.

items.q: You have no finance background. What do you think investment bankers actually do day to day?
p: Defines IB: M&A advisory plus raising equity and debt capital
Describes junior work: models, pitchbooks, diligence, documents, coordination
Mentions that fees are mostly success-based
Shows they have spoken to practising bankers
items.a: 'Investment bankers advise companies, promoters and funds on buying and selling businesses and on raising capital through IPOs, QIPs, block deals and debt. Senior bankers build relationships and win mandates; juniors execute. As an associate I would build and check models and valuations, draft pitchbooks, information memoranda and offer documents, run diligence and data rooms, and coordinate lawyers, auditors and the client. Most fees are success-based, so the work is about getting deals over the line. I have spoken with [names or roles at two banks], and what stood out was [how much time goes into coordination and drafting, not just modelling].'
items.t: Describing banking only as financial modelling, or confusing it with retail or commercial banking.
items.in: In India, ECM (IPOs, QIPs, OFS, block trades) is typically the largest fee pool for domestic banks, so juniors spend heavy time on offer documents and diligence.

items.q: Suppose I am running an IPO for a client. Briefly, what would I be doing?
p: Pre-filing: sizing, structure, diligence, valuation and offer document drafting
Regulatory filing and responding to regulator observations
Marketing: equity story, investor meetings, anchors, price band
Book-building, final pricing, allocation and listing
items.a: 'First you get the company ready: decide the size, the split between fresh issue and offer for sale, and the use of proceeds, and run legal and financial diligence with lawyers and auditors. Then you draft the offer document, file it with the regulator and respond to their comments. In parallel you build the equity story and valuation and meet investors early to test demand. Once cleared, you set the price band, run the roadshow, line up anchor investors and open the book for a few days. Based on demand you fix the final price, allocate shares across investor categories and list the stock.'
items.t: Skipping diligence and the regulatory filing stage and jumping straight to the roadshow and pricing.
items.in: Under SEBI ICDR: DRHP filed with SEBI, observations, RHP with the RoC, anchor book a day before opening, QIB/NII/retail quotas (typically 50/15/35), listing on T+3.

items.q: What do you know about the lifestyle in banking? How many hours a week do you expect to work?
p: Gives a realistic range, roughly 70 to 100 hours on live deals
Notes unpredictability: late calls, weekends, fixed filing deadlines
Cites bankers they spoke to as the source
Explains why they are prepared for it
items.a: 'From the bankers I have spoken to at [names or banks], a normal week is around [70 to 80] hours, and a live deal can push it to [90 or 100], including weekends. The bigger challenge is unpredictability: a 9 pm client call can change the next day's plan, and IPO filing or signing deadlines do not move. I have [worked similar stretches during audit busy season, a product launch and ISB's compressed terms], so I know how I cope: sleep discipline, planning and dropping non-essentials. I am going in with my eyes open, because the learning curve is the reason I want this.'
items.t: Claiming hours do not matter to you at all, or quoting a number with no source.

items.q: Your background is [IT services or consulting] with fairly regular hours. Tell me about a time you worked very long hours and made real sacrifices.
p: A specific stretch with hours or duration stated
Explains why the extra effort was necessary
Shows sustained output quality, not just presence
Links to banking workload without complaining
items.a: Address the doubt directly: they suspect you have never been stretched. Pick your toughest sustained stretch. 'During [a client go-live or audit busy season], I worked roughly [14-hour days for six weeks], including weekends, because [the deadline was fixed and we were two people short]. I [missed a family wedding] and cut almost everything else. What I learnt was how to keep quality up when tired: [checklists, a fixed review routine and short breaks]. We [delivered on time with zero escalations]. ISB's one-year programme has tested the same thing, balancing [classes, recruiting and club work].'
items.t: Saying you have never needed long hours, or presenting one all-nighter as a sustained stretch.

items.q: What product and industry groups does our bank have, and which one interests you most?
p: Distinguishes product groups (M&A, ECM, DCM) from sector coverage groups
Names the firm's actual teams and strengths from research
Picks one group and links it to their background
Stays accurate; does not guess the structure
items.a: Answer from research on that specific bank, structured as product versus coverage. 'Product groups execute transactions: M&A advisory, equity capital markets for IPOs, QIPs and block deals, and debt capital markets. Coverage or industry groups own client relationships in sectors such as [financial institutions, healthcare, consumer, technology and industrials]. From [your website, league tables and conversations with X], your strength is [ECM and mid-market M&A in consumer and healthcare], and junior teams are fairly [sector-agnostic]. I am most drawn to [your sector] because my [years in IT services] give me a head start on those business models.'
items.t: Guessing the bank's structure, or naming groups the firm does not actually have.
items.in: Many Indian banks and boutiques run lean, generalist junior teams; know the firm's actual structure and its IPO and M&A league table standing before the interview.

items.q: What goes into a pitchbook?
p: Bank credentials and relevant deal tombstones
Situation overview with company and industry context
Preliminary valuation, usually a football field
Strategic options, buyer list and process recommendation
items.a: 'A pitchbook is the deck a bank uses to win a mandate, so it is built around the client's problem. It usually has the bank's credentials and relevant deal tombstones; a situation overview of the company and its sector; market context such as trading levels and recent comparable deals; a preliminary valuation, typically a football field from trading comps, precedent transactions and a DCF; strategic options, for example a full sale versus an IPO versus a minority stake sale; for a sell-side pitch, a list of likely buyers with a proposed process and timeline; and finally the team and why we are the right advisor.'
items.t: Describing only the valuation pages and forgetting credentials, options and the process recommendation.

items.q: How does a company decide which investment bank to hire for a deal?
p: Relationship and trust with the senior banker
Sector expertise, recent credentials and league table position
Distribution: access to investors or buyers
Valuation view, fees and sometimes the lending relationship
items.a: 'It is a mix of relationship and capability. First, trust in the senior banker who will actually run the deal. Second, sector expertise and credentials: has the bank done similar deals recently, and where does it rank in league tables. Third, distribution: for an IPO, access to domestic mutual funds, insurers and foreign institutions; for M&A, access to strategic and private equity buyers. Fourth, the bank's view on valuation and execution, often tested in a bake-off where several banks pitch. Fees matter, and for large corporates the bank's lending relationship can help. Companies often appoint a syndicate, so getting included is itself a win.'
items.t: Saying companies simply pick the cheapest bank or the biggest brand.
items.in: Indian IPOs usually have several book running lead managers; promoter relationships and group connections weigh heavily in who gets mandated.

items.q: Walk me through a typical sell-side M&A process.
p: Preparation: valuation, teaser, information memorandum, buyer list
Round one: NDAs, IM, indicative non-binding bids
Round two: data room, management meetings, diligence, binding bids
Negotiation, signing, approvals and closing
items.a: 'In a broad auction, the bank first works with the client on valuation, the equity story and a buyer list of strategics and financial sponsors. We prepare a teaser and an information memorandum. Interested buyers sign NDAs, receive the IM and submit indicative, non-binding bids. A shortlist moves to round two: data room access, management presentations, site visits and full diligence, while the seller's lawyers circulate a draft purchase agreement. Buyers then submit binding bids with their markup of that agreement. We negotiate price and key terms with the preferred bidder, sign, obtain approvals and close. The whole process typically takes four to nine months.'
items.t: Skipping the two-round structure, or confusing indicative bids with binding offers.
items.in: Build in CCI approval above deal thresholds, a SEBI Takeover Code open offer when crossing 25% of a listed target, and FEMA pricing rules for foreign buyers.

items.q: Walk me through a typical buy-side M&A engagement.
p: Starts with client strategy and acquisition criteria
Screens and prioritises targets, then approaches owners
Valuation, synergies, accretion or returns, financing capacity
Diligence, bid strategy, negotiation, financing and closing
items.a: 'Buy-side starts with the client's strategy: why acquire, in which segments and at what size. We set criteria and screen a long list of targets down to a shortlist, then approach owners, often through the bank's relationships, or enter a sale process another bank is running. Once there is a live target, we value it on comps, precedents and a DCF, size synergies, and test accretion or dilution and financing capacity. We coordinate diligence with accountants, lawyers and consultants, advise on bid price and structure, negotiate terms and help arrange financing. Because the client can walk away, buy-side fees often include a retainer.'
items.t: Describing a sell-side auction from the buyer's seat and ignoring the strategy and target screening phase.
items.in: Listed Indian targets trigger SEBI Takeover Code open offers; promoter-controlled companies mean many deals are negotiated bilaterally with families rather than via auctions.

items.q: Walk me through how a bond or debenture issuance works for a corporate client.
p: Defines the need: size, tenor, security, fixed or floating, market
Credit rating obtained, which largely drives pricing
Documentation: offer document, covenants, trustee
Investor sounding, spread over government yield, bidding, allocation, settlement, listing
items.a: 'We start with the funding need: amount, tenor, use of proceeds, secured or unsecured, fixed or floating, and domestic or offshore. The issuer gets a credit rating, which largely drives pricing. Lawyers draft the offer document and covenants, and a trustee is appointed to protect bondholders. We then sound out investors such as mutual funds, insurers, pension funds and banks, and set price guidance as a spread over the comparable government bond yield. On issue day investors bid, the coupon is discovered, bonds are allocated, and they settle and list. It takes a few weeks, far faster than an IPO.'
items.t: Forgetting the credit rating and covenants, which drive pricing and investor appetite.
items.in: Larger Indian NCD private placements must use the exchanges' electronic bidding platform; key raters are CRISIL, ICRA, CARE and India Ratings; listed issues need a debenture trustee.

items.q: How are equity and debt capital markets teams different from M&A or industry coverage teams?
p: ECM and DCM are market-facing product teams executing financings
M&A is advisory on buying, selling and merging businesses
Coverage teams own relationships and originate across products
Different skills: market timing and demand versus valuation and negotiation
items.a: 'Coverage or industry groups own the relationship. They know the sector and the client's strategy, and they bring in whichever product the client needs. M&A is an advisory product: valuing businesses, running sale or acquisition processes and negotiating terms, so the work is model-heavy and deals can run for months. ECM and DCM sit between issuers and investors. They focus on market conditions, investor demand, pricing and timing, so their work is shorter-cycle and market-driven, with less deep company modelling. A typical IPO pitch combines the coverage banker, ECM for market view and distribution, and sometimes M&A if a stake sale is an alternative.'
items.t: Saying ECM and DCM do no analysis; they do valuation and credit work, just less deep modelling.

items.q: What is the difference between debt capital markets and leveraged finance?
p: DCM: investment-grade issuers, bonds, tighter spreads, lighter covenants
LevFin: sub-investment-grade, highly levered borrowers, often buyouts or acquisitions
LevFin uses leveraged loans and high-yield bonds with tighter covenants
LevFin needs deeper credit, cash flow and downside analysis
items.a: 'DCM mostly serves investment-grade issuers: large corporates, financial institutions and governments. Their debt is lower risk, priced at modest spreads over government bonds, and the work is about timing, pricing and distribution. Leveraged finance serves sub-investment-grade or highly levered borrowers, typically funding buyouts, acquisitions or recapitalisations. The instruments are leveraged loans and high-yield bonds, with wider spreads, security packages and tighter covenants. Because default risk is real, LevFin bankers spend much more time on cash flow modelling, leverage and interest coverage, and downside cases, and they work closely with private equity sponsors.'
items.t: Treating LevFin as DCM for bigger deals; the credit risk and the analysis are fundamentally different.
items.in: India has a thin high-yield market and historical RBI curbs on banks funding share acquisitions, so buyout debt often comes from NBFCs, private credit or offshore lenders.

items.q: What is a divestiture, and why would a company do one?
p: Sale or separation of a division, subsidiary or set of assets
Motives: focus, unlock value, deleverage, poor fit, regulation
Forms: outright sale, carve-out IPO, spin-off or demerger
Carve-out complexity: standalone costs, shared assets, transition services
items.a: 'A divestiture is when a company sells or separates part of itself: a division, subsidiary or set of assets. Reasons include sharpening focus on the core business, unlocking value when a conglomerate trades at a discount, raising cash to cut debt, exiting a business that no longer fits, or a regulatory requirement. It can be an outright sale to a strategic or private equity buyer, a partial IPO of the subsidiary, or a spin-off where shares go to existing shareholders. The hard part is the carve-out: separating shared people, IT and contracts, building standalone financials and agreeing transition services for the buyer.'
items.t: Assuming a divestiture always raises cash; a spin-off or demerger generates no proceeds for the parent.
items.in: In India, demergers run as NCLT-approved schemes under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act; business transfers are often structured as slump sales for tax.

items.q: If you had to build a one-slide company profile for an investor, what would you put on it?
p: Business description: segments, products, geography, key customers
Key financials: revenue, EBITDA, margins, PAT, growth, three to five years
Market data: share price, market cap, net debt, EV, multiples versus peers
Shareholding, management and recent developments, all sourced and dated
items.a: 'I would use four blocks. Top left: what the company does, its segments, products, geography and headquarters. Top right: key financials for the last three years plus forecasts, meaning revenue, EBITDA and margin, PAT and growth, ideally with a small chart. Bottom left: market and capital structure data, meaning share price, market cap, net debt, enterprise value, and EV/EBITDA and P/E against peers. Bottom right: shareholding pattern, key management, and recent developments such as acquisitions, fund raises or rating changes. Every number sourced and dated, units clear, and no clutter.'
items.t: Cramming in text and leaving numbers without sources, dates or currency units.
items.in: For Indian listed companies, always show promoter holding and any promoter pledge; investors read pledged shares as a governance and overhang risk.

items.q: A company hires you as financial advisor and asks for your view on its growth and M&A strategy. What value could you add?
p: Tests the strategy: organic versus inorganic, build versus buy
Market intelligence: targets, owner willingness, valuations, investor reaction
Quantifies options: valuation, synergies, EPS impact, leverage, returns versus cost of capital
Execution: approach, structure, financing, negotiation; willing to advise against a deal
items.a: 'First, I would pressure-test the strategy itself: is growth best achieved organically or through acquisitions, and which segments or geographies matter most. Second, I bring market intelligence the company lacks: who the realistic targets are, whether owners will sell, what similar businesses have traded at and how investors would react. Third, I quantify the options: valuation, synergies, the effect on earnings per share and leverage, and whether returns beat the cost of capital. Fourth, execution: approaching targets discreetly, structuring cash versus stock or earnouts, arranging financing and negotiating. The real value is an objective view, including telling the client when not to do a deal.'
items.t: Jumping straight to valuation without asking whether M&A is the right route at all.

items.q: When you get an open-ended investment or business question, such as how to invest Rs. 10 crore, what do you ask before answering?
p: Asks the goal: growth, income, capital preservation, control or exit
Asks constraints: horizon, risk tolerance, liquidity, tax, regulation
States assumptions out loud if no answers are given
Then gives a structured recommendation tied to those goals
items.a: 'Before recommending anything I would ask two sets of questions. First, goals: is the investor after capital growth, steady income or capital preservation; for a business, is the aim growth, profitability or an exit. Second, constraints: time horizon, risk tolerance, liquidity needs, tax position and any regulatory or mandate limits. A retiree needing monthly income and a 30-year-old with a ten-year horizon get very different answers. If the interviewer does not answer, I state assumptions out loud, say a five-year horizon and moderate risk, build the recommendation from there, and say what would change if those assumptions changed.'
items.t: Jumping straight to a stock or asset recommendation without clarifying goals and constraints.

items.q: Imagine you own a small business and a much larger company offers to buy it. How would you evaluate the offer and decide?
p: Compares offer to standalone value using cash flows and multiples
Examines structure: cash, stock, earnout, escrow, deferred payments
Weighs alternatives: keep running, other buyers, partial sale
Includes non-financial factors: employees, own role, risk appetite
items.a: 'I would compare the offer with what the business is worth if I keep it: the present value of the cash flows I expect, and what similar businesses sell for. Then I would look at structure: how much is cash upfront versus stock, earnouts or escrow, because deferred or contingent money is worth less. Next, alternatives: could I run a quick process with other buyers, or sell a minority stake and keep growing? I would ask why this buyer wants it, since synergies mean they can probably pay more. Finally, the personal side: my role afterwards, my employees and my risk appetite. I accept if the risk-adjusted offer beats my best alternative.'
items.t: Looking only at the headline price and ignoring structure, tax and alternatives.
items.in: For an Indian family business, also weigh capital gains tax on the sale, succession plans, and how the proceeds would be redeployed versus staying invested.

items.q: We work mostly with technology companies. Tell me about a tech trend or company that has caught your interest recently.
p: Picks one specific trend or company, not a list of buzzwords
Explains the business model and who makes money
Links to deal activity: IPOs, M&A, fundraising, financing
States a view and one key risk
items.a: Pick one topic you can defend for ten minutes, ideally linked to your background. Structure: what it is, why now, who wins, deal implications, risk. 'I have been following [Indian SaaS, digital payments, data centres or quick commerce]. The driver is [cheaper data and rising enterprise digitisation]. Money is made by [companies with recurring revenue and low churn], and the metrics that matter are [net revenue retention and customer acquisition payback]. For banks, this means [IPO pipelines, consolidation M&A and financing for capex-heavy players]. My concern is [valuations running ahead of profitability].' Check the latest data yourself before the interview rather than quoting stale figures.
items.t: Name-dropping AI or a famous company with no view on the business model or the deal angle.

items.q: If you had Rs. 8 crore to start any business you wanted, what would you start and why?
p: A specific idea with a clear customer and problem
Basic unit economics and how the capital is deployed
Why them: an edge from their background
Key risk and a cheap way to test the idea
