items.a: Show business judgement, not just enthusiasm. Structure: idea, customer, economics, edge, risks. 'I would start [a B2B procurement platform for small manufacturers in my home region]. The problem is [fragmented suppliers and poor access to credit]. Revenue comes from [a two to three percent take rate on transactions]. I would deploy roughly [Rs. 3 crore on technology and sales, Rs. 2 crore on working capital, and hold Rs. 3 crore as runway]. My edge is [my family business network or my supply chain background]. The main risk is [customer acquisition cost], so I would pilot with [twenty buyers] before scaling.'
items.t: Picking a vague passion project with no revenue model or plan for the funds.

items.q: Tell me about a company you admire and what makes it attractive to you.
p: Names the company and the one core reason
Explains competitive advantage with evidence: margins, ROCE, market share
Comments on capital allocation or management quality
Adds a risk or what could go wrong
items.a: Pick a company you can discuss in depth and analyse it like an investor, not a fan. Structure: what it does, its moat, the evidence, capital allocation and a risk. 'I admire [company] because [it built a durable advantage in a tough market]. Its moat is [distribution reach, brand or cost leadership], and you can see it in [consistently high return on capital and steady market share gains over a decade]. Management has [reinvested cash sensibly and avoided overpaying for acquisitions]. What I would watch is [new competition or key-person risk]. I got interested through [a work or personal link].' Verify any numbers before you quote them.
items.t: Picking a famous brand and praising its products as a consumer, with no financial or strategic analysis.

items.q: Suppose you want to start a business around laundry machines. How would you assess whether it is viable?
p: Clarifies the model: manufacturing, distribution or laundromat operation
Identifies demand: target customers, density, current alternatives
Builds unit economics: capex, revenue per machine, operating costs, payback
Checks payback against machine life, competition and financing
items.a: 'First I would clarify the model: making machines, distributing them or running self-service laundromats. Take laundromats in an Indian city. Demand comes from students, working bachelors and hostels in dense areas, so I would check what they pay today for a dhobi or home washing. Unit economics: a store with eight machines might cost about Rs. 30 lakh. At six washes per machine a day and Rs. 100 a wash, revenue is about Rs. 17.5 lakh a year. If rent, power, water, staff and maintenance cost about Rs. 10 lakh, the store earns Rs. 7.5 lakh, a four-year payback. That works only if machines last well beyond four years. Then I would test utilisation risk, competition and financing.'
items.t: Jumping to market size without first defining the business model and per-store unit economics.

items.q: Tell me about an M&A deal that caught your interest recently.
p: States parties, size, valuation multiple and structure accurately
Explains the strategic rationale for the buyer
Gives a clear view on whether it creates value
Mentions a risk, regulatory angle or implication for peers
items.a: Prepare two deals, ideally one Indian and one in the bank's sector, and verify every number before the interview. Structure: 'The deal is [acquirer] buying [target] for [Rs. X crore], about [Y times EBITDA], paid in [cash or stock]. The rationale is [scale, distribution, technology or consolidation]. I think it is [a good deal] because [the synergies look achievable and the multiple is below precedents]. The main risk is [integration, overpaying or CCI approval]. It signals [more consolidation in the sector], which matters for your [sector] coverage.' If you are unsure of a detail, say so rather than bluffing.
items.t: Getting basic facts wrong, or having no personal view on whether the deal creates value.

items.q: Pitch me a stock.
p: Clear call: buy or sell, with target price and horizon
Starts from current price and what the market already prices in
Two or three thesis points the market is mispricing
Valuation basis, catalysts, key risks and exit trigger
items.a: Lead with price and what is already priced in, then the thesis. 'I would buy [company] at [current price], trading at [X times forward earnings] versus peers at [Y times]. The market is pricing in [slow growth or margin pressure]. My thesis has three parts: [new capacity that lifts revenue], [margin recovery as input costs ease] and [a cleaner balance sheet]. Applying [Y times] to [two-year forward earnings] gives a target of [price], about [Z percent] upside over [12 to 18 months]. Catalysts are [quarterly results and a plant commissioning]. Key risks are [a demand slowdown and promoter pledge]; I would exit if [specific trigger].' Use only numbers you have verified yourself.
items.t: Pitching a famous large-cap with no variant view, or skipping valuation and risks.

items.q: Explain the 2008 subprime crisis in simple terms.
p: US lenders gave home loans to weak borrowers with lax standards
Loans were securitised and over-rated, spreading risk globally
House prices fell, defaults rose, leverage amplified the losses
Funding froze, Lehman failed, governments injected capital
items.a: 'In the mid-2000s, US lenders gave mortgages to borrowers with weak credit, often with low teaser rates and little documentation, assuming house prices would keep rising. These loans were pooled and sold as mortgage-backed securities and more complex structures, which rating agencies rated too generously, so banks and investors worldwide bought them, often with heavily borrowed money. When rates reset and house prices fell, borrowers defaulted, the securities lost value, and nobody knew who held the losses. Banks stopped lending to each other, Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008, and governments had to inject capital and guarantee funding to stop the system failing.'
items.t: Blaming only the borrowers and missing securitisation, ratings and leverage as the amplifiers.
items.in: Indian banks had little subprime exposure, but foreign outflows caused a liquidity squeeze; RBI cut the repo rate and CRR sharply from late 2008.

items.q: Do you support government rescues of failing banks, such as the US rescue package in 2008 or the Yes Bank rescue in India in 2020?
p: Takes a clear position with reasoning
Explains systemic risk: payments, deposits, credit freeze
Acknowledges moral hazard and taxpayer cost
Sets conditions: wipe out equity, replace management, recover costs
items.a: 'Broadly yes, when a failure threatens the system, but with conditions. A large bank collapsing can freeze payments, deposits and credit for healthy businesses, and that economic cost is usually far larger than the rescue. The 2008 US programme was largely repaid in the end. The real issue is moral hazard: if shareholders and managers are rescued, banks take more risk next time. So a good rescue protects depositors and the system but wipes out or heavily dilutes shareholders, replaces management and recovers money for taxpayers. I would also want strong capital rules and resolution regimes so that rescues are rarely needed.'
items.t: Giving a bare yes or no with no conditions, or ignoring moral hazard entirely.
items.in: In the 2020 Yes Bank scheme, SBI led the capital infusion, shareholders were diluted and AT1 bonds were written off (later litigated): a burden-sharing example.

items.q: How do I know you have properly researched banking? Who have you spoken to, and are you ready for the early-career trade-offs?
p: Names specific people or roles spoken to
Shares an insight only real conversations would give
Frames short-term sacrifice against a long-term goal
Shows actions taken because of what they learnt
items.a: Prove it with specifics. 'I have spoken to [six] bankers, including [an ISB alum who is a VP at X], [an associate at Y] and [an analyst at a boutique]. The most useful thing I learnt was [that associates at Indian banks spend a lot of time on offer document drafting and investor coordination, not just modelling], which is why I [took a capital markets elective and built two models on Indian IPOs]. I also asked about the downsides, mainly hours and unpredictability. I accept that trade-off for the next few years because my long-term goal is [to lead deals in your sector], and there is no faster way to build that judgement.'
items.t: Vague claims like 'I have read a lot about banking' with no names, insights or actions.

items.q: You have mostly worked in wealth management. Why move into investment banking now?
p: A positive pull towards IB, not an escape from wealth
Transferable skills: client handling, markets, products
The gap they want to fill: transactions, valuation, corporate finance
Timing explained: ISB as the deliberate pivot
items.a: Show a logical next step, not an escape. 'In wealth management at [firm], I advised [HNI and promoter] clients, and the most interesting conversations were around [promoter liquidity events such as IPOs, stake sales and block deals]. I realised I wanted to be on the other side, structuring the transaction rather than investing the proceeds. My client handling and market understanding carry over, but I needed deeper corporate finance and valuation skills, which is why I came to ISB and [took X and competed in Y]. The MBA is the natural switching point, and my promoter relationships and market sense are useful in ECM and mid-market M&A.'
items.t: Criticising wealth management or your previous employer instead of explaining the pull towards IB.

items.q: Markets are weak, deal volumes are down and banks are cutting staff. You have other options. Why still banking?
p: Acknowledges the cycle directly, without denial
Reason rests on long-term skills, not current deal flow
Notes downturns shift work: refinancing, restructuring, distressed M&A
Shows commitment despite the risk
items.a: 'I know the cycle matters, and [hiring and deal volumes are lower right now]. But my reason for banking is not this year's deal flow. I want to learn how companies are valued, financed and bought, and banking is the most intense training ground for that. Downturns also change the work rather than ending it: more refinancing, restructuring, distressed sales and stake sales, which build judgement. People who join in a slow market and learn the fundamentals are ready when activity recovers. I considered [consulting and corporate finance] and chose banking because [specific reason].'
items.t: Pretending the downturn is irrelevant, or giving a reason that depends on booming markets.
items.in: In an Indian downturn, work often shifts to IBC resolutions, stressed asset sales, QIPs for balance-sheet repair and promoter stake sales, all of which need advisers.

items.q: Finance is popular again and half of ISB seems to want banking. How do I know you are serious and not just following the crowd?
p: Evidence that predates the trend: actions, not statements
Specific preparation: models, deals followed, conversations
A consistent reason linked to their background
Calm and confident, not defensive
items.a: Answer with evidence, not adjectives. 'Fair question. My interest goes back to [your work at X, where you worked on a fundraise, audited a listed company or saw a family business acquisition]. Since then I have [cleared CFA Level I, built DCF models on three Indian companies and run a club initiative on IPOs], and I have spoken to [number] bankers about the day-to-day. I came to ISB specifically to make this move, and my [electives, competitions and projects] all point the same way. Someone following the crowd would not have [specific action] before it was popular.'
items.t: Getting defensive, or relying on enthusiasm alone without concrete proof.

items.q: Where did your interest in finance start?
p: A specific origin moment, not 'I always liked numbers'
Shows the interest grew through deliberate actions
Ends with why IB specifically
Kept to about 60 to 90 seconds
items.a: Tell a short story with a clear arc: spark, deepening, decision. 'It started with [watching my family business negotiate a bank loan, auditing a company that later went into insolvency, or an engineering project where the business case decided everything]. I realised [financial decisions drove outcomes more than technical ones]. I then [started investing, took CFA Level I and moved towards deal-related work at my firm]. It became banking specifically when [I worked alongside bankers on X or spoke to Y] and saw how they shaped the transaction. ISB was the deliberate step to make that switch.'
items.t: Starting with childhood anecdotes or 'I always loved numbers' with no specific trigger or later actions.

items.q: You enjoyed your previous role and could go back to your old employer. Why switch to investment banking instead?
p: Speaks positively about the past role
Explains what IB offers that the old path cannot
Specific reasons, not money or prestige
Shows a considered decision, not an impulse
items.a: Show you are choosing IB, not running away. 'I did enjoy [my role at X], and the option to return is real. What I liked most was [the client-facing analysis on deals and capital allocation], but that was a small part of my job. In banking it is the whole job: valuing companies, structuring transactions and advising promoters on the biggest decisions they make. My old path leads to [deeper specialisation in implementation or audit], which is a good career, but not what I want for the next ten years. ISB was my point to switch, and I would rather do it now than wonder later.'
items.t: Badmouthing the previous employer, or citing money and prestige as the main reason.

items.q: You were senior and well paid in your last role. Why take a step down, possibly a pay cut, and work far longer hours here?
p: Acknowledges the trade-off honestly
Long-term payoff outweighs the short-term cost
Specific pull factors of IB
Shows maturity: planned for it with family
items.a: 'You are right that it is a trade-off, and I have thought it through. In my last role at [firm] I was [senior and comfortable], but my learning curve had flattened. What I want long term is [to lead transactions in your sector], and that needs deal skills, a network and judgement you only build by doing deals. A few years of longer hours and less seniority is a reasonable price for that. [I have discussed it at home and planned for it financially], so it is not impulsive. My earlier experience also means I can [manage clients and juniors] sooner than a typical new associate.'
items.t: Claiming money does not matter at all; it sounds unconvincing. Address the trade-off honestly.

items.q: What is your biggest worry about working in investment banking?
p: A real but non-fatal concern
Shows awareness of the job's demands
Explains how they are preparing for it
Avoids a dealbreaker such as disliking long hours
items.a: Pick a genuine but manageable concern and show your plan. 'My main concern is [making errors under time pressure, given how much accuracy matters in models and offer documents]. I come from [consulting or engineering], where some iteration was normal, but in banking a wrong number in front of a client damages trust. So I have [built a checking routine: tying every number to source, cross-footing totals and re-reading outputs], and practised it on [ISB projects and modelling tests]. I also plan to ask seniors early how they want work checked. I see it as manageable with discipline.'
items.t: Naming a dealbreaker such as hours, pressure or Excel, or claiming you have no worries at all.

items.q: What is your Plan B if you do not land an investment banking role through placements?
p: Makes clear IB is Plan A with full commitment
Related Plan B: transaction advisory, corporate development or a boutique
Shows a route back into IB later
Not defeatist or scattered
items.a: Show commitment and a sensible fallback. 'IB is clearly my first choice, and that is where my preparation is focused. If it does not work out through placements, I would look for a role that builds the same skills and keeps the door open, such as [transaction advisory at a Big 4 firm, corporate development or a mid-market boutique], and I would keep applying to banks off-campus. Many bankers in India have come through those routes. I would not move to an unrelated field, because my goal of [working on transactions] stays the same.'
items.t: Naming an unrelated Plan B such as product management, which signals weak commitment to banking.

items.q: Another candidate has a near-perfect CGPA from an IIM and a top banking internship. Why should I hire you over them?
p: Stays calm and does not criticise the other candidate
States two or three specific differentiators with evidence
Ties differentiators to what an associate needs
Brief and confident, not arrogant
items.a: Do not attack the other candidate; sell what you uniquely bring. 'They clearly have a strong profile. I would add three things. First, [six years in IT services selling to enterprise clients], so I understand technology business models and client handling from the inside. Second, I have [delivered under real deadlines with real money at stake while managing a team of four]. Third, I have deliberately built the technical base: [CFA Level I, modelling projects at ISB and a live deal at X]. An associate has to manage clients and analysts early, and my experience lets me do that sooner.'
items.t: Getting defensive, criticising the other candidate, or failing to name concrete differentiators.

items.q: You are in a client meeting with your MD and spot an error in the materials while they are presenting. Do you point it out?
p: Judges materiality: does the error change the conclusion
Never contradicts the MD publicly in front of the client
Flags discreetly: a note to the MD or a natural break
Fixes the source afterwards and owns any personal mistake
items.a: 'It depends on how material the error is, but I would not correct the MD in front of the client. If it is minor, like a typo or a rounding difference, I would note it, tell the MD straight after the meeting and send corrected pages. If it is material, say a wrong valuation figure the client is about to rely on, I would pass the MD a short note or raise it quietly at a natural break so they can correct it themselves. Either way, I would fix the source, check the rest of the deck for the same error, and if it was my mistake, own it.'
items.t: Either interrupting the MD in front of the client, or staying silent on a material error.

items.q: I see a gap of [several months or two years] on your CV. What happened there?
p: Brief, honest explanation without over-sharing
Shows productive use of time where true
Moves quickly to what they learnt
Pivots to current readiness
items.a: Be short, honest and forward-looking. 'Between [dates], I [left my job to help run my family business, prepared for professional exams, handled a family responsibility or tried a start-up]. During that time I [managed the business's bank relationships and working capital, or cleared CFA Level I]. It taught me [how cash flow drives real decisions]. I then joined ISB to make the switch to finance, so the gap was part of the path rather than a break from it.' If the reason was personal, one sentence is enough; you do not owe details.
items.t: Over-explaining, sounding apologetic, or inventing activities that will not survive follow-up questions.

items.q: You got a weak grade in the core accounting course, or in [another finance-heavy subject]. Why, and should that worry me?
p: Owns it without excuses
Gives a brief, credible reason
Shows concrete remediation: course, certification, modelling practice
Demonstrates current competence, ideally inviting technical questions
items.a: Own it, explain briefly and prove it is fixed. 'That grade was my weakest point. In [term X], I [underestimated the course coming from engineering and prioritised other work]. I did not want that to stay a gap, so I [took the advanced accounting elective, cleared CFA Level I and built three-statement models for two Indian companies from their annual reports]. Today I am comfortable with [linking the statements, deferred tax and lease accounting under Ind AS 116]. I am happy to be tested on it.' Then make sure you can handle the technical questions that follow.
items.t: Blaming the professor or the grading curve, or claiming the grade does not matter.

items.q: You did [a pre-MBA internship or a live project] at [a firm] but did not get an offer to stay on. Why not?
p: Honest, brief reason without blaming the firm
Separates headcount or fit from performance, where true
Shows feedback sought and acted on
Cites a reference or achievement from the stint
items.a: Be honest and constructive. If it was not about performance, say so with evidence: '[The team had no full-time headcount that year], which my manager confirmed, and [she is happy to be a reference]. During the stint I [delivered X].' If performance was part of it, own the specific gap: 'Feedback was that I [was slow on modelling and did not ask questions early enough]. I took that seriously: I [did a modelling course, practised on Y] and now [check scope with seniors early].' The interviewer mainly wants to see that you take feedback and improve.
items.t: Blaming the manager or firm, or giving a vague answer that the interviewer can easily check.

items.q: You left your last job months before ISB started and nothing is listed for that time. What were you doing, and have you tried for banking roles before?
p: Concrete account of the period with outputs
Honest about any previous recruiting attempts
Shows what has changed since an earlier attempt
Links the period to IB preparation
items.a: Give a factual answer with outputs, and be straight about earlier attempts. 'After leaving [firm] in [month], I [spent three months preparing for CFA Level I, helped my family business with a bank refinancing and travelled for a month]. I did [apply to a couple of boutiques before ISB but did not convert, because I lacked the technical base]. Since then I have [worked through valuation and modelling and done X at ISB], so I am a much stronger candidate now.' Firms keep records, so never hide a previous application to the same firm.
items.t: Hiding previous recruiting attempts, or describing the period vaguely as 'personal time'.

items.q: Why are we your first choice? Would you not rather work at a global bank, or abroad in London, Singapore or Dubai?
p: Firm-specific reasons: deals, sector, team, culture
Positive case for India as a deal market
Mentions people spoken to at the firm
Honest, without disparaging other banks or locations
items.a: Give firm-specific reasons and a positive case for India, not a rejection of the alternatives. 'India is where I want to build my career: [deep domestic capital markets, promoter-led companies and active IPO and mid-market M&A activity], and my network and understanding are here. Within India, you are my first choice because of [your leadership in mid-market ECM or your consumer and healthcare M&A work, for example the X deal], and because [associates get early client exposure on lean teams]. When I spoke with [name], what stood out was [specific point]. Here I would see more of each deal, sooner.'
items.t: Generic praise that fits any bank, or implying you settled because abroad seemed unrealistic.

items.q: You have more experience than most incoming associates. Are you comfortable starting alongside younger colleagues and taking direction from people your age or younger?
p: Answers directly and comfortably
Frames experience as an asset: maturity, client handling
Shows humility and willingness to be managed
One example of working well under younger seniors
items.a: 'Yes, completely. I made this switch knowing I would start as an associate, and I am here to learn the craft. My experience helps in practical ways: I have [managed client relationships and small teams and handled pressure on real deadlines], so I can take ownership sooner. I have also [worked under a manager younger than me at [firm]], and what matters to me is competence, not age. I expect to learn modelling shortcuts from analysts who have done far more deals than I have, and I will be comfortable asking them.'
items.t: Sounding defensive, or implying you expect faster promotion because of your age or experience.

items.q: If you were an animal, which one would you be, and why?
p: Answers quickly without overthinking
Links one or two traits to the job
Light touch that shows personality
Under 30 seconds
items.a: Keep it light and quick, but tie it to traits a deal team values. 'Probably [an ant]. It is not glamorous, but ants work relentlessly, carry far more than their own weight and coordinate brilliantly as a team without any fuss. That is how I like to work: reliable under load and easy to work with. I would like to think I am a little friendlier than an ant, though.' Pick something you can explain in one breath, and avoid predators that suggest aggression.
items.t: Overthinking it, or choosing a predator such as a shark that implies ruthlessness.

items.q: Imagine your name is in a front-page newspaper headline some years from now. What is the story about?
p: Ambitious but credible story
Connects to career goals or values
Shows personality beyond work
Brief and positive
items.a: Make it ambitious but believable, and let it reveal your goals. 'Something like: [ISB alum advises on India's largest infrastructure IPO]. Or a more personal version: [banker funds a hundred schools in her home district]. The first is about wanting to lead landmark transactions that help Indian companies raise capital and grow. The second is about what I would do with that success. Either way, I would want the story to be about building something, not just about a title.'
items.t: Picking something unrealistic, negative, or unrelated to who you are.

items.q: Tell me a joke.
p: Has one short, clean joke ready
Inoffensive: no politics, religion, gender or region
Delivered confidently, then moves on
Ideally light finance or self-deprecating humour
items.a: Have one short, clean joke ready and deliver it calmly. A safe one for a banking room: 'How do you know a banker is planning a holiday? There is a base case, an upside case and a monsoon downside case, and the itinerary is in a pitchbook.' Smile, pause, and move on. The test is composure and judgement, not comedy. If your mind goes blank, a short self-deprecating line about your own Excel habits works too.
items.t: Telling an offensive, long or risque joke, or freezing and refusing to answer.

items.q: What is your personal beta?
p: Defines beta: sensitivity to market moves, market beta equals 1
Gives a number with a reason
Uses a twist: low beta to stress, high to opportunity
Short and slightly playful
items.a: Show you know the concept, then answer with a twist. 'Beta measures how much a stock moves relative to the market: the market is 1, above 1 is more volatile, below 1 is defensive. I would put my beta at about [0.7]: when things get chaotic, like a deal deadline being pulled forward, I stay steadier than the room. But when there is an opportunity to learn or take on more, I would like to think my beta is well above 1. So, a defensive stock with a growth option.'
items.t: Not knowing what beta measures, or giving a number with no explanation.

items.q: What is the riskiest thing you have ever done?
p: A real, calculated risk with genuine stakes
Explains how they sized the downside
States the outcome and the lesson
Nothing reckless or illegal
items.a: Choose a calculated risk, not a reckless one, and show how you weighed it. 'The riskiest decision was [leaving a stable role at X to join a start-up, or to do the MBA, or to launch a new line in the family business]. The downside was [losing a year's income and seniority]. I limited it by [saving twelve months of expenses and keeping a fallback], and judged that the upside, [new skills and a career switch], was worth it. It [worked, or partly worked], and I learnt [that sizing the downside first makes bold decisions easier]. That is how I would think about risk on a deal too.'
items.t: Describing physical recklessness or something illegal, which signals poor judgement.

items.q: You are given Rs. 8 crore, but you cannot invest it or use it to make more money. What would you spend it on?
p: A genuine, specific answer that reveals values
Some thought about allocation and impact
Not purely flashy consumption
Brief and personal
items.a: This tests values and personality, so answer honestly and specifically. 'I would split it three ways. The largest part, say [Rs. 5 crore], would fund [scholarships for students from my district], because I have seen what access to education changed for [people around me]. Around [Rs. 2 crore] would go to my family, for example [a home for my parents]. The rest I would spend on experiences, such as [travelling to every continent with my family]. Even without returns, I would want to know where each rupee went and what it achieved.'
items.t: Listing only luxury purchases, or sneaking in an investment, which ignores the rule in the question.

items.q: Pick one deal from your resume and walk me through it, from what the client wanted to where it ended up.
p: Opens with a one-line summary: parties, size, deal type, outcome
States the strategic rationale for the client
Explains own role and one concrete output
Covers outcome and one lesson in under two minutes
items.a: Structure it in five beats. First, the headline: 'At [firm], I worked on [a sell-side / acquisition / fundraise / diligence] for a [client type] in [sector], roughly Rs. [X] crore.' Second, why the client did it: [growth, exit, deleveraging]. Third, the process: [number of parties, key stages, timeline]. Fourth, my role: 'I owned [the model / a diligence workstream / the management presentation]; one output was [specific analysis], which showed [finding].' Fifth, outcome and lesson: '[Signed / closed / paused] in [month]; I learned [one insight].' If you came from Big 4 or consulting, say clearly you were the diligence or advisory team, not the banker, and describe the client by sector and size rather than name.
items.t: Rambling chronologically for five minutes, or overstating your role so the follow-up questions expose you.

items.q: This deal sounds like it was mostly research. Did you actually do any quantitative work on it?
p: Names a specific model or analysis built, not just 'Excel'
Quantifies the output: a number, range or sensitivity
Links the numbers to a decision the client made
Stays calm and specific; does not get defensive
items.a: Do not argue; answer with specifics. 'Fair question. The research fed into numbers. I built [a revenue build by segment / a working capital analysis / a comps set of [N] peers]. For example, I [normalised EBITDA for one-offs of Rs. [X] crore / ran sensitivities on price and volume], which moved the valuation range from [A] to [B]. That changed [the client's bid / the negotiation on the working capital peg].' If your role genuinely was qualitative, say so honestly and pivot: 'My quant work was lighter there, but on [other project] I built [model].' Then prove you can do it now by explaining the method crisply.
items.t: Bluffing a model you did not build; interviewers will ask you to walk through it line by line.

items.q: On the deal you worked on, why did the company or its owners decide to sell?
p: Separates the owner's motive from the company's situation
Gives one primary reason, not a list of five
Explains why the timing made sense then
Connects the motive to the type of buyers targeted
items.a: Give the primary reason and why now. Typical motives: owners want liquidity or an exit (a PE fund near the end of its fund life, a promoter with no successor); the business needs capital or capabilities it cannot build alone; a parent is divesting a non-core unit to focus or deleverage; or valuations are high and the window is open. So: 'The [promoter / PE fund / parent] wanted to sell because [reason]. Timing mattered because [fund life / a debt maturity / sector multiples near a peak]. That shaped the buyer list: we targeted [strategics for synergies / financial sponsors].' Show you understood the seller's incentives, not just the transaction.
items.t: Saying 'to make money' or listing generic reasons without the specific trigger for this seller.
items.in: In India, common triggers are promoter succession gaps, PE funds exiting within fund life, groups selling non-core units to cut debt, and stress from pledged promoter shares.

items.q: Why did your client want to acquire the target rather than grow organically?
p: States the strategic rationale: capability, market, scale or product
Explains buy versus build: speed, cost or execution risk
Mentions synergies and their rough size
Gives a view on whether the price was justified
items.a: Frame it as buy versus build. 'The client wanted [access to a new geography / a product it lacked / procurement scale / a technology capability]. Building it would have taken [years] and carried execution risk; buying got there in [months].' Then the economics: 'We estimated synergies of about Rs. [X] crore, mostly [cost / revenue], and the deal was [accretive / dilutive] to EPS in year [N].' Add one risk you discussed: integration, culture or overpaying. Close with whether you thought the price was justified, because interviewers want to see judgment, not just the press release rationale.
items.t: Repeating the press release without discussing buy versus build or whether the price made sense.

items.q: Describe how the deal process actually ran, stage by stage.
p: Correct sequence: preparation, outreach, first round, second round, signing, closing
Mentions key documents: teaser, NDA, information memorandum, SPA
Gives rough timeline and number of parties at each stage
Names approvals or conditions needed before closing
items.a: For a typical sell-side auction: preparation (four to six weeks: model, teaser, information memorandum, buyer list); outreach (teasers out, NDAs signed, memorandum shared); first round (non-binding indicative bids, usually a valuation range); second round (three to five shortlisted parties get management meetings, data room access and diligence, then submit binding bids with a marked-up SPA); then negotiation, signing, and closing once conditions precedent such as regulatory approvals are met. Map your deal to this: 'We contacted [N] parties, [N] signed NDAs, [N] bid in round one, [N] in round two; signing took [X] months.' If it was a negotiated one-to-one deal, say so and explain why.
items.t: Reciting a textbook process without anchoring it to what actually happened on your deal.
items.in: For listed Indian targets, acquiring 25% or more triggers a SEBI takeover code open offer; larger deals need CCI approval; foreign buyers face FEMA pricing rules and sectoral caps.

items.q: What made your client attractive to buyers or investors? What were its key selling points?
p: Three crisp selling points, not ten
Each backed by a number: growth, margin or market share
Explains why each matters to the buyer universe
Explains why the advantage is durable
items.a: Pick three investment highlights and back each with data. 'First, [market position]: number [two] in [segment] with [X]% share. Second, [growth]: revenue compounding at [X]% over three years versus [Y]% for the market. Third, [margin or cash conversion]: EBITDA margin of [X]% with low capex needs, so strong free cash flow.' Then tie it to buyers: 'For a strategic, that meant [distribution / capability] synergies; for a PE fund, predictable cash flow to support leverage.' Mention why the advantage lasts, such as [contracts, brand, licences]. That shows you could write the investment highlights page of an information memorandum.
items.t: Listing adjectives like 'great management, strong brand' with no numbers or buyer-specific angle.

items.q: Now the flip side: what were the client's weaknesses, and why might investors have hesitated?
p: Names real weaknesses: concentration, cyclicality, governance or margins
Quantifies at least one weakness
Explains how the team mitigated or positioned it
Sounds balanced, not like a sales pitch
items.a: Be candid; an adviser who sees no weaknesses is not credible. 'The main concerns were [customer concentration: the top three customers were [X]% of revenue], [margin pressure from raw material costs], and [dependence on the promoter].' Then how you handled them: 'We addressed concentration by showing [long-term contracts and renewal history], and positioned margin risk with [pass-through clauses]. Some buyers still discounted for it, which showed up as [lower bids / an earnout].' This tells the interviewer you can anticipate diligence questions, which is exactly what an analyst on either side of a deal must do.
items.t: Claiming there were no real weaknesses, or criticising the client in a way that breaches confidentiality.
items.in: Indian buyers often probe promoter related-party transactions, tax litigation and governance gaps in family-run firms; these frequently lead to escrows or specific indemnities.

items.q: What were the biggest obstacles to getting the deal done, and how were they resolved?
p: Names one or two specific obstacles, not generic 'delays'
Explains root cause: valuation gap, diligence finding, approval or financing
Describes the fix: earnout, escrow, price change or structure
States the outcome honestly, including if the deal died
items.a: Pick the one or two issues that really mattered. Common ones: a valuation gap between buyer and seller, a diligence finding (a tax exposure, a change-of-control clause in a key contract, working capital below what was represented), financing, or a regulatory approval. Then the resolution: 'The bid-ask gap was about Rs. [X] crore. We bridged it with an earnout tied to [next year's EBITDA], and a specific indemnity backed by an escrow for the [tax] issue.' If it failed, say so: 'The deal broke because [reason]; in hindsight, [lesson].' A dead deal explained clearly impresses more than a vague success story.
items.t: Claiming nothing went wrong, or blaming the other side without explaining the economics of the gap.

items.q: What kind of standalone operating model did you build for the client, and what did it drive?
p: Describes revenue drivers: volume, price, segments or units
Covers cost structure, capex, working capital and debt
Mentions scenarios: base, upside, downside
Says what the model fed: valuation, bid or financing
items.a: Describe the structure, then the use. 'It was a three-statement model with [five]-year projections. Revenue was built bottom-up from [volumes by plant / stores and same-store growth / customers times revenue per customer]. Costs were split into variable and fixed so margins moved with volume. Capex was linked to capacity, working capital to receivable, inventory and payable days, and there was a debt schedule.' Then scenarios: 'Base, management and downside cases, with sensitivities on [price, utilisation].' And the output: 'It fed the DCF, the leverage buyers could raise, and the [lender / buyer] presentation.' If you did not build it, say which parts you owned.
items.t: Saying 'a three-statement model' without explaining a single driver or how the output was used.

items.q: Where did the deal stand when you left your previous firm?
p: Gives a clear status: closed, signed, paused or dead
Mentions timing and what was still pending
Shows you followed it after leaving
Respects confidentiality on non-public details
items.a: Keep it short and factual. 'When I left in [month, year], we had [received second-round bids / signed the SPA and were awaiting regulatory approval / paused because of market conditions].' Then show continued interest: 'I followed it afterwards; it [closed in [month] at a reported Rs. [X] crore / is still pending].' If the deal is not public, say: 'It has not been announced, so I will keep it at that level.' Be precise about what happened during your time versus after you left. This question tests honesty and discretion as much as deal knowledge.
items.t: Claiming credit for a closing that happened long after you left, or leaking non-public details.

items.q: What did you look at during due diligence on this deal?
p: Covers financial, commercial, legal and tax workstreams
Mentions quality of earnings and normalised EBITDA
Gives one specific finding and its impact on price or terms
Separates own workstream from other advisers' work
items.a: Organise by workstream, then give a finding. Financial: quality of earnings, normalised EBITDA, net debt and debt-like items, and the working capital trend for the peg. Commercial: market size, customer concentration, churn and pricing power. Legal: material contracts, change-of-control clauses, litigation and licences. Tax: direct and indirect tax exposures. Also HR, IT and environmental where relevant. Then: 'My piece was [financial diligence on revenue recognition]. We found [one-off income of Rs. [X] crore inside EBITDA / an unrecorded liability], which [cut the price / went into an indemnity].' Ex-Big 4 candidates should lean on this question; it is where your strongest story usually sits.
items.t: Listing workstreams like a textbook without one finding that actually changed the deal.
items.in: Indian diligence adds promoter related-party transactions, GST and income-tax disputes, land title, labour law compliance, and FEMA filings for any foreign shareholding.

items.q: Tell me about the industry your client operated in.
p: Market size and growth rate, with numbers
Key players and the client's position
Two or three demand drivers and the main risk
How industry dynamics affected valuation or buyer interest
items.a: Give a 45-second industry snapshot. 'The [sector] market in India is about Rs. [X] crore, growing [Y]% a year, driven by [formalisation / rising incomes / government capex]. It is [fragmented / consolidated]: the top [N] players hold [Z]%. Our client was [number three, focused on segment A].' Then the economics: 'Margins depend on [raw material pass-through and capacity utilisation], and the main risk is [regulation / import competition].' Close with the deal link: 'Consolidation pressure is why strategics were interested, and sector multiples of around [X] times EBITDA anchored the valuation.'
items.t: Giving stale or vague numbers; know size, growth, structure and margin drivers cold.

items.q: How did you narrow down the list of potential buyers, targets or investors?
p: Starts with a long list, then applies explicit filters
Filters: strategic fit, ability to pay, deal appetite, conflicts
Separates strategic buyers from financial sponsors
Gives numbers from long list to short list
items.a: Explain the funnel. 'We started with a long list of about [60] names: strategics in [the sector and adjacent sectors], PE funds with [a sector focus and cheque size of Rs. X to Y crore], and family offices. We filtered on strategic fit (synergies, product or geographic overlap), ability to pay (balance sheet strength or fund dry powder), track record of actually closing deals, and conflicts (competitors we did not want to see our data). That got us to [25] contacted and [8] serious.' For a buy-side mandate, the same logic applies to targets: size range, margins, owners willing to sell, and fit with the client's strategy.
items.t: Saying 'we used a database' without explaining the criteria and judgment applied.

items.q: How did you value the client or target on this deal?
p: Names the methods: comps, precedents, DCF, LBO where relevant
Gives the key multiple or assumption that drove value
Explains which method got most weight and why
States the range and where the final price landed
items.a: 'We triangulated three methods. Trading comps: [N] listed peers at [X to Y] times EV/EBITDA, adjusted for size and growth. Precedent transactions: [N] deals at higher multiples, reflecting a control premium. A DCF with a WACC of about [X]% and terminal growth of [Y]%. We weighted [precedents] most because [it was a control sale with active strategic buyers].' Then the result: 'The football field gave Rs. [A to B] crore; bids came in at [C], about [X] times EBITDA.' If a PE fund bid, mention the LBO analysis as a floor. Be ready to defend why a given peer or assumption was in or out.
items.t: Naming methods without the driving assumption, or being unable to explain why bids differed from your range.
items.in: Indian deals often need a registered valuer or merchant banker report, and cross-border share transfers must respect FEMA pricing guidelines based on fair value.

items.q: What exactly did you personally contribute to this deal?
p: Uses 'I', not 'we', with specific tasks
Names one output that changed a decision
Shows ownership beyond the assigned tasks
Stays honest about scope; no inflation
items.a: Switch from 'we' to 'I' and be specific. 'I owned three things: [the operating model / the comps and precedents / the diligence tracker]. The one I am proudest of: [I found receivables over 180 days of Rs. [X] crore, which led to a working capital adjustment / I rebuilt revenue by plant, which showed the management case needed [Y]% utilisation, and we reset the bid].' Add one ownership moment: '[I coordinated the data room for 12 bidders / I drafted the market section of the memorandum].' Keep it honest; your interviewer may know someone who worked on that deal.
items.t: Hiding behind 'we' throughout, or claiming senior-level decisions you could not have made.

items.q: What do you understand a restructuring banker actually does day to day?
p: Advises distressed companies or creditors on fixing the capital structure
Mentions liquidity forecasting, such as a 13-week cash flow
Mentions valuation, recovery analysis and stakeholder negotiation
Names tools: exchange offers, amend and extend, Chapter 11 or IBC
items.a: Restructuring bankers advise either a distressed company or its creditors when the capital structure no longer fits the business's cash flows. The work has three layers. Analysis: a short-term liquidity forecast, often a 13-week cash flow, debt capacity, enterprise valuation, and recovery waterfalls showing what each creditor class gets under different outcomes. Transactions: amend and extend deals, exchange offers, debt-for-equity swaps, rescue financing, distressed asset sales, and in-court processes such as Chapter 11, or IBC in India. Negotiation: brokering a deal among lenders, bondholders, equity and sometimes the court. As an associate I would expect heavy modelling, a lot of reading of credit agreements, and fast turnaround, because liquidity sets the clock.
items.t: Describing it as 'M&A for bankrupt companies'; most of the work is capital structure negotiation.
items.in: In India, much stressed-asset work runs through IBC (CIRP led by a resolution professional, with the CoC deciding) or the RBI June 2019 framework; bankers often advise bidders or lenders.

items.q: Restructuring mandates come from two sides. What are they, and which side does our team mostly advise?
p: Debtor side: advising the company
Creditor side: advising a lender group or creditor committee
Explains how the work differs between the two sides
Has researched the firm's actual mix of mandates
items.a: The two sides are debtor-side and creditor-side. Debtor-side means advising the company: building the business plan, running liquidity analysis, designing the restructuring proposal, raising rescue or DIP financing, and running any sale. Creditor-side means advising a lender group, an ad hoc bondholder group or an official creditors' committee: testing the company's plan, valuing the business to argue for a bigger recovery, and negotiating terms. Creditor work often means more mandates at once, because groups form in many situations. On your team's mix, I would say: 'From my research, you have been more active on the [debtor / creditor] side, for example [recent mandate], but I would like to hear how the split looks today.'
items.t: Guessing the firm's side without research; check recent mandates and league tables before the interview.
items.in: Under IBC, the board is suspended and the CoC of financial creditors controls the process, so Indian advisory leans toward lenders and resolution applicants rather than the debtor.

items.q: Beyond the fact that restructuring is busy right now, why does it genuinely interest you?
p: Gives a reason that outlasts the current cycle
Links to own background with one specific experience
Shows understanding of the work: capital structure, negotiation, legal process
Under 60 seconds and ends on the role
items.a: Structure: what draws you, proof from your past, and fit. 'Three things. First, it is the most technical corner of banking: you need valuation, credit documents and legal process together. Second, the outcomes matter; a good restructuring keeps a viable business and its jobs alive. Third, it is counter-cyclical work, so the skills hold value across cycles. I saw this first-hand at [Big 4 / bank / family business], where [you worked on a stressed borrower's audit / a credit review / a customer going into insolvency] and saw [specific detail]. That is why I want to start in restructuring rather than generalist M&A.'
items.t: Saying 'it is hot right now' or 'I like complexity' with no evidence from your own background.

items.q: How would restructuring experience help you reach your longer-term career goals?
p: States a credible long-term goal in one line
Names transferable skills: credit analysis, valuation, negotiation
Signals commitment to the role for several years
Avoids framing restructuring as a mere stepping stone
items.a: Structure: goal, skills, commitment. 'Long term I see myself in [credit or special situations investing / corporate finance leadership / staying in advisory]. Restructuring builds exactly what those need: reading credit documents, valuing businesses when the base case is broken, understanding where value breaks in a capital structure, and negotiating with several stakeholders at once. Those skills are scarce and they compound. But I want to build them properly here first, over several years and a few cycles of mandates.' Then tie back to your background: '[My CA training / my risk role / my audit work] gave me the base; this is the logical next step.'
items.t: Making it sound like a two-year stopover before a buy-side move; banks hire for commitment.

items.q: If a distressed company needs a restructuring adviser, how does it choose between banks?
p: Track record in comparable situations and sectors
Relationships and credibility with the relevant creditor groups
No conflicts from advising the other side
Can run all options in parallel; sensible fee structure
items.a: The board, often nudged by lenders, weighs five things. Track record: has the bank handled situations of similar size, complexity and sector? Relationships: does it know the key lenders, distressed funds and their counsel, and is it credible with them and the court? Conflicts: it cannot already advise a creditor group in the same situation. Breadth: can it run every option in parallel, from rescue financing to a sale to a court process, so the company keeps negotiating leverage? And practicality: bandwidth to move within days, and fees, typically a monthly retainer plus a success fee on completing the restructuring or sale. Chemistry with the senior banker matters a lot in a crisis.
items.t: Saying 'the best brand' or 'the lowest fees'; credibility with creditors and conflicts matter more.
items.in: Once CIRP starts, the board is suspended and the resolution professional, with CoC approval, appoints advisers, so Indian company-side mandates mostly happen before admission or in out-of-court restructurings.

items.q: Why do companies end up in bankruptcy or insolvency in the first place?
p: Distinguishes a liquidity problem from a solvency problem
Too much debt for the cash flows, often LBO or capex-led
Operational decline: competition, disruption, cost shocks
Refinancing wall or maturity mismatch as the trigger
items.a: Companies fail when they cannot pay obligations as they fall due, so the trigger is cash, not accounting losses. The root causes usually combine. Over-leverage: debt sized for a best-case plan, from an LBO or an aggressive capex cycle. Operational decline: lost market share, disruption, input cost spikes or the loss of a key customer. Liquidity and refinancing: a large maturity when credit markets are shut, or long-dated assets funded with short-term borrowing. External shocks: recession, a commodity price crash, regulatory change or litigation. Sometimes fraud or governance failure. A company can be solvent but illiquid, or liquid today with an unsustainable capital structure; advisers diagnose which before choosing a fix.
items.t: Saying 'they lose money'; many loss-making companies survive while profitable ones fail on liquidity.
items.in: India's stressed-asset wave came from over-leveraged infrastructure, power and steel capex funded by banks, project delays and regulatory shocks; IL&FS in 2018 showed asset-liability mismatch.

items.q: A company can no longer meet its debt obligations. What options does it have?
p: Out of court: waivers, amend and extend, exchange offers, refinancing
Raise liquidity: asset sales, rescue financing, equity injection
Sell the whole company in a distressed M&A process
In court: Chapter 11 reorganisation or Chapter 7 liquidation
items.a: I would group them from least to most drastic. First, buy time: covenant waivers or an amend and extend with existing lenders. Second, raise liquidity: refinance, raise rescue financing (usually secured and expensive), sell non-core assets, or get an equity injection from the sponsor or promoter. Third, fix the balance sheet out of court through a distressed exchange, swapping debt for new debt with lower face value, or for equity. Fourth, sell the whole company in a distressed M&A process. Fifth, go to court: Chapter 11 to reorganise with the automatic stay and the ability to bind holdouts, including a prepackaged plan or a 363 sale, or Chapter 7 liquidation if the business is not viable.
items.t: Jumping straight to bankruptcy and forgetting the cheaper out-of-court options companies try first.
items.in: Indian equivalents: restructuring under the RBI June 2019 framework with an inter-creditor agreement, one-time settlements, sale to ARCs, SARFAESI enforcement, IBC CIRP, prepacks for MSMEs, or liquidation.

items.q: Take those options one by one. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of each?
p: Waivers or amend and extend: cheap and fast, but only buys time
New money or asset sales: liquidity, but costly or value-destructive
Exchange offer: cheaper than court, but holdouts free-ride
Chapter 11: binds dissenters, but slow, costly, public
items.a: Waivers and amend and extend: quick, cheap, equity survives; but higher spreads and fees, and they only buy time. Refinancing or rescue capital: preserves ownership; but it is expensive, dilutive or primes existing lenders, and may not be available. Asset sales: cash without court; but fire-sale prices and a smaller business. Out-of-court exchange: faster, cheaper and less stigma than court; but it needs high consent, and holdouts get paid in full while others take haircuts. Distressed sale: certainty and a clean exit; but a low price, and equity is usually wiped out. Chapter 11: automatic stay, DIP financing, cram-down of holdouts, rejection of bad contracts; but costly, slow and public. Chapter 7: final, but lowest value.
items.t: Ignoring the holdout problem, which is the main reason out-of-court deals fail.
items.in: Under IBC, admission usually means promoters lose control (board suspended, Section 29A may bar them from bidding), so Indian promoters strongly prefer out-of-court settlements first.

items.q: From the creditors' side, what strategies can they use to recover their money from a distressed borrower?
p: Negotiate: waivers or amendments for higher pricing, fees and covenants
Enforce: accelerate, foreclose on collateral, or force a bankruptcy
Exit: sell the debt to distressed investors at a discount
Seek control: DIP financing, debt-for-equity, credit bid
items.a: Creditors have four broad plays. Negotiate: grant waivers or an amend and extend in exchange for higher spreads, fees, more collateral and tighter covenants. Enforce: accelerate the debt, foreclose on collateral, or file an involuntary bankruptcy petition to force a process. Exit: sell the loan or bonds to a distressed fund at a discount and take the loss now. Or go for control: organise an ad hoc group, provide DIP or rescue financing to gain priority and influence, swap debt for equity, or credit bid their secured claim to buy the assets. The choice depends on seniority, collateral coverage, the cost of holding the position, and their view of going-concern value versus liquidation value.
items.t: Treating all creditors alike; secured and unsecured creditors have very different leverage and incentives.
items.in: Indian lenders use SARFAESI enforcement, IBC filings under Section 7 (financial creditors) or Section 9 (operational creditors), sale to ARCs, DRT recovery, or RBI framework resolution.

items.q: How is a restructuring deal different from a normal M&A or financing transaction?
p: Many stakeholders with conflicting claims, not one buyer and seller
Focus on liabilities and capital structure, not just enterprise value
Valuation allocates a fixed pie; negotiation is largely zero-sum
Liquidity sets the timeline; heavy legal and court involvement
items.a: Four big differences. Stakeholders: M&A has a buyer and a seller; restructuring has the company, several creditor classes, sometimes a sponsor, employees and a court, each with different priority and incentives. Focus: the liabilities side, meaning who holds what, what the documents allow, and where value breaks, not just enterprise value. Valuation: it is used to allocate a fixed pie, so a higher valuation helps junior classes and a lower one helps senior classes; that makes the negotiation largely zero-sum. Clock and process: liquidity runs out, so cash sets the timeline, and legal documents and court procedure drive much of the work. Fees differ too: usually a monthly retainer plus a completion fee.
items.t: Saying only 'the company is in trouble' without explaining the multi-party, value-allocation nature of the work.

items.q: What is the difference between Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the US?
p: Chapter 7: liquidation by a trustee; the business generally stops
Chapter 11: reorganisation; debtor in possession keeps operating
Chapter 11 plan voted by classes; cram-down can bind dissenters
Distributions follow absolute priority
items.a: Chapter 7 is liquidation. A trustee is appointed, the business generally stops operating, assets are sold, and proceeds are distributed by priority: secured creditors from their collateral, then administrative and priority claims, then unsecured creditors, with equity last. Chapter 11 is reorganisation. Management usually stays in control as debtor in possession, the automatic stay halts creditor enforcement, the company can raise DIP financing and reject burdensome contracts, and it proposes a plan of reorganisation that creditor classes vote on. A class accepts with two-thirds in amount and more than half in number of those voting, and the court can cram down a dissenting class if the plan is fair and equitable. Chapter 11 can also end in a 363 asset sale.
items.t: Thinking Chapter 11 always saves the company; many cases end in asset sales or conversion to Chapter 7.
items.in: IBC parallels these: CIRP and liquidation, but creditor-in-control. A resolution professional replaces the board; the CoC approves a plan at 66%; the 330-day limit is often exceeded; failure means liquidation.

items.q: What is debtor-in-possession financing, and how does a company in bankruptcy use it?
p: New money lent during Chapter 11, approved by the court
Super-priority status, often priming liens over existing secured debt
Funds operations and case costs; reassures suppliers and customers
Often from existing lenders; can include roll-ups and milestones
items.a: DIP financing is new money lent to a company after it files Chapter 11, approved by the court. Because the borrower is already in trouble, the law gives DIP lenders protection to attract them: super-priority administrative claim status, liens on unencumbered assets and, if existing secured lenders consent or are adequately protected, priming liens ranking ahead of them. The company uses it to fund payroll, suppliers, working capital and professional fees while it restructures, which also reassures customers and vendors. DIP loans are short-dated, expensive and carry tight covenants and milestones for a plan or sale. Existing lenders often provide it defensively, sometimes rolling up prepetition debt, and it is usually refinanced by exit financing.
items.t: Calling it just 'a loan to a bankrupt company' without the priority that makes lenders willing to lend.
items.in: IBC's equivalent is interim finance, raised by the resolution professional with CoC approval; it counts as a CIRP cost, paid first in the Section 53 waterfall.

items.q: When modelling or valuing a distressed company, how would you adjust its three financial statements?
p: Income statement: strip one-offs, normalise underinvestment, treat unpaid interest carefully
Balance sheet: write down assets, surface hidden or reclassified liabilities
Cash flow: tighter supplier terms, catch-up capex, restructuring cash costs
Builds a short-term liquidity forecast such as 13-week cash flow
items.a: Income statement: remove one-offs such as restructuring charges and advisory fees to get normalised EBITDA, but also add back costs the company has been starving, like maintenance, marketing or R&D, and reflect lost customers. Treat interest carefully: accrued but unpaid, PIK or default interest. Balance sheet: write down overstated assets such as aged receivables, obsolete inventory and goodwill; recognise contingent and off-balance-sheet liabilities; reclassify debt as current if covenants are breached; show debt at claim value. Cash flow: model suppliers tightening terms so payables shrink, catch-up capex, cash restructuring costs and possibly lost tax shields. Practically, you also build a 13-week cash flow, because survival depends on near-term liquidity.
items.t: Only adding back one-offs, which inflates EBITDA; normalising underinvestment pushes it down.
items.in: In India, check corporate guarantees given to group companies, invoked bank guarantees, and disputed operational creditor claims; these often sit outside reported debt.

items.q: Would those adjustments look different for a public versus a private distressed company?
p: Economic adjustments are the same in principle
Public: more disclosure, plus market prices for debt and equity
Private: weaker data, more diligence, owner-related normalisations
Information gap changes the method, not the logic
items.a: The logic is the same: normalise earnings, mark assets and liabilities to realistic values, and focus on liquidity. What differs is information. A public company files audited, regular disclosures, so you start from better data, and you get market signals: traded bond and loan prices show where the market thinks value breaks, and the share price shows remaining option value. A private company may have less frequent, less reliable or unaudited numbers, so you do more diligence, rely on management data, and normalise owner-related items such as above-market promoter salaries, related-party transactions and personal expenses run through the company. Without market prices, you lean more on comparables and your own recovery analysis.
items.t: Calling the adjustments completely different, or completely identical without noting the information gap.
items.in: Listed Indian companies disclose material events, including loan defaults, under SEBI LODR; private companies' MCA filings often lag, and promoter-group related-party flows need deep scrutiny.

items.q: If a distressed company's debt is worth more than its assets, what happens to the value of its equity?
p: Intrinsic equity value is zero; creditors own the economic value
Equity cannot go negative because of limited liability
Listed shares may still trade above zero: option value
Restructuring usually wipes out or heavily dilutes equity
items.a: Economically, equity is out of the money: if claims ranking ahead of it exceed what the assets are worth, nothing is left for shareholders, so intrinsic value is zero. It cannot go below zero, because of limited liability; the shortfall falls on creditors. But listed shares often still trade at a small positive price, because equity behaves like a call option on the firm's assets: if the business recovers before the debt comes due, shareholders keep the upside. That option value shrinks as maturities approach. In a restructuring, equity is usually wiped out or massively diluted as creditors convert debt into new equity. Strictly, it is the face value of debt that exceeds assets; market prices already reflect expected recovery.
items.t: Saying equity value turns negative, or ignoring the option value that keeps the share price above zero.

items.q: In a bankruptcy, in what order do claims get paid out of the company's assets?
p: Absolute priority: seniors paid in full before juniors get anything
Secured creditors first, but only up to collateral value
Administrative and priority claims, then unsecured, then subordinated
Preferred equity, then common equity last
items.a: The principle is absolute priority: a class is paid only after the classes above it are paid in full. In US practice, roughly: DIP financing and super-priority claims; secured creditors up to the value of their collateral, first lien before second lien; administrative claims such as professional fees and post-filing obligations; priority claims such as certain taxes and capped employee wages; senior unsecured debt, trade claims and secured deficiency claims; subordinated debt; preferred equity; and finally common equity. Any secured claim above its collateral value becomes an unsecured deficiency claim. In negotiated plans, junior classes sometimes receive a small recovery to win their consent, a deliberate deviation from strict priority.
items.t: Ranking all debt ahead of everything and forgetting secured lenders are protected only up to collateral value.
items.in: IBC Section 53: process costs; workmen's dues (24 months) with secured creditors relinquishing security; other employees (12 months); unsecured financial creditors; government dues and secured shortfall; other debts; preference; equity.

items.q: How would you estimate cost of debt for a company so distressed that no investor will lend it new money?
p: Start from yields on its existing traded debt, with caution
Promised yield overstates expected return; adjust for default and recovery
Alternatives: distressed peer yields, synthetic rating, rescue or DIP pricing
Deep distress: debt is equity-like; cost approaches cost of equity
items.a: Start with the market yield on its existing bonds or loans: a bond trading at 55 implies a very high yield to maturity. But that is a promised yield that assumes full repayment, so it overstates the expected return. Better: adjust for the probability of default and expected recovery, or use yields on comparable distressed issuers, or a synthetic rating based on interest coverage. You can also look at what rescue or DIP lenders charge, since that is the true marginal cost of new money. Conceptually, as distress deepens, debt carries equity-like risk, so its cost converges toward the cost of equity. Many practitioners value the business on a post-restructuring capital structure instead.
items.t: Plugging the coupon, or the raw distressed yield, into WACC as the cost of debt.
items.in: Indian corporate bond markets are thin, so use rating-based spreads over G-secs for comparable stressed issuers, or private credit pricing for stressed borrowers.

items.q: How does valuation change when the company you are valuing is distressed?
p: Focus shifts to enterprise value and the fulcrum security
Liquidation value becomes a key floor against going-concern value
Distressed comps, normalised EBITDA, scenario-weighted projections
Equity often near zero; valuation allocates recoveries between classes
items.a: Three shifts. First, the question changes from 'what is the equity worth' to 'what is the enterprise worth and who is entitled to it'. You run value through the waterfall to find the fulcrum security, the class where value runs out, since that class usually becomes the new owner. Second, you add liquidation value as a floor and compare it with going-concern value, because creditors only support a reorganisation that beats liquidation. Third, the methods adapt: comps and precedents from distressed or recovered peers, normalised EBITDA, DCFs with restructuring costs and scenario weights, and debt trading prices as a cross-check. Equity value is often near zero, and valuation becomes a negotiating tool between classes.
items.t: Running a normal DCF and subtracting face-value debt, ignoring liquidation value and the fulcrum.
items.in: IBC requires two registered valuers to estimate fair value and liquidation value; a resolution plan must give dissenting financial creditors at least their liquidation value.

items.q: How would you adapt a DCF for a company in distress?
p: Projections include restructuring costs, catch-up capex, working capital outflows
Scenario or probability-weighted cash flows, including a downside or liquidation case
Unlevered cash flows; WACC on target post-restructuring structure
Enterprise value run through the claims waterfall; value tax losses
items.a: Several changes. Cash flows: management cases in distress are usually optimistic, so build your own with explicit restructuring cash costs, severance, catch-up capex, and working capital outflows as suppliers tighten terms. Use scenarios, or probability-weight a going-concern case against a liquidation case, rather than one base case. Discounting: use unlevered free cash flow and a WACC built on the target post-restructuring capital structure, not today's broken one, with a cost of equity reflecting higher risk. Terminal value: apply it only once the business is normalised, which may need a longer projection period. Add value for tax losses that survive. Then run enterprise value through the claims waterfall rather than simply subtracting net debt.
items.t: Using today's distressed capital structure in WACC, which double counts distress and distorts value.
items.in: Indian tax law restricts carry-forward of losses after a change in ownership, with relief for IBC-approved resolution plans; verify the current position before valuing the loss shield.

items.q: A distressed company hires you to sell it. How would that sale process differ from selling a healthy company?
p: Compressed timeline set by the liquidity runway
Buyer universe: distressed funds, cash-rich strategics, existing lenders
Creditor consent or court approval, often a 363 sale with stalking horse
As-is terms with limited reps and indemnities; certainty over price
items.a: Five differences. Timing: weeks, not months, because the cash runway sets the deadline; diligence is shorter and the information package thinner. Buyers: fewer patient strategics, more distressed and special situations funds, strategics with strong balance sheets, and sometimes existing lenders. Stakeholders: creditors effectively control the outcome, so their consent or a court process is needed; in Chapter 11 the sale often runs under Section 363, with a stalking horse bid, court-approved bid procedures and an auction. Terms: as-is, with limited reps, warranties and indemnities, since the seller may not survive to stand behind them. Price: often below the face value of debt, and certainty of closing matters as much as headline value.
items.t: Treating it as a normal auction with full indemnities; time and creditor consent dominate everything.
items.in: Under IBC, the resolution professional runs the process for the CoC: Form G, information memorandum, resolution plans, 66% CoC vote, NCLT approval; Section 29A screens bidders; 330-day limits often overrun.

items.q: We always want multiple bidders in a sell-side process. Why are they especially important when the seller is distressed?
p: Seller has little leverage; walking away is not an option
Competition is the only defence against lowball bids
Court and creditors need a market test to approve the sale
Backup bidders protect certainty if the lead bidder walks
items.a: A distressed seller has almost no bargaining power: every buyer knows cash is running out and the alternative is liquidation, so competition is the only thing that disciplines price. Second, the outcome needs a market test: in a 363 sale the court approves the highest or otherwise best offer after an auction, and the board, whose duties tilt toward creditors near insolvency, needs evidence that value was maximised to withstand creditor challenges. Third, certainty: distressed bidders often retrade or walk when diligence surfaces problems, so a backup bidder protects against a failed process. A stalking horse bid sets the floor, and other bidders must top it, including the break fee.
items.t: Answering only 'to get a higher price' and missing the market test and deal certainty points.
items.in: In CIRP, multiple resolution applicants give the CoC competitive tension; some processes run challenge rounds or a Swiss challenge to improve the best bid.

items.q: What is the difference between a stock purchase and an asset purchase, and which would the buyer and the seller each prefer in a distressed sale?
p: Stock purchase: buys the entity and inherits all liabilities
Asset purchase: chosen assets and liabilities; the rest stays behind
Distressed buyer prefers assets, ideally free and clear via a 363 sale
Seller prefers a stock sale, but rarely has leverage in distress
items.a: In a stock purchase, the buyer acquires the shares, so it inherits the whole company: every asset, contract and liability, known or unknown. In an asset purchase, the buyer chooses which assets and liabilities to take; everything else stays with the seller entity. A distressed buyer strongly prefers an asset deal: it avoids hidden liabilities, cherry-picks the good assets and, in the US, usually gets a tax basis step-up. Through a 363 sale it also buys free and clear of liens and claims, with court protection. The seller normally prefers a stock sale for a clean exit, but in distress it rarely has the leverage, and proceeds left in the shell go to creditors by priority.
items.t: Saying the seller prefers an asset sale; it leaves the seller holding the liabilities in a shell.
items.in: IBC resolution plans usually acquire the company itself, but NCLT approval binds all stakeholders and extinguishes claims outside the plan, giving a clean slate; outside IBC, slump sales transfer businesses.

items.q: If a distressed sale does not end in a normal stock or asset purchase, what other outcomes are possible?
p: Debt-for-equity swap: creditors become owners via a plan or exchange
Credit bid by secured lenders using their claim as currency
Liquidation, piecemeal or by division
Prepackaged plan, sponsor rescue, or merger with a stronger player
items.a: Several. Creditors can take the keys: in a plan of reorganisation or an out-of-court exchange, debt converts into new equity and the fulcrum class ends up owning the company. Secured lenders can credit bid in a 363 sale, using the face value of their claim instead of cash, which often sets a floor and can win the auction. Distressed investors can run a loan-to-own strategy, buying debt cheaply to convert into control. The company can liquidate under Chapter 7, piecemeal or by selling divisions. A prepackaged plan agreed before filing can recapitalise it quickly. Or the existing sponsor injects equity in exchange for creditor concessions, or the company merges with a stronger competitor.
items.t: Forgetting credit bids and debt-for-equity swaps, the two most common non-cash outcomes.
items.in: If CIRP fails, the company is liquidated, though a going-concern sale is still possible; outside IBC, lenders restructure under the RBI framework or sell loans to ARCs.

items.q: M&A processes are normally confidential. Why might a distressed company publicly announce it has hired a banker to run a sale?
p: Distress is already public; an announcement controls the narrative
Reassures suppliers, customers, staff and lenders there is a plan
Brings in more bidders quickly under a short timeline
May be required disclosure for listed companies
items.a: Because confidentiality has little value once the market already knows the company is in trouble: bond prices, rating downgrades and supplier gossip have seen to that. Announcing a process controls the narrative: it tells suppliers, customers, employees and lenders that management has a credible plan, which can stop suppliers demanding cash in advance and help keep key staff. It widens the buyer universe fast, which matters when there are only weeks of runway and competition is the main price lever. It can also buy goodwill and standstill time from creditors. For listed companies, a strategic review may need disclosure anyway. The trade-off is that it signals weakness, so bidders may lowball.
items.t: Insisting it should never be announced; in distress the benefits usually outweigh the signalling cost.
items.in: Listed Indian companies must disclose material events and loan defaults under SEBI LODR; once CIRP starts, the resolution professional publicly invites expressions of interest through Form G.

items.q: In a distressed sale or bankruptcy, are existing shareholders likely to get anything back?
p: Usually little or nothing under absolute priority
Equity is paid only after all creditors are paid in full
Exception: liquidity crisis with value above claims
Token recoveries for consent, such as warrants or small stakes
items.a: Usually very little or nothing. Under absolute priority, shareholders recover only after every creditor class is paid in full, and in most distressed cases enterprise value is below total claims, so equity is wiped out and creditors become the new owners. There are exceptions. If the problem is liquidity rather than solvency, for example a maturity that cannot be refinanced in a frozen market, value may exceed claims and equity keeps something. And in negotiated plans, senior creditors sometimes give shareholders a small recovery, such as warrants or a few percent of new equity, to avoid litigation and speed up confirmation. Buying equity in a distressed company is essentially buying an out-of-the-money option.
items.t: Assuming shareholders share in sale proceeds just because they own the company.
items.in: Under IBC, resolution plans typically cut existing equity to near zero through capital reduction and fresh issuance, and Section 29A usually bars defaulting promoters from bidding back.

items.q: A company wants to sell itself or restructure its debt out of court. Why might it still be forced into Chapter 11?
