p: Holdout creditors block deals needing high or unanimous consent
Chapter 11 binds dissenters via class votes and cram-down
Automatic stay stops enforcement when liquidity runs out
Buyers want 363 free-and-clear protection; ability to reject contracts
items.a: Mainly because out-of-court deals need near-universal consent, and some creditors hold out. Changing payment terms on US public bonds typically needs each affected holder's consent, so holdouts can demand full payment while others take haircuts. Chapter 11 fixes this: a class is bound if two-thirds by amount and more than half by number of voting claims accept, and the court can cram down dissenting classes. Second, liquidity: if cash runs out or a creditor starts enforcing, the automatic stay is the only way to stop it. Third, buyers often insist on a 363 sale to get assets free and clear of liens and claims. Fourth, the company may need to reject burdensome leases or contracts.
items.t: Saying 'because it cannot pay' without explaining the holdout problem that court processes solve.
items.in: IBC binds dissenters once 66% of the CoC approves and NCLT sanctions; out of court, the RBI framework binds signatory lenders when 75% by value and 60% by number agree.

items.q: A distressed company repurchases Rs. 100 crore face value of its own debt in the market at 50% of face. Why do it, and how do the three statements change?
p: Retires Rs. 100 crore of face value for Rs. 50 crore cash
Pre-tax gain of 50; net income up 37.5 at 25% tax
Operating cash flow down 12.5 after removing gain; financing down 50
Cash down 62.5, debt down 100, equity up 37.5
items.a: Motivation: the company deleverages cheaply, retiring Rs. 100 crore of face value for Rs. 50 crore, cutting future interest and refinancing needs and improving leverage covenants. It works when the market prices the debt as if default is likely but the company has spare cash. Accounting, assuming 25% tax paid in cash: the income statement shows a Rs. 50 crore gain on extinguishment, so net income rises Rs. 37.5 crore. Cash flow: start with 37.5, subtract the non-cash gain of 50, so operating cash flow is minus 12.5 (the tax); financing cash flow is minus 50 for the repurchase. Cash falls 62.5. Balance sheet: assets down 62.5; debt down 100 and equity up 37.5. It balances.
items.t: Forgetting the gain is taxable, or leaving the gain inside operating cash flow.
items.in: Under Ind AS 109 the gain on derecognition also goes to profit and loss; Indian borrowers more often achieve this through one-time settlements with lenders, so check tax treatment.

items.q: What kind of companies are most likely to buy back their own debt at a discount?
p: Has spare cash or capital access despite distressed debt prices
Debt trades well below par on fear, not true insolvency
Debt documents permit repurchases
Often cyclicals or sponsor-backed firms in a downturn
items.a: Companies whose debt trades at a deep discount but which still have liquidity: cash on the balance sheet, an asset sale in hand, or a sponsor willing to inject equity. That typically happens in a market-wide sell-off or in cyclical sectors during a downturn, when bond prices fall on broad fear rather than a truly broken business. A company with no cash cannot do it, which is why the deeply insolvent rarely do. The documents matter too: loan agreements often restrict repurchases or require pro rata offers to all lenders, so bonds are usually easier to buy back in the open market. Sponsor-backed firms and companies facing a near-term maturity they want to shrink are common users.
items.t: Saying the most distressed companies do it; they lack the cash and creditors would object.

items.q: Why would a creditor ever agree to take a loss on money it lent to a distressed company?
p: Enterprise or collateral value is below its claim
A haircut now beats lower, slower liquidation recovery
Can be bound by class vote or cram-down anyway
Junior or unsecured position means value runs out first
items.a: Because the alternative is usually worse. If the company's enterprise value, or the value of the collateral, is below the creditor's claim, a full recovery is not available. A negotiated haircut often recovers more than liquidation, which destroys going-concern value and adds legal costs and years of delay, and time value matters. Junior and unsecured creditors sit where value runs out, so they are impaired first. They can also be forced: a class vote or cram-down in Chapter 11 can bind a dissenting creditor. Taking equity for debt may mean a book loss today but upside if the business recovers. And banks may prefer crystallising a loss to carrying a non-performing asset.
items.t: Assuming secured creditors are always made whole; they are protected only up to collateral value.
items.in: Indian lenders have accepted large haircuts under IBC because liquidation recoveries are typically far lower and NPAs carry rising provisioning requirements.

items.q: What is the ultimate goal of a financial restructuring?
p: Sustainable capital structure the cash flows can service
Enough liquidity runway to execute the business plan
Preserves going-concern value rather than liquidating
Allocates value by priority so the deal wins support
items.a: To leave the company with a capital structure its cash flows can actually support, and enough liquidity to run the business, so it survives as a going concern. Concretely: cutting debt to a sustainable leverage level, extending maturities, reducing cash interest, and adding new money if needed. It should also maximise total value for stakeholders, because a viable business is usually worth more than its liquidated parts, and allocate that value in line with priority so the deal gets enough support. A good restructuring is done once and deep enough that the company does not come back for a second round. It fixes the balance sheet; operational problems need a separate turnaround plan.
items.t: Saying the goal is to repay creditors in full or to protect shareholders.

items.q: How is a distressed M&A deal different from a restructuring deal?
p: Distressed M&A: sale of the company or assets to a new owner
Restructuring: changes the liabilities side, the capital structure
In restructuring, ownership may pass to creditors via debt-for-equity
Distressed M&A can be one tool inside a restructuring
items.a: Distressed M&A is a change of ownership: the company or some of its assets are sold to a new buyer under time pressure, usually because it cannot fix its finances alone. The work looks like a compressed sell-side or buy-side process. A restructuring changes the right-hand side of the balance sheet: amending, extending, exchanging or converting debt so the existing company survives with a sustainable capital structure. Ownership may change there too, but through creditors swapping debt for equity rather than a third-party purchase. The two overlap: a restructuring may include a sale of non-core units or a 363 sale of the whole business, and a distressed sale is often the exit from a failed restructuring.
items.t: Treating them as the same; one sells the business, the other fixes its capital structure.

items.q: What is the difference between buying only a company's assets and buying them on a 'current liabilities assumed' basis?
p: Assets only: buyer pays for assets; seller keeps all liabilities
Current liabilities assumed: buyer also takes payables and accruals
Cash price falls by roughly the liabilities assumed
Assuming liabilities keeps suppliers and operations running
items.a: In a pure asset purchase, the buyer pays for the assets and takes no liabilities; the seller keeps them all and settles what it can from the proceeds. On a current liabilities assumed basis, the buyer takes the assets plus the operating current liabilities, such as payables, accrued expenses and sometimes customer advances, so it is effectively buying fixed assets plus net working capital. The price adjusts: if the assets are worth Rs. 500 crore and current liabilities are Rs. 120 crore, the buyer pays about Rs. 380 crore in cash. Why do it? Paying suppliers keeps them shipping and customers served, so the business keeps running, which matters a lot in distress. Long-term debt still stays behind.
items.t: Thinking the buyer pays the same cash in both cases; assumed liabilities are part of the consideration.

items.q: How could a falling share price push a company toward bankruptcy, given that equity is not a debt claim?
p: Share price itself creates no payment obligation
Closes equity and refinancing routes; dilution becomes prohibitive
Margin calls on share-backed loans; confidence spiral with suppliers
Convertibles stay unconverted and must be repaid in cash
items.a: The share price itself does not force a default; it works through channels. Funding: if the company needs to refinance or recapitalise, a collapsed share price makes equity raising prohibitively dilutive, and lenders read it as a distress signal, so refinancing dries up too. Collateral: loans secured on shares, especially holding company or promoter loans, face margin calls, and forced selling pushes the price lower and can cost the group control. Convertible bonds expected to convert stay out of the money and must be repaid in cash. Confidence: suppliers tighten terms, customers hesitate, employees leave and rating agencies downgrade, which can trip covenants. That spiral turns a valuation problem into a liquidity problem.
items.t: Saying a falling share price directly drains the company's cash; it acts through financing and confidence.
items.in: Promoter share pledges are the classic Indian channel: falling prices trigger margin calls, lenders invoke pledges, and promoters can lose control; SEBI requires pledge disclosures.

items.q: What tends to happen to accounts payable days at a distressed company, and why?
p: First rises as the company stretches suppliers to conserve cash
Suppliers react: shorter terms, cash in advance, credit insurance cut
Then payable days fall sharply, draining liquidity
Model this reversal in the liquidity forecast, not historical days
items.a: It moves in two phases. First, payable days usually rise: the company delays supplier payments to conserve cash, which temporarily flatters operating cash flow. Then suppliers notice; trade credit insurers cut limits, and suppliers shorten terms or demand cash on delivery or payment in advance. Payable days then fall sharply, and that unwind is a large cash outflow exactly when liquidity is tightest; it is often what tips a company over. So in a distressed model or a 13-week cash flow, I would not assume historical payable days; I would model a reversion toward tighter terms and treat any stretched payables at the starting point as quasi-debt.
items.t: Giving only one direction; interviewers want the stretch and then the supplier reaction.
items.in: Under the MSMED Act, buyers must pay micro and small suppliers within 45 days at most, and income tax rules defer deductions for overdue dues to them, limiting the stretch.

items.q: A distressed company wants to fix its problems by raising new debt or equity instead of selling or filing. Why might that fail?
p: Covenants and existing liens block new borrowing; little free collateral
Lenders unwilling, or pricing worsens the problem
Equity at a depressed price means massive dilution
Debt overhang: new equity mainly makes creditors safer
items.a: New debt: existing credit agreements and bond documents usually cap additional debt and restrict new liens, and the best assets are already pledged, so there is little collateral to offer. Any lender willing to lend would charge rates that worsen the problem, and an already high leverage ratio cannot absorb more. New equity: at a depressed share price, raising enough means massive dilution, and existing shareholders may refuse to approve it. More fundamentally there is debt overhang: near insolvency, much of the value of new equity flows to creditors by making their claims safer, so new investors demand a huge discount or stay away. Time is also short; raises take weeks the company may not have.
items.t: Saying 'nobody wants to invest' without explaining covenants, collateral and the debt overhang problem.
items.in: SEBI's floor price for preferential issues uses trailing average prices, which can sit above a collapsing market price; banks are also reluctant to lend fresh money to NPA accounts.

items.q: For a distressed company, would adjusted EBITDA usually be higher or lower than reported EBITDA?
p: Usually higher: adds back restructuring, severance, advisory costs
Adds back losses from closed units or exited contracts
Can be lower: normalising starved maintenance, marketing, staff costs
Buyers and lenders challenge add-backs, especially recurring 'one-offs'
items.a: Usually higher. Distressed companies book many items management argues are non-recurring: restructuring and severance costs, advisory and legal fees, losses from closed plants or stores, inventory write-downs and one-off litigation. Adding those back lifts EBITDA. Note that impairments of goodwill and fixed assets sit below EBITDA anyway, so they do not change it. But an honest adjustment can also cut EBITDA: distressed companies often starve maintenance, marketing, R&D or staffing to save cash, and normalising those costs reduces it. So management's adjusted number is usually higher, while a buyer or lender will challenge the add-backs, especially 'non-recurring' charges that appear every year, and may land lower than reported.
items.t: Answering 'higher' without noting that normalising underinvestment can cut EBITDA, and add-backs get challenged.

items.q: Since a distressed company is weighed down by debt, should its DCF use levered free cash flow?
p: No: use unlevered free cash flow to value the enterprise
The current capital structure will change; interest may not be paid
Value operations independent of financing, then allocate via waterfall
Levered view only once post-restructuring structure is fixed
items.a: No, generally you use unlevered free cash flow. The whole point of a restructuring is that the capital structure will change: debt will be cut, converted or extended, and interest may not even be paid in the meantime. Levered cash flows depend on interest and repayments that are not reliable, so a levered DCF on today's structure produces a meaningless equity value. Instead, value the operating business independently of its financing: discount unlevered free cash flow at a WACC based on a sustainable target structure, get enterprise value, then run it through the claims waterfall to see what each class recovers. A levered view becomes useful only once the post-restructuring capital structure is set.
items.t: Saying 'yes, because it has debt'; that debt is exactly what is being renegotiated.

items.q: In a liquidation valuation, why not just use book shareholders' equity? It is assets minus liabilities, after all.
p: Book values are historical cost, not forced-sale proceeds
Goodwill and most intangibles recover little or nothing
Liquidation adds new claims: severance, termination damages, wind-down costs
Priority waterfall decides distribution; equity usually gets zero
items.a: Because book values are accounting numbers, not what a forced sale delivers. On the asset side, each class sells at a discount to book: some receivables go uncollected, inventory goes at clearance prices, specialised plant fetches near-scrap value, and goodwill and most intangibles are worth almost nothing. On the liability side, liquidation creates new claims: severance, contract and lease termination damages, professional and wind-down costs, plus contingent liabilities that were never on the balance sheet. So you apply recovery rates asset by asset, deduct liquidation costs, and run the proceeds through the priority waterfall. In most distressed cases that leaves nothing for equity, even when book equity is positive.
items.t: Assuming book equity approximates what shareholders would actually receive in a wind-down.

items.q: In a liquidation analysis, what recovery rates would you typically assume for different asset classes?
p: Cash near 100%; receivables roughly 70 to 90%
Inventory roughly 30 to 60%; finished goods above work in progress
PP&E varies by specialisation; land can approach market value
Goodwill, most intangibles and prepaids near zero; deduct liquidation costs
items.a: These are rules of thumb that depend on asset quality. Cash: close to 100%. Receivables: roughly 70 to 90%, lower for aged, disputed or concentrated balances, since customers often stop paying a dying supplier. Inventory: roughly 30 to 60%; raw materials and finished goods recover more than work in progress, and perishable or fashion items much less. PP&E: very wide; general-purpose equipment and vehicles do better, specialised plant may fetch little more than scrap, while land and buildings can approach market value. Prepaid expenses: near zero. Goodwill and most intangibles: near zero, unless there is a saleable brand, licence or IP. Always deduct liquidation costs before distributing.
items.t: Using one blended haircut for all assets, or giving goodwill a meaningful recovery.
items.in: IBC requires two registered valuers to estimate liquidation value; in India, land and buildings often carry most recoverable value, while plant and receivables realise slowly.

items.q: How would an LBO model for a distressed company differ from a standard LBO?
p: Lower leverage and more equity; lenders wary of unstable cash flows
Uses include restructuring costs, catch-up capex, working capital, DIP repayment
Returns from turnaround and multiple recovery, not debt paydown
Wide scenarios; entry may be via buying debt to convert
items.a: Several differences. Capital structure: lenders will not fund normal leverage against unstable cash flows, so the deal carries much more equity, and some existing debt may be rolled over or reinstated rather than refinanced. Sources and uses: add restructuring and severance costs, catch-up capex, working capital rebuilding, contract cure costs and any DIP repayment. Entry: control may come from buying the fulcrum debt at a discount and converting it, a loan-to-own route, rather than buying equity. Returns: driven by the operational turnaround and multiple expansion from a depressed entry multiple, not by paying down debt. Hence wide downside and upside scenarios, and higher target IRRs to compensate for the risk.
items.t: Applying standard leverage multiples and assuming steady debt paydown from day one.
items.in: Under IBC, buyers bid through resolution plans with upfront and deferred payments; Section 29A bars ineligible bidders, and domestic bank acquisition finance has historically been limited.

items.q: Before we get into specifics: what are the core accounting ideas a banker must have cold, from the three statements to accrual versus cash and capitalising versus expensing?
p: Names IS, BS and CFS and what each one measures
Explains links: net income, cash, retained earnings, PP&E, debt
Accrual: revenue when earned, expenses matched to that revenue
Capitalise if the benefit lasts over a year; otherwise expense
items.a: Five things. First, the three statements: the income statement shows profitability over a period, the balance sheet shows what the company owns and owes at a point in time, and the cash flow statement shows actual cash movement. Second, the links: net income starts the cash flow statement, ending cash goes to the balance sheet, and net income less dividends flows into retained earnings. Third, accrual accounting: revenue is recorded when earned and expenses are matched to it, regardless of when cash moves. Fourth, capitalise spending that benefits more than a year, like a plant, and expense the rest. Fifth, knowing what items like goodwill, intangibles and shareholders' equity actually represent.
items.t: Treating the cash flow statement as a separate report rather than the bridge between two balance sheets.
items.in: Indian companies follow Ind AS (IFRS-converged) and present under Schedule III of the Companies Act, so labels differ: Revenue from operations, Other equity, Exceptional items.

items.q: Name the key line items you would expect to see on each of the three financial statements.
p: IS: revenue, COGS, SG&A, D&A, interest, tax, net income
BS: cash, receivables, inventory, PP&E, payables, debt, equity
CFS: operating, investing and financing sections with examples
Mentions less obvious items like goodwill or deferred revenue
items.a: On the income statement: revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, operating expenses like SG&A and R&D, depreciation and amortisation, operating income, interest expense, taxes and net income. On the balance sheet, assets include cash, receivables, inventory, prepaid expenses, PP&E, goodwill and other intangibles; liabilities include payables, accrued expenses, deferred revenue and short and long-term debt; equity includes share capital, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings and treasury stock. The cash flow statement starts with net income, adds back non-cash items like D&A and stock-based compensation, adjusts for working capital, then shows capex and acquisitions in investing, and debt and equity raised, buybacks and dividends in financing.
items.t: Listing only income statement items and forgetting the investing and financing sections of the cash flow statement.
items.in: Schedule III labels: Revenue from operations, Other income, Finance costs, Exceptional items; equity shows Equity share capital and Other equity. Treasury shares appear only for ESOP trust holdings.

items.q: How are the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement connected?
p: Net income is the first line of the cash flow statement
Adds back non-cash items and adjusts for working capital changes
Ending cash on the CFS becomes balance sheet cash
Net income less dividends flows into retained earnings
items.a: Net income from the income statement is the starting point of the cash flow statement. From there you add back non-cash charges like depreciation and adjust for changes in balance sheet working capital items, such as receivables, inventory and payables, to get cash from operations. Investing and financing activities capture capex, acquisitions, debt and equity movements. The net change in cash is added to opening cash to give closing cash on the balance sheet. On the equity side, net income less dividends flows into retained earnings. Other links: PP&E rises with capex and falls with depreciation, and debt moves with borrowings and repayments. Once both sides move by the same amount, the balance sheet balances.
items.t: Forgetting the retained earnings link, so the balance sheet does not balance after the cash change.

items.q: If you could review only one financial statement to judge a company's overall health, which would you pick and why?
p: Picks the cash flow statement
Shows actual cash generation, not accounting profit
Reveals reinvestment, borrowing and payouts to shareholders
Acknowledges the limit: no full view of assets and liabilities
items.a: I would choose the cash flow statement. It shows how much cash the business actually generates, which is harder to manipulate than accounting profit. Operating cash flow tells me whether profits convert into cash, investing flows show how much it reinvests, and financing flows show whether it is funding itself by borrowing or raising equity, or returning cash to shareholders. It also starts from net income, so I still get a sense of profitability. A company with rising net income but persistently negative operating cash flow is a red flag. The limitation is that I would not see the full stock of debt or assets, but for a health check, cash is what keeps a company alive.
items.t: Picking the income statement; profit can look fine while the company runs out of cash.
items.in: Indian listed companies publish the balance sheet and cash flow statement only half-yearly under SEBI LODR; quarterly results are mainly the P&L, so cash checks often lag.

items.q: Now you get two statements instead of one to judge a company's prospects. Which two do you choose, and why?
p: Picks the income statement and the balance sheet
Can rebuild the cash flow statement from those two
Notes it needs opening and closing balance sheets
items.a: The income statement and the balance sheet, because I can rebuild the cash flow statement from them. With an opening and a closing balance sheet plus the income statement for the period, I start from net income, add back depreciation and other non-cash charges, and take the change in each working capital item, PP&E, debt and equity to derive operating, investing and financing cash flows. So with those two I effectively have all three. The income statement also gives me revenue growth and margins, which matter most for prospects, while the balance sheet shows leverage and liquidity.
items.t: Choosing the cash flow statement plus one other, which leaves you unable to reconstruct the third.

items.q: Depreciation increases by Rs.10. Walk me through the effect on all three statements.
p: Operating income down 10; net income down 7.5 at 25% tax
CFS: net income -7.5, add back 10, cash up 2.5
BS: PP&E down 10, cash up 2.5, total assets down 7.5
Retained earnings down 7.5, so both sides fall 7.5
items.a: Assuming a 25% tax rate. On the income statement, operating income falls by Rs.10 and, after the tax saving of Rs.2.5, net income falls by Rs.7.5. On the cash flow statement, net income is down Rs.7.5, but depreciation is a non-cash expense so I add back Rs.10, and cash from operations is up Rs.2.5. Net change in cash: up Rs.2.5. On the balance sheet, cash is up Rs.2.5 and PP&E is down Rs.10, so total assets fall by Rs.7.5. On the other side, retained earnings fall by Rs.7.5 because of the lower net income. Both sides are down Rs.7.5, so it balances.
items.t: Saying cash is unchanged because depreciation is non-cash, ignoring the Rs.2.5 tax saving.

items.q: Depreciation involves no cash outflow. So why does a higher depreciation charge change the company's cash balance?
p: Depreciation is tax deductible, so it lowers taxes paid
Rs.10 extra depreciation saves Rs.2.5 of cash at 25%
The cash left earlier, at capex, not at depreciation
Mentions book versus tax depreciation and deferred tax
items.a: Because depreciation reduces taxable income. The charge itself uses no cash; the cash went out when the asset was bought. But it lowers pre-tax profit and therefore the tax bill. With a 25% tax rate, Rs.10 of extra depreciation reduces taxes by Rs.2.5. On the cash flow statement, net income falls by Rs.7.5 and we add back the full Rs.10, so cash rises by Rs.2.5. That Rs.2.5 is the depreciation tax shield. This assumes the depreciation is deductible for tax; where book and tax depreciation differ, the cash effect follows the tax figure and the gap sits in deferred taxes.
items.t: Saying depreciation itself generates cash; only the tax saving does.
items.in: In India the real shield comes from tax depreciation under Income Tax Act WDV block rates, not Schedule II book depreciation; Section 115BAA companies cannot claim additional depreciation.

items.q: Where would you normally find depreciation on the income statement?
p: Often embedded in COGS and operating expenses, not separate
Some companies show D&A as its own line
Always sits above EBIT; full figure is on the CFS
items.a: It depends on how the company presents its expenses. Many companies, especially those reporting by function, embed depreciation within cost of goods sold for manufacturing assets and within SG&A or operating expenses for offices and other assets, so there is no separate line. Others show depreciation and amortisation as a distinct line above operating income. Either way, it sits above EBIT, which is why EBITDA adds it back. If it is buried in other lines, I take the total from the cash flow statement or the notes to get the full D&A figure.
items.t: Assuming a D&A line on the income statement always captures the full charge.
items.in: Ind AS Schedule III requires a by-nature P&L, so Indian companies show Depreciation and amortisation expense as a separate line, making EBITDA easier to compute.

items.q: Accrued compensation rises by Rs.10. What happens across the three statements?
p: Assumes expense recognised now, unpaid (e.g. a bonus)
Expense up 10; net income down 7.5 at 25% tax
CFS: net income -7.5, accrued liability +10, cash up 2.5
BS: cash +2.5; liabilities +10, retained earnings -7.5
items.a: I assume this is compensation expense recognised now but not yet paid, for example a year-end bonus. On the income statement, operating expenses rise by Rs.10, so pre-tax income falls by Rs.10 and net income by Rs.7.5 at a 25% tax rate. On the cash flow statement, net income is down Rs.7.5, but the increase in accrued compensation, a liability, adds Rs.10 to operating cash flow, so cash is up Rs.2.5. On the balance sheet, cash rises Rs.2.5 on the asset side. On the other side, accrued compensation is up Rs.10 and retained earnings are down Rs.7.5, a net Rs.2.5. Both sides up Rs.2.5, so it balances.
items.t: Treating it as a pure balance sheet move with no expense; the accrual exists because an expense was recognised.
items.in: Section 43B allows bonus only when paid, but payment before the return filing due date counts for the same year; only if unpaid then does a deferred tax asset arise.

items.q: Inventory goes up by Rs.10 and the company pays cash for it. What changes on each statement?
p: No income statement impact until the goods are sold
CFS: inventory increase cuts operating cash flow by 10
BS: inventory up 10, cash down 10; total assets unchanged
items.a: Nothing happens on the income statement, because buying inventory is not an expense; it only hits COGS when the goods are sold. On the cash flow statement, the increase in inventory is a use of working capital, so cash from operations falls by Rs.10 and the net change in cash is minus Rs.10. On the balance sheet, cash falls by Rs.10 and inventory rises by Rs.10, so total assets are unchanged. Nothing moves on the liabilities and equity side, so it balances.
items.t: Putting the inventory purchase in investing activities; it is an operating working capital item.

items.q: Why doesn't a change in inventory show up on the income statement?
p: Inventory is an asset until it is sold
Matching: cost moves to COGS when revenue is recognised
Cash effect appears on the CFS as working capital
Exception: write-downs to net realisable value hit the P&L
items.a: Because under accrual accounting, buying inventory just swaps one asset, cash, for another, inventory. The cost only becomes an expense when the goods are sold, at which point it moves into cost of goods sold, matched against the revenue it helped generate. Until then there is no income or expense to record. The cash effect shows up on the cash flow statement as a working capital change instead. The exception is when inventory loses value through obsolescence or damage and must be written down to net realisable value; that write-down does hit the income statement.
items.t: Saying inventory never affects profit; it does, through COGS when sold and through write-downs.
items.in: Under Ind AS 2, LIFO is not permitted; companies use FIFO or weighted average cost and carry inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

items.q: An electronics manufacturer buys Rs.100 crore of new factories, funded entirely with debt. At the start of Year 1, before anything else happens, how do the three statements change?
p: No income statement impact yet
CFS: capex -100 in investing, debt +100 in financing
Net change in cash is zero
BS: PP&E +100, debt +100; balances
items.a: There is no change on the income statement yet, since no depreciation or interest has been incurred. On the cash flow statement, capital expenditure of Rs.100 crore appears as an outflow in investing activities and the new borrowing of Rs.100 crore appears as an inflow in financing activities, so the net change in cash is zero. On the balance sheet, PP&E rises by Rs.100 crore on the asset side and debt rises by Rs.100 crore on the liabilities side, so both sides go up by the same amount and it balances.
items.t: Recording interest or depreciation before any time has passed.
items.in: Under Ind AS 23, interest during construction is capitalised into the asset until the plant is ready for use, so early interest may not hit the P&L.

items.q: Move forward one year to the start of Year 2. No principal is repaid, interest is 10% a year and the factories depreciate at 10% a year. Walk me through the statements.
p: Interest 10 plus depreciation 10: pre-tax income down 20
Net income down 15 at 25% tax
CFS: -15 plus 10 depreciation add-back; cash down 5
BS: cash -5, PP&E -10; retained earnings -15; debt unchanged
items.a: Assuming 25% tax. On the income statement, there is Rs.10 crore of interest expense, 10% of Rs.100 crore of debt, and Rs.10 crore of depreciation, 10% of the factories. Pre-tax income falls by Rs.20 crore and, after a Rs.5 crore tax saving, net income falls by Rs.15 crore. On the cash flow statement, net income is down Rs.15 crore and I add back Rs.10 crore of depreciation, so operating cash flow and net cash are down Rs.5 crore. On the balance sheet, cash is down Rs.5 crore and PP&E is down Rs.10 crore, so assets fall Rs.15 crore. Debt is unchanged, and retained earnings fall Rs.15 crore. Both sides fall Rs.15 crore.
items.t: Adding back interest as if it were non-cash; interest is paid in cash and stays in net income.
items.in: Under Ind AS 7 many Indian companies classify interest paid in financing: CFO becomes +5 crore and financing -10 crore; net cash is still down Rs.5 crore.

items.q: At the start of Year 3 the factories break down and are written down to zero, and the Rs.100 crore loan must be repaid now. Walk me through the three statements.
p: Carrying value after two years of depreciation is 80, not 100
Write-down 80; net income down 60 at 25% tax
CFS: -60 + 80 add-back, -100 repayment; cash down 80
BS: cash -80, PP&E -80; debt -100, retained earnings -60
items.a: After two years of 10% depreciation the factories are carried at Rs.80 crore, so that is the write-down. (Year 2 repeats Year 1: net income down Rs.15 crore, cash down Rs.5 crore.) Income statement: an Rs.80 crore loss cuts pre-tax income by Rs.80 crore and, at 25% tax, net income by Rs.60 crore. Cash flow statement: net income down Rs.60 crore, add back the non-cash write-down of Rs.80 crore, so operating cash is up Rs.20 crore; repaying the loan is a Rs.100 crore financing outflow; net cash is down Rs.80 crore. Balance sheet: cash down Rs.80 crore and PP&E down Rs.80 crore, assets down Rs.160 crore; debt down Rs.100 crore and retained earnings down Rs.60 crore, also Rs.160 crore. It balances.
items.t: Writing down Rs.100 crore and forgetting two years of accumulated depreciation.
items.in: In India an impairment is generally not tax deductible; the tax benefit comes later via tax depreciation or on disposal, so expect a Rs.20 crore deferred tax asset, not cash.

items.q: Different scenario: the same company orders Rs.10 crore of extra component inventory, paid from cash on hand. Nothing has been made or sold yet. What happens on the three statements?
p: No income statement impact; nothing sold yet
CFS: inventory increase reduces operating cash by 10
BS: inventory +10, cash -10; total assets unchanged
If bought on credit, payables rise and cash is unchanged
items.a: Nothing on the income statement, since no goods have been sold and no cost has been expensed. On the cash flow statement, the increase in inventory is a working capital outflow, reducing cash from operations by Rs.10 crore, so net cash is down Rs.10 crore. On the balance sheet, inventory goes up Rs.10 crore and cash goes down Rs.10 crore; total assets are unchanged. Liabilities and equity do not move, so it balances. If instead the supplier gave credit, accounts payable would rise by Rs.10 crore and cash would not change at all.
items.t: Recording the purchase as COGS before any sale has happened.
items.in: Under Ind AS 2, purchase cost includes non-refundable duties but excludes recoverable GST, which sits as an input tax credit asset, not inventory.

items.q: The company now sells those goods for Rs.20 crore, at a cost of Rs.10 crore. Walk me through the three statements.
p: Revenue 20, COGS 10, pre-tax +10, net income +7.5
CFS: +7.5 plus 10 inventory decrease; cash up 17.5
BS: cash +17.5, inventory -10; retained earnings +7.5
States assumptions: cash sale, tax paid in cash
items.a: Assuming a cash sale and 25% tax. Income statement: revenue up Rs.20 crore, COGS up Rs.10 crore, so pre-tax income rises Rs.10 crore and net income Rs.7.5 crore after Rs.2.5 crore of tax. Cash flow statement: net income up Rs.7.5 crore, and the Rs.10 crore decrease in inventory is a source of cash, so operating cash flow and net cash rise Rs.17.5 crore. Balance sheet: cash up Rs.17.5 crore, inventory down Rs.10 crore, so assets up Rs.7.5 crore; retained earnings up Rs.7.5 crore. It balances. If the sale were on credit, receivables would rise Rs.20 crore and cash would fall Rs.2.5 crore for tax, with assets still up Rs.7.5 crore.
items.t: Deducting the Rs.10 crore cost as a cash outflow again; the inventory was paid for earlier.

items.q: Can a company's shareholders' equity be negative? What would that tell you?
p: Yes: accumulated losses exceed the capital raised
Or debt-funded dividends, leveraged recaps or large buybacks
Not automatically distress; check cash flow and debt service
items.a: Yes. The most common reason is sustained losses: if accumulated losses exceed the capital shareholders put in, equity turns negative, which usually signals distress. But it can also happen in healthy companies. A leveraged recapitalisation or a private equity dividend recap pays out large dividends funded with debt, pushing equity below zero. Some large, highly profitable consumer companies abroad have negative book equity because years of buybacks exceeded retained earnings. So negative equity is not a verdict by itself. I would look at what caused it, whether operating cash flow comfortably covers interest and debt maturities, and whether the business is stable enough to carry that leverage.
items.t: Assuming negative equity always means bankruptcy; strong cash generators with heavy buybacks can show it.
items.in: Rare in India via buybacks: Section 68 caps buybacks at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves and post-buyback debt-equity at 2:1. Net worth erosion alarms lenders and rating agencies.

items.q: What is working capital, and how do bankers and lenders use it?
p: Current assets minus current liabilities
Operating version excludes cash and short-term debt
Measures liquidity and cash tied up in operations
Increase in working capital consumes cash; decrease releases it
items.a: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. In valuation and modelling we usually use operating working capital, which excludes cash and short-term debt: receivables plus inventory plus prepaid expenses, less payables, accrued expenses and deferred revenue. It tells you two things. First, liquidity: whether the company can meet obligations due within a year. Second, how much cash is tied up in running the business. What matters for cash flow is the change: if working capital rises, say receivables grow faster than payables, it consumes cash; if it falls, it releases cash. That change feeds directly into free cash flow in a DCF and is a big focus in deals through the working capital peg.
items.t: Including cash and debt in working capital when calculating the change for free cash flow.
items.in: Indian banks fund working capital through cash credit and overdraft limits, with drawing power set by stock and receivable statements submitted by the borrower.

items.q: A company has negative working capital. Is that necessarily a warning sign?
p: Means current liabilities exceed current assets
Often positive: customers pay before suppliers are paid
Examples: FMCG, restaurants, airlines, subscription businesses
Bad if driven by short-term debt or overdue payables
items.a: Not necessarily. Negative working capital means current liabilities exceed current assets. In many strong businesses it signals bargaining power: customers pay upfront or in cash while suppliers give credit. Restaurants, airlines that sell tickets in advance, subscription software and some large FMCG companies run this way, and growth actually releases cash for them. It is a bad sign when it comes from stress: short-term borrowings funding long-term assets, payables stretched because the company cannot pay, or current debt maturities it cannot refinance. So I would check the composition, and whether operating cash flow is healthy, before calling it good or bad.
items.t: Calling negative working capital automatically bad without checking whether it comes from customer advances or debt.
items.in: Indian FMCG leaders such as HUL and Nestle India run negative working capital through distributor terms; contrast infrastructure contractors, where government receivables stretch working capital.

items.q: Banks sometimes take large write-downs on loans or investments. Walk me through a Rs.100 crore asset write-down across the three statements.
p: Pre-tax down 100; net income down 75 at 25% tax
CFS: -75 plus 100 add-back; cash up 25
BS: asset -100, cash +25; retained earnings -75
Flags the tax deductibility assumption and DTA alternative
items.a: Assuming the write-down is tax deductible at 25%. Income statement: a Rs.100 crore loss reduces pre-tax income by Rs.100 crore and net income by Rs.75 crore. Cash flow statement: net income down Rs.75 crore, add back the Rs.100 crore non-cash write-down, so operating cash flow is up Rs.25 crore, the tax saving. Balance sheet: the asset falls Rs.100 crore and cash rises Rs.25 crore, so assets are down Rs.75 crore; retained earnings fall Rs.75 crore. It balances. If the write-down is not deductible for tax yet, which is common, cash does not change and a Rs.25 crore deferred tax asset is created instead.
items.t: Forgetting the tax effect, or assuming cash itself is lost in the write-down.
items.in: Indian banks provide for bad loans under RBI prudential norms, and the tax deduction for provisions is capped, so deferred tax assets build up.

items.q: The government injects Rs.100 crore into a struggling company as a bailout. How does it affect the three statements?
p: Depends on structure: equity, preference shares or debt
Equity: no IS impact; financing inflow 100
BS: cash +100, equity +100
Debt: cash and debt +100; future interest hits the IS
items.a: It depends on how the bailout is structured. If the government buys common equity, there is no income statement impact. On the cash flow statement, Rs.100 crore of equity issuance appears in financing activities, so cash rises Rs.100 crore. On the balance sheet, cash is up Rs.100 crore and share capital plus securities premium are up Rs.100 crore combined, so it balances. If it comes as a loan, cash and debt each rise Rs.100 crore, and interest hits the income statement later. Preference shares need care: redeemable ones with a fixed dividend are usually classified as liabilities under IFRS and Ind AS, so they behave like the loan case. A grant, by contrast, would eventually flow through income.
items.t: Recording the bailout as revenue or income on the income statement.
items.in: India recapitalised PSU banks partly via recap bonds: banks subscribed to government bonds and the government used the money to buy bank equity, so investments and equity both rose.

items.q: A lender agrees to write off Rs.100 crore of the company's debt. Walk me through the effect on the three statements.
p: Gain of 100 on IS; net income up 75 after 25% tax
CFS: +75, subtract non-cash gain of 100; cash down 25
BS: cash -25; debt -100, retained earnings +75
No financing outflow, since nothing is paid to the lender
items.a: Assuming the gain is taxable at 25%. Income statement: the company records a Rs.100 crore gain on extinguishment of debt, so pre-tax income rises Rs.100 crore and net income Rs.75 crore. Cash flow statement: net income is up Rs.75 crore, but the gain is non-cash, so I subtract Rs.100 crore; operating cash flow is down Rs.25 crore, which is the tax paid. Balance sheet: cash down Rs.25 crore on the asset side; debt down Rs.100 crore and retained earnings up Rs.75 crore, a net Rs.25 crore fall. Both sides down Rs.25 crore, so it balances. In practice, many tax regimes exempt or defer tax on such gains.
items.t: Treating the debt reduction as a financing cash outflow; no cash is paid to the lender.
items.in: Under IBC, lender haircuts in resolution plans create large write-back gains; whether a loan waiver is taxable depends on facts (Mahindra & Mahindra, Supreme Court 2018).

items.q: When would a company receive cash from a customer but not book it as revenue?
p: Payment received before goods or services are delivered
Examples: subscriptions, advance tickets, tuition, project advances
Recorded as deferred revenue, a liability
Also deposits and indirect taxes collected for government
items.a: When the customer pays before the company has delivered what it promised. Revenue is recognised when the performance obligation is satisfied, not when cash arrives. Examples: an annual software subscription paid upfront, an airline ticket bought for travel next month, a coaching institute collecting a full year's fees, or advances on a construction or real estate project. Until delivery, that cash sits as deferred revenue, a liability. Other cases include refundable security deposits and indirect taxes collected from customers, which belong to the government and are passed on, not revenue.
items.t: Thinking cash receipt equals revenue; under accrual accounting delivery, not payment, drives recognition.
items.in: GST collected is a liability, not revenue. Real estate developers collect large advances, recognised under Ind AS 115 over time or on completion depending on contract terms.

items.q: If cash received from a customer is not booked as revenue, where does it go and how does it flow through the statements?
p: Cash up; deferred revenue liability up by the same amount
No income statement impact at receipt
Increase in deferred revenue adds to operating cash flow
Recognised monthly as delivered; Rs.1 lakh per month example
items.a: It becomes deferred revenue, also called a contract liability. Say a SaaS company collects Rs.12 lakh upfront for a 12-month subscription. On receipt, cash rises Rs.12 lakh and deferred revenue rises Rs.12 lakh; there is no income statement impact. On the cash flow statement, net income is unchanged, but the increase in deferred revenue adds Rs.12 lakh to operating cash flow. Each month, Rs.1 lakh moves from deferred revenue into revenue as the service is delivered. At that point the income statement shows revenue, and the cash flow statement shows a matching decrease in deferred revenue, so there is no further cash.
items.t: Recording the full Rs.12 lakh as revenue on day one.
items.in: Ind AS 115 calls it a contract liability; advances for services also attract GST at receipt, which is a separate liability from the deferred revenue.

items.q: How is accounts receivable different from deferred revenue?
p: AR: revenue recognised, cash not yet received; an asset
Deferred revenue: cash received, not yet earned; a liability
AR increase uses cash; deferred revenue increase provides cash
items.a: They are mirror images. Accounts receivable arises when the company has delivered and recognised revenue but the customer has not paid yet, so it is an asset: money owed to the company. Deferred revenue arises when the customer has paid but the company has not yet delivered, so it is a liability: an obligation to provide goods or services. When receivables increase, cash lags profit, so operating cash flow falls; when deferred revenue increases, cash runs ahead of profit, so operating cash flow rises. A subscription business with large deferred revenue is effectively financed by its customers.
items.t: Calling deferred revenue an asset because cash has come in.

items.q: Roughly how long does a company take to collect its receivables, and what drives that?
p: Measured by DSO: receivables / revenue x 365
Typically 30 to 60 days, varying by industry
Retail near zero; B2B and government contracts much longer
Rising DSO can flag collection or revenue quality issues
items.a: It is usually measured as days sales outstanding: receivables divided by revenue, times 365. For many businesses it is somewhere in the range of 30 to 60 days, in line with typical credit terms. But it varies a lot. Consumer retail and restaurants collect almost immediately. B2B companies and IT services firms often sit at 60 to 90 days, and infrastructure companies or those selling to government or state utilities can take much longer. What matters is the trend and the peer comparison: a DSO that rises faster than revenue can mean weaker customers, looser credit terms or aggressive revenue recognition.
items.t: Quoting one universal number without saying it depends on industry and customer type.
items.in: Section 43B(h) defers deductions for dues to micro and small enterprises until paid if unpaid beyond MSMED Act limits (15 days, or up to 45 by agreement).

items.q: Explain the difference between cash-basis and accrual accounting.
p: Cash basis: record transactions when cash moves
Accrual: revenue when earned, expenses matched to revenue
Accrual creates receivables, payables, deferred revenue, depreciation
Companies use accrual; cash basis only for very small entities
items.a: Under cash-basis accounting, revenue is recorded when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid. Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when it is earned, that is when the goods or services are delivered, and expenses are recorded in the period they relate to, matched with the revenue they help generate. So accrual accounting needs items like receivables, payables, accrued expenses, deferred revenue and depreciation to bridge the timing gap between cash and profit. Cash basis is simpler and used by very small businesses or individuals, but accrual gives a truer picture of performance, which is why companies use it, and why we need a cash flow statement alongside the income statement.
items.t: Saying accrual accounting ignores cash; the cash flow statement exists precisely to reconcile the two.
items.in: Section 128 of the Companies Act requires every company to keep books on accrual basis under double entry, so cash basis is not an option for Indian companies.

items.q: A customer buys a Rs.50,000 TV from an electronics retailer and pays by credit card. How is this recorded under cash-basis versus accrual accounting?
p: Cash basis: revenue only when the card network settles cash
Accrual: revenue at sale, receivable from the card acquirer
Receivable turns into cash on settlement, no further P&L impact
Card fee (MDR) expensed; TV cost moves to COGS
items.a: Under cash basis, the retailer records nothing at the point of sale, because the card payment is not cash in hand yet. Revenue is recorded only when the acquiring bank settles the money into the retailer's account, typically a day or two later. Under accrual accounting, the retailer records Rs.50,000 of revenue at the moment of sale, because the TV has been delivered, along with a receivable from the card acquirer. When settlement arrives, the receivable turns into cash with no further income statement impact. The merchant discount rate the bank keeps is recorded as an expense, and the cost of the TV moves from inventory to COGS at the sale.
items.t: Treating the receivable as owed by the customer; it is owed by the card network or acquiring bank.
items.in: Revenue excludes GST: at 18% GST on a Rs.50,000 invoice, revenue is about Rs.42,373 and GST payable about Rs.7,627.

items.q: How do you decide whether a purchase should be capitalised or expensed?
p: Capitalise if the benefit extends beyond one year
Expense items consumed within the year
Capitalised cost is depreciated or amortised over useful life
Aggressive capitalisation inflates near-term EBITDA and profit
items.a: The test is whether the spending creates an asset with benefits beyond the current year. Buying machinery, building a factory or acquiring multi-year software licences is capitalised: it goes on the balance sheet as PP&E or intangibles and is depreciated or amortised over its useful life, so the cost is matched to the years it helps generate revenue. Items consumed within the year, like salaries, rent, utilities and routine repairs, are expensed immediately. Companies also set materiality thresholds, so small items are expensed. As an analyst, I watch for aggressive capitalisation, since it inflates current EBITDA and profit while pushing the cost into future depreciation.
items.t: Forgetting that capitalised spending still hits cash immediately, through capex in investing activities.
items.in: Under Ind AS 38, development costs are capitalised once technical feasibility and other criteria are met, unlike US GAAP where most R&D is expensed; check this in pharma and tech.

items.q: Why do companies report adjusted or non-GAAP earnings alongside their statutory numbers?
p: Strips out non-recurring or non-cash items for comparability
Examples: restructuring, impairments, SBC, acquisition amortisation
Used in comps and valuation multiples
Risk of management bias; reconcile to reported figures
items.a: Statutory earnings include items that can distort the picture of ongoing performance: restructuring charges, impairments, gains or losses on asset sales, acquisition-related amortisation and often stock-based compensation. Companies report adjusted earnings and adjusted EBITDA to show what they see as underlying, recurring profitability, which makes year-on-year and peer comparisons cleaner. Analysts and bankers use adjusted figures for comps and valuation multiples too. The catch is that management chooses the adjustments, and some recurring costs get labelled as one-offs every year. So I always reconcile adjusted numbers back to reported figures and question any adjustment that keeps reappearing.
items.t: Accepting management's adjustments blindly, especially recurring one-off charges or stock-based compensation.
items.in: Indian results show Exceptional items as a separate Schedule III line, and EBITDA is a voluntary disclosure, so adjusted figures need reconciling to the Ind AS P&L.

items.q: A company has reported positive EBITDA every year for a decade, yet it has just gone bankrupt. How is that possible?
p: EBITDA ignores interest, principal, capex, tax and working capital
Heavy debt: interest and maturities exceed cash generation
Capex or working capital can absorb all the cash
Liquidity crunch: unable to refinance maturing debt
items.a: EBITDA is not cash flow, and it ignores several things that can sink a company. First, debt: if the company is heavily leveraged, interest and principal repayments can exceed its cash generation, and a refinancing failure at maturity triggers default even when operations are fine. Second, capex: a capital-intensive business can show positive EBITDA while spending more than that on maintaining its assets. Third, working capital: rising receivables or inventory can absorb all the cash. Taxes, lease payments and one-off liabilities like litigation also sit below EBITDA. So a company can look profitable at the EBITDA level and still run out of cash.
items.t: Treating EBITDA as a proxy for cash flow without deducting capex, interest and working capital.
items.in: Many Indian IBC cases in power, steel and infrastructure had positive EBITDA but unsustainable debt; a default of just Rs.1 crore lets a financial creditor file under Section 7.

items.q: Goodwill usually sits unchanged on the balance sheet. Why would it be impaired, and what does an impairment mean?
p: Goodwill not amortised; tested at least annually
Impaired when recoverable value falls below carrying value
Signals the acquirer overpaid
Rs.100 crore impairment: NI -100 if non-deductible; cash unchanged
items.a: Goodwill is the excess of purchase price over the fair value of net identifiable assets acquired. It is not amortised; instead it is tested at least annually. If the acquired business underperforms, through lost customers, falling margins or a market downturn, its recoverable value can drop below its carrying value including goodwill, and the excess is written off. Essentially it admits the buyer overpaid. Take a Rs.100 crore impairment: pre-tax and net income fall Rs.100 crore, since it is usually not tax deductible; it is added back on the cash flow statement, so cash is unchanged; goodwill and retained earnings both fall Rs.100 crore. If deductible, net income would fall Rs.75 crore and cash rise Rs.25 crore.
items.t: Thinking goodwill can be written back up later; goodwill impairments are never reversed.
items.in: Ind AS 36 tests goodwill at cash-generating unit level and bans reversal. For tax, goodwill is not depreciable since Finance Act 2021, so impairment gives no tax shield.

items.q: In what situations would goodwill on a company's balance sheet go up?
p: New acquisitions paid above fair value of net assets
Measurement-period adjustments to purchase price allocation
Currency translation of foreign subsidiaries' goodwill
Internally generated goodwill is never recognised
items.a: Mainly when the company makes a new acquisition and pays more than the fair value of the target's identifiable net assets; that excess is added to goodwill. Goodwill can also change when the acquirer finalises the purchase price allocation during the measurement period, up to a year after the deal, for example if acquired assets turn out to be worth less, which pushes goodwill up. For goodwill sitting in foreign subsidiaries, currency movements can increase the reported rupee amount. What does not increase goodwill: organic growth, brand building or a rising share price. Internally generated goodwill is never recognised, and impaired goodwill cannot be written back.
items.t: Saying goodwill rises when the company's own brand or market value grows.
items.in: Unlike IFRS, Ind AS 103 sends a bargain purchase gain to OCI and then capital reserve, or directly to capital reserve, not to profit.

items.q: How does book accounting for financial reporting differ from accounting for tax purposes?
p: Book follows accounting standards; tax follows tax law
Different depreciation methods and useful lives
Temporary differences create deferred tax; permanent ones do not
Book tax expense differs from cash taxes paid
items.a: Financial reporting follows accounting standards and aims to show economic performance to investors, while tax accounting follows tax law and determines the tax actually payable. The two differ in timing and scope. The classic example is depreciation: companies usually use straight-line depreciation in their books but accelerated depreciation for tax, so taxable income is lower than book income in early years. Other differences include provisions deductible only when paid, and items never deductible, like certain penalties. Timing differences create deferred tax assets and liabilities; permanent differences change the effective tax rate. That is why book tax expense on the income statement often differs from cash tax paid.
items.t: Assuming the tax expense on the income statement equals the cash tax paid.
items.in: Indian books follow Ind AS with Schedule II useful lives; tax follows Income Tax Act WDV blocks. Under Section 115BAA the effective rate is about 25.17%, with no MAT.

items.q: What are deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities, and how do they arise?
p: Arise from temporary book-tax differences that reverse
DTL: pay less tax now, more later (accelerated tax depreciation)
DTA: pay more now, less later (losses, provisions)
Example: Rs.10 crore timing gap at 25% gives Rs.2.5 crore
items.a: They come from temporary differences between book income and taxable income that reverse over time. A deferred tax liability arises when a company pays less tax today than its book tax expense implies, and will pay more later. Example: book depreciation of Rs.10 crore but tax depreciation of Rs.20 crore. Taxable income is Rs.10 crore lower, so at 25% cash tax is Rs.2.5 crore lower, and a Rs.2.5 crore DTL is recorded; book tax expense is unchanged and cash is Rs.2.5 crore higher. A deferred tax asset is the reverse: the company pays more tax now and less later, for example from carried-forward losses or provisions deductible only when paid. Changes in DTL or DTA are non-cash adjustments on the cash flow statement.
items.t: Getting the direction wrong: higher tax depreciation than book creates a liability, not an asset.
items.in: Under Ind AS 12, DTAs on losses need convincing evidence of future taxable profit; companies moving to Section 115BAA remeasured deferred taxes and often wrote off MAT credit.

items.q: Walk me through how you would build a revenue model for a company.
p: Bottom-up: volume times price, by segment
Top-down: market size times market share
Uses company-specific drivers: stores, utilisation, customers
Sanity-checks against history, guidance and consensus
items.a: I start by understanding how the company actually makes money and pick its true drivers. The bottom-up approach builds revenue from units: for a quick service restaurant chain, number of stores times revenue per store, with new openings and same-store sales growth; for a cement company, capacity times utilisation times realisation per tonne; for a SaaS firm, customers times average revenue per customer, with churn and upsell. The top-down approach takes market size and applies a market share assumption. I usually build bottom-up and cross-check top-down, then sanity-check the result against historical growth, management guidance and broker estimates, and run sensitivities on the key drivers.
items.t: Just growing total revenue at a flat percentage without identifying the underlying drivers.

items.q: Walk me through how you would build an expense model for a company.
p: Splits fixed versus variable costs
Variable costs as % of revenue or cost per unit
Employee costs: headcount times cost per head, with increments
D&A from the PP&E schedule, interest from the debt schedule
items.a: I separate costs by behaviour. Variable costs like raw materials and freight are tied to the revenue drivers, either as a percentage of revenue or as cost per unit times volume, adjusted for commodity price views. Employee costs I build from headcount times cost per employee, with annual increments and hiring linked to growth; in an IT services firm, that is the biggest line, tied to utilisation and pricing. Fixed overheads like rent and admin grow with inflation plus step-ups for new capacity. Depreciation comes from the PP&E schedule, driven by capex, and interest from the debt schedule. Finally I check implied margins against history and peers so operating leverage looks sensible.
items.t: Projecting every expense as a flat percentage of revenue, which hides operating leverage.
items.in: Indian P&Ls under Schedule III are by nature: cost of materials, employee benefits, finance costs, D&A, other expenses, so models usually follow those lines rather than COGS and SG&A.

items.q: Suppose the company's disclosures are too thin to build these revenue and expense models properly. What would you do?
p: Uses peers' disclosures and industry benchmarks as proxies
Mines earnings calls, investor presentations, management guidance
Industry reports, expert calls, channel checks
Simplifies assumptions and runs sensitivities
items.a: I would fill the gaps from other sources and be transparent about assumptions. First, look at peers that disclose more and use their metrics as proxies, such as revenue per store or cost per employee. Second, mine everything the company says outside statutory filings: earnings call transcripts, investor presentations, analyst meets and management guidance. Third, use industry reports, trade data, expert calls and broker research. If none of that works, I simplify: model revenue at the segment or total level with growth tied to market growth, use margins rather than detailed cost lines, and run sensitivities on the key assumptions so the client sees the range.
items.t: Inventing precise-looking drivers with no source instead of simplifying and stating assumptions.
items.in: DRHPs are gold mines: they include commissioned industry reports (CRISIL, Redseer, Technopak). For private Indian companies, MCA filings give audited financials and shareholding.

items.q: Walk me through the main components of shareholders' equity.
p: Common stock at par plus APIC: capital raised from shares
Retained earnings: cumulative net income less dividends
Treasury stock reduces equity
Mentions AOCI and non-controlling interest
items.a: There are a few main pieces. Common stock records the par or face value of shares issued, and additional paid-in capital records what investors paid above par; together they are the capital raised from shareholders. Retained earnings is the cumulative net income the company has kept rather than paid out as dividends. Treasury stock, where it exists, is a negative item for shares bought back and held. Accumulated other comprehensive income captures gains and losses that bypass the income statement, such as currency translation and certain investment revaluations. In consolidated accounts, non-controlling interest shows the portion of subsidiaries owned by outside shareholders, presented within equity.
items.t: Confusing book equity with market capitalisation; book equity is an accounting residual.
items.in: Ind AS splits equity into Equity share capital and Other equity (securities premium, retained earnings, general reserve, OCI reserves). Bought-back shares are extinguished; treasury shares arise only via ESOP trusts.

items.q: What flows into retained earnings over a period?
p: Opening balance plus net income less dividends
Policy changes, error corrections, some buybacks hit it directly
Most OCI and share issuances do not flow into it
items.a: Retained earnings rolls forward simply: opening balance, plus net income for the period, less dividends declared. If opening retained earnings is Rs.500 crore, net income is Rs.100 crore and dividends are Rs.30 crore, closing retained earnings is Rs.570 crore. A net loss reduces it. A few other items can hit it directly: retrospective adjustments from accounting policy changes or error corrections, and the portion of a buyback or share retirement charged to retained earnings. Most other comprehensive income items sit in separate reserves, though Indian companies often show actuarial remeasurements within retained earnings. Capital raised goes to share capital and premium, not here.
items.t: Adding share issuance proceeds or all OCI to retained earnings.
items.in: Dividends are now taxed in shareholders' hands (DDT abolished in 2020). Buybacks out of free reserves require a transfer to a capital redemption reserve under Section 69.

items.q: What flows into additional paid-in capital, or securities premium as it is called in India?
p: Issue price above par: 10 lakh shares, Rs.10 face, Rs.200 price
Share capital +1 crore, premium +19 crore, cash +20 crore
Stock-based compensation expense credited to APIC or reserve
Option exercise proceeds; equity issue costs deducted
items.a: APIC captures money from shareholders above the par value of shares. If a company issues 10 lakh shares of face value Rs.10 at Rs.200, share capital rises by Rs.1 crore and APIC by Rs.19 crore, with cash up Rs.20 crore. It also moves with stock-based compensation: the expense recognised on the income statement is credited to APIC or a share options reserve, so total equity is unchanged while retained earnings fall through lower net income. When employees exercise options, the exercise price received and the related reserve move into share capital and APIC. Issue costs on equity raises are deducted from it.
items.t: Thinking APIC moves with the share price after issuance; it only reflects issue transactions.
items.in: Section 52 limits securities premium use to bonus shares, issue expenses, redemption premium or buybacks; Ind AS 102 ESOP cost goes to a share options outstanding account.

items.q: What is the statement of shareholders' equity, and why is it useful?
p: Reconciles opening to closing balance of each equity component
Shows net income, dividends, issuances, buybacks, SBC, OCI
Helps build the equity roll-forward and spot dilution
items.a: It reconciles the opening and closing balance of each component of equity over the period: share capital, APIC, retained earnings, treasury stock, other comprehensive income and non-controlling interest. You can see net income added, dividends paid, shares issued for cash or acquisitions, buybacks, stock-based compensation and currency translation movements. It is useful because the balance sheet only shows end-of-period totals; this statement explains why equity changed. In modelling, it helps build the equity roll-forward, and in analysis it reveals capital allocation choices, dilution from share issuance and how much value is being returned to shareholders.
items.t: Dismissing it as unimportant; it is where buybacks, dilution and OCI movements become visible.
items.in: Ind AS 1 requires a full Statement of Changes in Equity, usually split between Equity share capital and each reserve within Other equity.

items.q: Which non-recurring items would you typically add back to EBIT or EBITDA when normalising a company's earnings?
p: Restructuring and severance charges
Impairments and one-off asset or inventory write-downs
Legal settlements, M&A and transaction costs
Adjusts both ways: deducts one-off gains like asset sale profits
items.a: The aim is to show sustainable operating profit, so I adjust for items that will not repeat. Common add-backs are restructuring and severance charges, impairments of goodwill or other assets, inventory write-downs from a one-off event, legal settlements and litigation costs, acquisition and transaction fees, and losses on the sale of assets or businesses. Adjustments run both ways: one-off gains, such as profit on selling land or an insurance recovery, should be deducted. I also check that impairments are not double counted with D&A in EBITDA. The key test is whether it genuinely will not recur; if the company restructures every year, that is a cost of doing business.
items.t: Only adding back one-off losses and ignoring one-off gains that inflate earnings.
items.in: Start with Schedule III Exceptional items, but also scan Other income (treasury gains, one-off interest) and the notes; VRS costs and fair value gains are common Indian adjustments.

items.q: In a three-statement model, how would you project balance sheet items like receivables and accrued expenses?
p: Receivables via DSO on revenue
Inventory and payables via days on COGS
Accrued expenses as % of operating expenses
Example: Rs.365 crore revenue at 45 DSO gives Rs.45 crore
items.a: I tie each working capital item to the income statement line that drives it, using historical ratios. Receivables are projected with days sales outstanding: revenue divided by 365, times DSO. So with Rs.365 crore of revenue and a 45-day DSO, receivables are Rs.45 crore. Inventory uses days inventory on COGS, and payables use days payable on COGS or purchases. Accrued expenses are usually a percentage of operating expenses, and prepaid expenses a percentage of revenue or opex. Deferred revenue is projected as a percentage of revenue or bookings. I hold ratios near historical averages unless there is a reason to change them, and the year-on-year changes feed the cash flow statement.
items.t: Growing each balance at a flat rate unlinked to the revenue or cost line that drives it.

items.q: How should depreciation and capital expenditure be projected in a model?
p: Capex from guidance or % of revenue; maintenance vs growth
PP&E roll-forward: opening plus capex less depreciation
Depreciation as % of PP&E or a capex waterfall
Mature firms: capex near depreciation; growth firms: above it
items.a: Capex usually comes from management guidance where available; otherwise as a percentage of revenue based on history, split between maintenance and growth capex for capacity-driven businesses like cement or power. Depreciation is driven by the asset base: either as a percentage of opening gross or net PP&E, or with a waterfall schedule depreciating each year's capex over its useful life. The PP&E roll-forward ties it together: opening PP&E plus capex less depreciation equals closing PP&E. Sanity checks: a mature business should have capex roughly in line with depreciation, a growing one higher, and depreciation as a share of revenue should not drift wildly.
items.t: Cutting capex in outer years while depreciation stays high, inflating terminal free cash flow.
items.in: Book depreciation follows Schedule II useful lives, usually straight-line; tax depreciation uses Income Tax Act WDV block rates, so model them separately for cash tax and deferred tax.

items.q: How do net operating losses affect a company's three financial statements?
p: NOLs offset future taxable income, cutting cash taxes
Recognised as a DTA if future profits are probable
Using NOL: book tax 10, cash tax 0, DTA falls 10
Rs.40 crore profit: NI 30, cash +40, DTA -10
items.a: A net operating loss can be carried forward to offset future taxable income. Assume Rs.100 crore of losses, already recognised as a Rs.25 crore deferred tax asset at 25%, and Rs.40 crore of pre-tax profit this year, all received in cash. Income statement: book tax expense is still Rs.10 crore, so net income is Rs.30 crore, but cash tax is zero. Cash flow statement: net income Rs.30 crore plus the Rs.10 crore decrease in the DTA, so operating cash flow is Rs.40 crore. Balance sheet: cash up Rs.40 crore, DTA down Rs.10 crore, so assets up Rs.30 crore, matched by retained earnings up Rs.30 crore. If no DTA was recognised, tax expense itself would be zero.
items.t: Cutting book tax expense when a DTA was already recognised; the saving shows up in cash, not net income.
items.in: Business losses carry forward 8 years, unabsorbed depreciation indefinitely. Section 79 forfeits losses of closely held companies on a change of over 49% in voting ownership, relevant in acquisitions.

items.q: What is the difference between finance (capital) leases and operating leases?
p: Finance lease transfers substantially all risks and rewards
Tests: ownership transfer, bargain option, most of life, 90% PV
US GAAP: both on balance sheet as ROU asset and liability
Finance: depreciation plus interest; operating: single straight-line cost
items.a: A finance or capital lease is effectively a financed purchase: the lessee gets substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset. The classic US tests are ownership transferring at the end, a bargain purchase option, a lease term covering most of the asset's life, often taken as 75%, or present value of payments of at least 90% of fair value. Under current US GAAP both types go on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. The difference is in the income statement: a finance lease shows depreciation plus interest, front-loaded, while an operating lease shows a single straight-line lease cost within operating expenses, so EBITDA is lower.
items.t: Saying operating leases are still off-balance sheet; that changed under ASC 842 and IFRS 16.
items.in: Ind AS 116 has one lessee model: nearly all leases become ROU depreciation plus interest, lifting EBITDA. Principal repayments move to financing cash flow, flattering CFO for retailers and airlines.

items.q: Why might the D&A figure on the income statement not match the D&A on the cash flow statement?
p: D&A often embedded in COGS and opex on the IS
CFS adds back the full non-cash charge
CFS may include financing fee amortisation or other items
Uses CFS or notes figure, cleaned, for EBITDA
items.a: Usually because the income statement does not show all of it as one line. Many companies allocate depreciation into cost of goods sold and operating expenses, so the separate D&A line, if any, captures only part of the charge, while the cash flow statement adds back the full non-cash amount. The cash flow figure can also include items that are not operating D&A, such as amortisation of debt issuance costs, which sits in interest expense, or amortisation of acquired intangibles shown separately. Depreciation capitalised into inventory or construction work also creates timing differences. For EBITDA, I take the cash flow or notes figure and strip out anything financing-related.
items.t: Calculating EBITDA from a partial income statement D&A line and understating it.
items.in: Schedule III's by-nature P&L shows D&A separately, so gaps are smaller in India; remaining differences usually come from depreciation capitalised into capital work-in-progress or inventory.

items.q: Why do bankers look at both enterprise value and equity value when valuing a company?
p: EV values core operations, available to all capital providers
Equity value is the claim of common shareholders only
EV is capital-structure neutral, so peers with different leverage compare cleanly
Equity value converts into a per-share price or offer price
items.a: They answer different questions. Enterprise value is what the core operating business is worth to everyone who funds it: lenders, preference holders, minority holders and common shareholders. Because it ignores how the business is financed, I can compare two companies with very different debt levels on the same footing. Equity value is the slice left for common shareholders once the other claims are settled, and that is what turns into a share price. So in practice I value the operations at the EV level, then walk across the bridge, adjusting for debt, cash and other claims, to get equity value and a value per share.
items.t: Calling one measure 'better'; they serve different purposes and a valuation needs both.

items.q: When you evaluate the acquisition of a company, do you focus more on enterprise value or equity value?
p: Equity value is what is paid to selling shareholders
EV reflects the true economic cost, since the buyer inherits debt and cash
Private deals are priced cash-free, debt-free, i.e. on an EV basis
Multiples like EV/EBITDA anchor the negotiation
items.a: Enterprise value is the better measure of what the business really costs. If I buy the shares, I also take on the target's debt, which I usually have to refinance or repay at change of control, and I get its cash, which offsets that. So the economic price is EV. That is also why private deals are usually agreed cash-free, debt-free: the headline is an EV, often set as a multiple of EBITDA, and the equity cheque is derived from it after net debt and working capital adjustments. Equity value still matters because it is what shareholders actually receive and, for a listed target, what the per-share offer price is based on.
items.t: Saying only equity value matters because 'that is the purchase price', ignoring assumed debt.
