items.in: Buying 25% or more of a listed Indian company triggers a SEBI SAST open offer priced per share, so equity value sets that cheque.

items.q: What is the formula for enterprise value?
p: Starts from diluted equity value, not basic market cap
Adds debt, preferred stock and minority (non-controlling) interest
Subtracts cash and non-operating assets such as investments and associates
Explains the logic: claims added, non-core assets removed
items.a: Enterprise value equals diluted equity value, plus total debt, plus preferred stock, plus minority interest, minus cash and cash equivalents. A fuller version also subtracts other non-operating assets, such as investments in associates or surplus land, and adds other debt-like items, such as lease liabilities or unfunded pension obligations, when the metric you divide by excludes them. The logic is simple: add every claim on the operating business other than common equity, and remove anything the company owns that does not drive its operating earnings, so the numerator matches operating metrics like EBITDA.
items.t: Using basic shares instead of diluted shares, or forgetting to subtract non-operating assets like associates.
items.in: Ind AS calls minority interest non-controlling interest. Add Ind AS 116 lease liabilities to debt when EBITDA is post-Ind AS 116 (lease rent excluded).

items.q: Why do you add minority interest when you calculate enterprise value?
p: Parent consolidates 100% of a majority-owned subsidiary's revenue and EBITDA
Equity value only reflects the parent's share of that subsidiary
Adding minority interest makes numerator and denominator consistent
Ideally use market value of minority stake if subsidiary is listed
items.a: It is a consistency fix. If a company owns, say, 80% of a subsidiary, accounting rules make it consolidate 100% of that subsidiary's revenue and EBITDA. But the parent's equity value only captures the 80% it owns. If I then divide EV by consolidated EBITDA, the numerator covers 80% of the subsidiary while the denominator covers 100%, so the multiple looks artificially low. Adding minority interest puts the 20% owned by outsiders back into EV, so both sides of the multiple describe the whole subsidiary. Book value is the default, but if the subsidiary is listed, the market value of the outside stake is more accurate.
items.t: Saying it is added because minority holders are 'owed money' like lenders; the real reason is matching consolidated metrics.
items.in: Ind AS calls it non-controlling interest. Listed subsidiaries are common in Indian groups (Bajaj Finserv consolidates Bajaj Finance), so value NCI at market, not book.

items.q: How do you calculate a company's fully diluted share count?
p: Starts with latest basic shares outstanding, not weighted average from EPS
Adds in-the-money options and warrants using the treasury stock method
Adds RSUs and in-the-money convertibles on an if-converted basis
Out-of-the-money instruments are excluded
items.a: Start with the latest basic shares outstanding from the most recent filing, not the weighted average used in EPS. Then add dilution from securities that would convert into shares. For in-the-money options and warrants, use the treasury stock method: assume they are exercised, the company collects the exercise price, and uses that cash to buy back shares at the current price; only the net new shares are added. Restricted stock units are added in full since there is no exercise price. In-the-money convertibles are added on an if-converted basis. Anything out of the money is ignored. In an M&A context, use the offer price rather than the market price for these tests.
items.t: Using the weighted average share count from the income statement instead of the latest outstanding figure.
items.in: Take basic shares from the latest exchange shareholding pattern and option counts and exercise prices from the annual report's ESOP disclosures under SEBI SBEB Regulations.

items.q: A company has 100 shares at Rs.10 each and 10 options with an exercise price of Rs.5. What is its fully diluted equity value?
p: Options are in the money: Rs.5 strike below Rs.10 price
Exercise proceeds of Rs.50 buy back 5 shares
Net new shares are 5, so diluted shares are 105
Fully diluted equity value is Rs.1,050
items.a: The options are in the money because the Rs.5 exercise price is below the Rs.10 share price, so I include them using the treasury stock method. All 10 options are exercised, creating 10 new shares, and the company receives 10 times Rs.5, which is Rs.50. It uses that Rs.50 to repurchase shares at Rs.10, retiring 5 shares. Net new shares are 10 minus 5, which is 5. Diluted shares are 100 plus 5, so 105, and fully diluted equity value is 105 times Rs.10, which is Rs.1,050.
items.t: Adding all 10 option shares to get Rs.1,100 and forgetting the buyback funded by exercise proceeds.

items.q: Same company: 100 shares at Rs.10, but the 10 options now have an exercise price of Rs.15. What is its fully diluted equity value?
p: Options are out of the money: Rs.15 strike above Rs.10 price
Out-of-the-money options are excluded from diluted shares
Diluted shares stay at 100
Fully diluted equity value is Rs.1,000
items.a: Here the exercise price of Rs.15 is above the current share price of Rs.10, so the options are out of the money. No rational holder would pay Rs.15 for a share worth Rs.10, so they would not be exercised today and I exclude them from the diluted share count. Diluted shares stay at 100, and fully diluted equity value is 100 times Rs.10, which is Rs.1,000. If this were an acquisition at an offer price above Rs.15, I would rerun the test at the offer price, since the options could then be in the money.
items.t: Running the treasury stock method mechanically and getting negative net shares, or counting the options anyway.

items.q: Why do you subtract cash when calculating enterprise value, and is that always appropriate?
p: Cash is a non-operating asset; interest income sits outside EBITDA
An acquirer effectively gets the cash back, lowering the net cost
Only excess cash should be subtracted, not minimum operating cash
Trapped, restricted or customer cash should not be subtracted
items.a: EV is meant to value the operating business, and cash is not an operating asset: the income it earns sits below EBITDA. A buyer who acquires the company also acquires its cash and can use it to repay debt or return it to itself, so the net cost of the business is lower by that amount. It is not always accurate, though. Only truly excess cash should come off. Cash needed to run day-to-day working capital, cash trapped in overseas subsidiaries or blocked by regulation, restricted cash such as margin deposits, and customer money held as float are not freely available, so subtracting them overstates the cash and understates EV.
items.t: Subtracting the entire cash balance without asking whether the business needs some of it to operate.
items.in: Check Ind AS 'other bank balances': Indian companies often hold earmarked cash (unpaid dividend accounts, margin money, escrow, lien-marked deposits) that is not free cash.

items.q: Is it always correct to simply add the company's debt to equity value when calculating enterprise value?
p: Usually yes: a buyer must repay or assume the debt
Use market value if debt trades well below par, e.g. distress
Include debt-like items: leases, pensions, deferred consideration, if consistent with EBITDA
For banks and NBFCs, debt is operating, so EV is not used
items.a: Usually yes, because the debt is a claim the buyer must repay or assume. But a few refinements matter. First, if the debt trades well below par, as in distress, its market value is a better measure of the claim. Second, reported borrowings are not the whole story: lease liabilities, unfunded pensions, deferred acquisition payments and some provisions behave like debt and should be added if the metric you divide by excludes their cost. Third, consistency: if EBITDA already deducts lease rent, do not also add lease liabilities. Finally, for banks and lenders, debt is raw material rather than financing, so EV is not a meaningful measure there at all.
items.t: Treating only long-term borrowings as debt and missing short-term facilities or debt-like items.
items.in: Indian mid-caps rely on working capital lines (cash credit, overdraft, buyer's credit, acceptances); treat them as debt even when acceptances sit inside trade payables.

items.q: Can a company have a negative enterprise value? What would that tell you?
p: Yes, when cash exceeds equity value plus debt and other claims
Market values the operating business below zero
Signals expected cash burn, doubt the cash is real, or poor governance
Rarely a free lunch; investigate why before calling it cheap
items.a: Yes. If a company's cash and non-operating assets exceed its market cap plus debt and other claims, the formula gives a negative EV. That means the market is valuing the operating business at less than zero: it expects the business to burn through its cash with operating losses, or it doubts the cash is genuinely available to shareholders, for example because it is trapped, tied up in litigation or controlled by management that will not return it. It shows up in distressed small caps and cash-rich biotech or tech companies with failing products. In theory it looks like buying the cash at a discount, but usually the market is flagging a real problem.
items.t: Concluding a negative EV is automatically a bargain without asking why the market distrusts the cash.
items.in: Seen in some Indian promoter-controlled small caps with large reported cash; the market discounts cash it doubts will reach minority shareholders.

items.q: Can a company have a negative equity value? What would that mean?
p: Market equity value cannot go below zero due to limited liability
Book shareholders' equity can be negative: losses, buybacks, recaps
Implied equity value from EV minus net debt can be negative
Negative implied equity means equity is worthless except option value
items.a: Market equity value cannot be negative, because shares cannot trade below zero and shareholders' liability is limited to what they invested. Book shareholders' equity can be negative, from years of accumulated losses or from large dividends and buybacks funded with debt. In a valuation, though, the implied equity value from subtracting net debt and other claims from EV can come out negative. That means the debt and other claims exceed the value of the business, so equity is worth nothing on fundamentals. The shares may still trade above zero because of option value: the chance of a turnaround before the debt falls due.
items.t: Confusing negative book equity with a negative market value; the two are very different.
items.in: Under IBC, when implied equity is negative, resolution plans typically extinguish or heavily dilute existing shareholders while creditors take haircuts.

items.q: Why is preferred stock added when moving from equity value to enterprise value?
p: Preferred ranks ahead of common shareholders
Pays a fixed dividend, behaving more like debt than equity
Usually must be redeemed or paid out in an acquisition
It is a funding source whose returns come from pre-dividend profits
items.a: Preferred stock is a claim on the business that ranks ahead of common shareholders. It typically carries a fixed dividend and a liquidation preference or redemption amount, so economically it behaves much more like debt than common equity. In an acquisition, the buyer normally has to pay out or redeem the preferred holders. Since EV represents the value available to all capital providers, and the profits that pay preferred dividends sit within EBITDA, it has to be added in. The exception is preferred that is convertible and in the money; then you treat it as converted into common shares instead, not both.
items.t: Adding convertible preferred as preferred and also counting its conversion shares in diluted equity.
items.in: Companies Act 2013 bans irredeemable preference shares, so Indian preference capital is redeemable. Startup CCPS normally go into the diluted share count on conversion.

items.q: How do you treat convertible bonds when calculating enterprise value?
p: Test whether share price exceeds the conversion price
In the money: add conversion shares to diluted shares, not debt
Out of the money: treat the bond as debt
Never count the same bond as both debt and shares
items.a: It depends on whether they are in the money. Compare the current share price, or offer price in a deal, with the conversion price. If the share price is higher, holders would convert, so I add the shares they would receive to the diluted share count and do not count the bond as debt. If the share price is below the conversion price, holders would rather take repayment, so the bond stays in debt at its face value. The key point is consistency: a convertible is either equity or debt in the bridge, never both, or you double count it.
items.t: Counting an in-the-money convertible as debt while also adding its conversion shares.
items.in: Indian issuers use FCCBs and compulsorily convertible debentures (CCDs). CCDs must convert, so they usually go into diluted shares; FCCBs follow the in-the-money test.

items.q: A company has 1 million shares at Rs.100 each and Rs.10 million of convertible bonds, Rs.1,000 par, conversion price Rs.50. What are diluted shares outstanding?
p: Convertible is in the money: Rs.100 price above Rs.50 conversion price
10,000 bonds, each converting into 20 shares
200,000 new shares; diluted shares are 1.2 million
Bonds removed from debt in the EV bridge
items.a: First check if conversion makes sense: the share price of Rs.100 is above the Rs.50 conversion price, so holders convert. Number of bonds is Rs.10 million divided by Rs.1,000 par, which is 10,000 bonds. Each bond converts into Rs.1,000 divided by Rs.50, which is 20 shares. So conversion creates 10,000 times 20, or 200,000 new shares. Equivalently, Rs.10 million divided by Rs.50 gives 200,000. Diluted shares are 1 million plus 200,000, which is 1.2 million, and diluted equity value is Rs.120 million. Since the bonds are treated as converted, I would not also include the Rs.10 million as debt in enterprise value.
items.t: Dividing Rs.10 million by the Rs.100 share price instead of the Rs.50 conversion price, giving 100,000 shares.

items.q: What is the difference between equity value and shareholders' equity?
p: Equity value is market value: share price times diluted shares
Shareholders' equity is book value from the balance sheet
Market value is forward-looking; book value is historical
Ratio of the two is price-to-book; book equity can be negative
items.a: Equity value is a market measure: share price times diluted shares, reflecting what investors think the company's future cash flows are worth. Shareholders' equity is an accounting measure from the balance sheet: share capital plus retained earnings and other reserves, essentially historical capital put in and profits kept. For a healthy, growing company equity value is usually well above book because the market prices in future earnings and intangibles not on the balance sheet. The two can diverge sharply: book equity can be negative while market value is large, and a distressed company or a weak bank can trade below book.
items.t: Treating book equity as the value of the company or using it in EV calculations instead of market cap.
items.in: Under Ind AS, book equity shows as equity share capital plus other equity; for Indian banks and NBFCs, P/BV links the two and is the main multiple.

items.q: Is there anything wrong with the simple enterprise value formula you just gave me?
p: Simple formula omits debt-like items: leases, pensions, earnouts, provisions
Omits non-operating assets: associates, investments, surplus land, tax losses
Test: include an item if its cost or income sits outside EBITDA
Book vs market value choices can distort the result
items.a: Yes, it is a simplification. It misses debt-like items such as lease liabilities, unfunded pensions, deferred or contingent acquisition payments and large legal or environmental provisions. It also misses non-operating assets beyond cash: stakes in associates, financial investments, surplus land and sometimes tax losses. The guiding test is consistency with the metric you are dividing by. If an item's cost or income is excluded from EBITDA, its value should be in the bridge; if it already runs through EBITDA, leave it out to avoid double counting. And it mixes market value for equity with book value for most other items, which can matter for distressed debt or listed subsidiaries.
items.t: Adding every liability on the balance sheet, including payables, which are operating and already in working capital.
items.in: Indian groups carry large cross-holdings, associates and disputed tax demands (shown as contingent liabilities); each needs a deliberate in-or-out call, often at market value for listed stakes.

items.q: Should you use book values or market values for each item when calculating enterprise value?
p: Equity value always at market: share price times diluted shares
Debt at book unless trading well away from par
Minority interest at book by convention; market if subsidiary listed
Investments at fair or market value where available
items.a: In theory, market value for everything, because EV is a market measure. In practice it is a mix. Equity value is always market: share price times diluted shares. Debt is usually taken at book value, because most loans are not traded and book is close to market for a healthy company; I would switch to market value if bonds trade well below par, as in distress, or if rates have moved a lot on long fixed-rate debt. Minority interest and preferred are generally at book or liquidation value, but if a subsidiary is listed I would use market value of the outside stake. Cash is at book, and listed investments at market.
items.t: Using book shareholders' equity instead of market capitalisation as the starting point.
items.in: Most Indian corporate debt is bank loans or unlisted NCDs without liquid prices, so book value is the practical default except for listed bonds or distress.

items.q: What level of dilution to equity value from options and convertibles would you consider 'too high'?
p: No hard rule; mature companies typically see low single-digit dilution
Above roughly 10% warrants checking inputs and instrument treatment
High dilution is common in tech and startups with large ESOP pools
Matters for per-share value and acquirer's cash-out cost
items.a: There is no fixed threshold, but there is a sense check. For a mature company, dilution from options and RSUs is typically small, in the low single digits as a percentage of basic shares. If my diluted count is more than roughly 10% above basic, I go back and check: are convertibles that should be debt being converted, are out-of-the-money options sneaking in, is the share count date right? If it holds up, it is real information. It usually means heavy equity-based pay, common in tech and newly listed companies, or a large convertible. That dilution lowers value per share and raises the cost for an acquirer, who must cash out or roll over those instruments.
items.t: Giving a single magic number with confidence instead of explaining the sense check and drivers.
items.in: Recently listed Indian new-age tech companies often carry sizeable ESOP pools; check the SBEB disclosures in the annual report before finalising diluted shares.

items.q: What are the three main valuation methodologies?
p: Comparable companies (trading comps)
Precedent transactions
Discounted cash flow analysis
Notes two are relative, DCF is intrinsic
items.a: The three core methods are comparable companies, precedent transactions and discounted cash flow. Comparable companies values the business using trading multiples of similar listed peers, such as EV/EBITDA or P/E. Precedent transactions uses the multiples paid in past acquisitions of similar businesses, so it builds in a control premium. A DCF values the company intrinsically, by projecting its unlevered free cash flows, adding a terminal value and discounting everything back at the cost of capital. The first two are relative methods that tell you what the market pays; the DCF tells you what the cash flows are worth on your own assumptions.
items.t: Listing the methods without saying what each captures or how they differ.

items.q: Rank the three main valuation methodologies from highest to lowest expected value.
p: Precedent transactions usually highest due to control premium and synergies
Comparable companies usually lowest: minority, liquid stake pricing
DCF is the most variable, depending on assumptions
States this is a tendency, not a rule
items.a: As a general tendency, precedent transactions come out highest, because acquirers pay a control premium and often price in synergies. Comparable companies tends to be lowest, because trading multiples reflect the value of small, liquid minority stakes with no control. The DCF is the hardest to place: it is the most assumption-driven, and because management projections are often optimistic and the terminal value dominates, it frequently lands near or above precedents, but it can just as easily sit below comps. I would always stress that this ordering is a tendency, not a rule; market conditions and the quality of the deal set can flip it.
items.t: Presenting the ranking as a fixed law without explaining why each method sits where it does.
items.in: Indian precedent sets are thin and often minority PE stakes without control premia, so precedents do not always exceed listed comps.

items.q: When would a DCF not be an appropriate valuation method?
p: Unpredictable or negative cash flows, e.g. early-stage startups
Banks and financial institutions: debt is operating, use DDM or P/BV
Distressed companies where liquidation value matters more
Notes terminal value dominance makes output unreliable
items.a: I would avoid relying on a DCF when cash flows cannot be forecast with any confidence. Early-stage or pre-revenue companies are the clearest case: almost all value sits in the terminal value, so the answer is just your assumptions. Banks and other financial institutions are another: debt and interest are part of operations, so unlevered free cash flow and WACC do not make sense, and you use a dividend discount model, residual income or price-to-book. Distressed companies near liquidation are better valued on asset recovery. Highly cyclical commodity businesses can also produce misleading DCFs if you anchor to a single point in the cycle.
items.t: Saying 'never use a DCF for a loss-making company'; a turnaround with visible cash flows can still be modelled.
items.in: For Indian banks and NBFCs, use P/BV linked to sustainable ROE, or residual income; for early-stage startups, round pricing and the VC method dominate.

items.q: Apart from the three main methods, what other valuation methodologies are there?
p: LBO analysis and sum-of-the-parts
Liquidation or net asset value, replacement cost
Dividend discount model or residual income for financials
Market reference points: 52-week range, analyst targets, premiums paid
items.a: Beyond comps, precedents and DCF, there are several. An LBO analysis tells you what a financial sponsor could pay and still hit its target return. Sum-of-the-parts values each division separately. Liquidation value or net asset value looks at what the assets would fetch, and replacement cost asks what it would take to build the business from scratch. For financial institutions, a dividend discount model or residual income model replaces the DCF. Early-stage companies use the VC method. And bankers show market reference points: the 52-week trading range, broker target prices and premiums paid in past public takeovers.
items.t: Listing methods without saying when each is useful.
items.in: Indian merger schemes need a registered valuer report weighting income, market and asset approaches; SEBI ICDR sets a VWAP-based floor for preferential issues.

items.q: When would you use a liquidation valuation?
p: Distress or insolvency, when going concern is doubtful
Creditor recovery analysis and setting a floor value
Assets valued at realisable values with haircuts
Proceeds distributed by priority of claims
items.a: I use it when the company may not survive as a going concern: insolvency, a distressed sale, or creditors assessing recovery. It also serves as a floor in any valuation, the minimum the assets are worth if the business shuts. The method is to take each asset at what it would realistically fetch in a sale: cash near full value, receivables at a discount for collectibility, inventory at a deeper discount, and fixed assets often well below book. Then subtract liabilities in order of priority to see how much each class of creditor recovers and whether anything is left for equity, which in distress is often nothing.
items.t: Using book values instead of realisable values with haircuts.
items.in: Under IBC, registered valuers compute fair and liquidation value; resolution plans must give dissenting financial creditors at least liquidation value, and Section 53 governs the liquidation waterfall.

items.q: When would you use a sum-of-the-parts valuation?
p: Conglomerates or companies with distinct divisions
Divisions with different growth, margins and peer multiples
Value each part separately, then sum and adjust for holdco items
Mentions conglomerate or holding company discount
items.a: Sum-of-the-parts fits a company with distinct businesses that have different growth rates, margins, risk and peer groups, so a single blended multiple would mislead. I value each division separately, using its own comps, precedents or DCF, and value listed stakes at market. I then add the parts, subtract holding company costs and net debt at the parent level, and often apply a conglomerate discount because investors cannot buy the pieces separately and capital allocation across divisions may be inefficient. It is also useful to show a client the value that could be unlocked through a demerger or sale of a division.
items.t: Forgetting to deduct central costs and parent-level net debt after adding up the divisions.
items.in: Very common for Indian conglomerates such as Reliance, L&T and Grasim; analysts often apply a holding company discount, typically 20 to 50%, to listed stakes.

items.q: When would you include an LBO analysis in a valuation?
p: When private equity firms are likely bidders
Shows the maximum price a sponsor can pay for its target IRR
Acts as a floor in a sell-side process
Needs stable cash flows and debt capacity
items.a: I include it whenever a financial sponsor is a realistic buyer, which is most sell-side processes for businesses with stable cash flows and some debt capacity. The LBO works backwards: given a sponsor's target return, say a 20% IRR, a realistic amount of debt and an assumed exit multiple, what is the most it could pay today? That gives a reference point, often treated as a floor, because if strategic buyers are not willing to pay more, sponsors will set the price. It is also useful on the buy side to sanity-check whether a sponsor can compete with a strategic acquirer.
items.t: Treating the LBO as an intrinsic value; it depends on the sponsor's return target and leverage.
items.in: Domestic bank acquisition finance in India has historically been restricted, so Indian buyouts use less leverage (NCDs, private credit), lowering LBO-implied values.

items.q: What are the most commonly used valuation multiples?
p: EV/Revenue, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT
P/E for equity value
P/BV for banks and financial institutions
Pairs EV with pre-interest metrics, equity value with post-interest metrics
items.a: The workhorses are EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, EV/Revenue and P/E. EV/EBITDA is the most common for operating companies because it is independent of capital structure and depreciation policy. EV/EBIT adds capital intensity back in. EV/Revenue is used when a company is not yet profitable. P/E, equity value over net income, is widely used by equity investors for mature companies. For banks and insurers, price-to-book is standard. The rule underneath all of them is matching: enterprise value goes with metrics before interest, available to all capital providers, and equity value goes with metrics after interest, belonging to shareholders.
items.t: Pairing equity value with EBITDA or EV with net income.
items.in: Indian sell-side research quotes P/E heavily and P/BV or P/ABV for lenders; bankers still lead with EV/EBITDA for operating companies.

items.q: Give some examples of industry-specific valuation multiples.
p: Telecom: EV/subscriber; hotels: EV/room; airlines: EV/EBITDAR
Oil and gas: EV/reserves or EV/production
Real estate: P/FFO or P/NAV; SaaS: EV/ARR
Financials: P/BV, insurers on price-to-embedded value
items.a: Many sectors use operating metrics that capture value better than accounting earnings. Telecom and internet businesses use EV per subscriber or per monthly active user. Hotels use EV per room, hospitals EV per bed. Airlines and retailers have historically used EV/EBITDAR to neutralise lease versus own decisions. Oil and gas uses EV per barrel of reserves or of daily production, and metals and cement EV per tonne of capacity. REITs use price to funds from operations or to NAV. Software uses EV to annual recurring revenue. Banks use price-to-book, and life insurers price to embedded value.
items.t: Listing exotic metrics without explaining why they suit that industry.
items.in: Indian favourites: cement on EV per tonne of capacity, hospitals on EV per bed, life insurers on P/EV, NBFCs on P/ABV, power on EV per MW.

items.q: For industry-specific multiples like EV per subscriber or EV per researcher, why use enterprise value instead of equity value?
p: Operating metric is generated by the whole business
It is not affected by capital structure
Numerator and denominator must cover the same capital providers
Equity value would vary with leverage, distorting comparisons
items.a: Because the denominator is an operating metric that belongs to the whole business, not just to shareholders. Subscribers or researchers are generated using capital from both lenders and shareholders, and their number does not change if the company swaps equity for debt. Equity value does change with leverage: two identical telecom operators with different debt would show very different equity value per subscriber despite identical operations. EV strips out the financing effect, so the numerator and denominator describe the same thing: the value of the operations relative to an operational driver. That is the same logic as pairing EV with EBITDA.
items.t: Saying 'EV is just more standard' without the capital-structure-neutral reasoning.

items.q: Would an LBO analysis or a DCF usually give a higher valuation?
p: DCF usually higher
LBO discounts at sponsor's target IRR, higher than WACC
LBO is constrained by debt capacity and exit multiple
Caveat: depends on assumptions; LBO often treated as a floor
items.a: Usually the DCF gives the higher value. Both are cash flow based, but an LBO effectively discounts the cash flows at the sponsor's target return, often 20% or more, while a DCF discounts at the WACC, which is much lower. The LBO is also constrained by how much debt the business can carry and by a conservative exit multiple. That is why the LBO is often read as a floor valuation: what a financial buyer could pay. It is not guaranteed, though; with very aggressive leverage or a high assumed exit multiple, or a DCF with a high WACC and low terminal growth, the order can flip.
items.t: Saying they should be equal because both use cash flows, ignoring the different required returns.

items.q: How would you present the results of these valuation methodologies to a client or its investors?
p: Football field chart with a range per method
Show market reference points: 52-week range, analyst targets
Mark current price and proposed offer price
Explain which methods are weighted most and why
items.a: I would use a football field: a chart with one horizontal bar per method showing a value range, not a point. Typically that includes the 52-week trading range, broker target prices, trading comps, precedent transactions, a DCF range from sensitivity tables, and an LBO range if sponsors are relevant. I would show the values per share or as EV, with vertical lines for the current share price and any proposed offer. Then I would talk the client through it: which methods deserve more weight for this business, where the ranges overlap, and what that implies for a negotiating range or a fairness view.
items.t: Presenting one precise number instead of overlapping ranges with reasoning.

items.q: How would you value an apple tree?
p: DCF of apple cash flows over the tree's productive life
Comparables: prices of similar trees or orchards
Replacement cost of growing a new tree to maturity
Mentions risks: weather, disease, apple prices
items.a: I would treat it like a small business. First, a DCF: estimate apples per year, times the price, minus costs like water, fertiliser and labour, over the tree's productive life, plus any value of the wood at the end, discounted at a rate that reflects risks like weather, pests and price swings. Second, comparables: what similar trees or orchards have sold for, perhaps expressed per tree or per kilo of annual yield. Third, replacement cost: what it would cost to plant a sapling and nurture it until it bears fruit, adjusted for the years of lost harvest. I would triangulate the three into a range.
items.t: Giving one method only, or forgetting the time and risk element of the cash flows.

items.q: Why is Equity Value / EBITDA not a valid multiple, while EV / EBITDA is?
p: EBITDA is before interest, available to all capital providers
Equity value covers only common shareholders
Mismatch makes leveraged companies look cheap
Pair equity value with post-interest metrics like net income
items.a: Because the numerator and denominator would describe different groups of investors. EBITDA is earned before any interest payments, so it is available to lenders, preferred holders and shareholders alike. Equity value represents only the common shareholders' claim. Dividing one by the other means a highly leveraged company looks cheap simply because its equity value is small relative to EBITDA, even though much of that EBITDA goes to lenders. If you want an equity value multiple, use a metric after interest, like net income or levered free cash flow. If you use EBITDA, EBIT or revenue, pair it with enterprise value.
items.t: Saying 'it is just convention' without explaining the capital provider mismatch.

items.q: When might a liquidation valuation give the highest value of all methods?
p: Assets worth more sold off than used in the business
Business earns returns below its cost of capital
Valuable real estate or assets carried at low book value
Market multiples depressed for the sector
items.a: When the assets are worth more broken up than kept running. That happens if the business earns returns below its cost of capital, so cash flow methods give little value, while the assets themselves have a strong resale market. Classic examples are companies sitting on valuable land or real estate bought decades ago, businesses holding inventory or equipment with a liquid secondary market, or firms in a sector whose trading multiples have collapsed. In those cases, closing down and selling the assets returns more to owners than continuing, which is effectively the argument activists or asset-stripping buyers make.
items.t: Saying liquidation value is always the lowest without considering asset-rich, low-return businesses.
items.in: Classic Indian case: defunct Mumbai textile mills, whose central-city land was worth far more as real estate than the operating businesses.

items.q: Think of Facebook in 2004, or an Indian consumer app today: fast user growth, no revenue, no profit. How would you value it?
p: Comparable companies and recent funding rounds on user metrics
EV per user or per monthly active user
Long-horizon DCF: users times future ARPU, discounted at high rate
VC method: exit value discounted at target return
items.a: With no revenue or profit, earnings multiples are useless, so I would value it on its user base and future potential. First, comparables and precedents on operating metrics: what similar platforms are valued at per user or per monthly active user, including recent funding rounds and acquisitions. Second, a long-horizon DCF: project users, assume when and how it monetises, through ads or subscriptions, apply a mature-stage revenue per user and margin, then discount at a high venture-style rate. Third, the VC method: estimate an exit value at year five to seven and discount it at a target return of 30 to 50%. I would sanity-check engagement, retention and cost to acquire users.
items.t: Forcing a standard DCF with precise short-term projections or applying P/E to a loss-making company.
items.in: Shares issued by Indian startups to foreign investors need a fair value report under FEMA pricing rules, typically DCF-based, which sets a floor price.

items.q: If you use a free cash flow multiple, should it be paired with equity value or enterprise value?
p: Unlevered FCF (FCFF) pairs with enterprise value
Levered FCF (FCFE) pairs with equity value
Levered FCF is after interest and debt repayment
Logic: match the capital providers the cash flow belongs to
items.a: It depends which free cash flow. Unlevered free cash flow is calculated before interest, so it is available to all capital providers and pairs with enterprise value. Levered free cash flow is after interest and mandatory debt repayments, so it belongs only to shareholders and pairs with equity value. The test is always the same: whose cash flow is it? If lenders have not been paid yet, use EV; if they have, use equity value. Mixing them, for example EV over levered FCF, distorts the multiple in favour of whichever company is more leveraged.
items.t: Giving one answer without asking whether the free cash flow is levered or unlevered.

items.q: You almost never use Equity Value / EBITDA, but are there cases where Equity Value / Revenue makes sense?
p: Generally avoid: revenue is pre-interest, so EV/Revenue is consistent
Financial institutions: interest is operating, EV not meaningful
Banks and insurers use equity value multiples like P/BV
Little practical difference when a company has negligible net debt
items.a: Usually no, for the same reason: revenue is available to all capital providers, so it pairs with EV. The main exception is financial institutions. For banks and insurers, borrowing and interest are part of operations, so enterprise value is not meaningful and every multiple is on equity value: price-to-book, P/E, and sometimes price to revenue or total income. Price-to-sales also appears in equity research for companies with little or no net debt, where EV and equity value are nearly identical, so the mismatch does not matter. For a leveraged operating company, though, I would stick to EV/Revenue.
items.t: Saying it is never acceptable, missing the financial institutions case.
items.in: For Indian banks and NBFCs, P/BV, P/ABV and P/E dominate; EV-based multiples are not used.

items.q: How do you choose the companies for a comparable companies analysis or a precedent transactions set?
p: Screen by industry and business model first
Then size, geography, growth and margin profile
Precedents: also recency (3 to 5 years) and deal type
Aim for a focused set and tier closest comparables
items.a: Start with the business: same industry, similar products, customers and business model. Then narrow by financial profile: size by revenue or market cap, geography, growth rate and margins. For precedents I add transaction filters: deals in the last three to five years so market conditions are relevant, control deals rather than minority stakes, and similar deal size. I aim for a focused set, often five to ten names, and tier them: a core group of the closest peers and a wider group for context. If the set is thin, I relax geography or size before I relax business model, since that drives economics most.
items.t: Picking peers on industry label alone without checking business model, size or growth.
items.in: Indian listed peer sets are often small; bankers add global or EM peers and screen out illiquid, promoter-heavy stocks with low free float.

items.q: How do you apply the three valuation methodologies to arrive at a value for the company?
p: Comps and precedents: apply a multiple range to target's metric
Uses interquartile range, positioned by relative growth and margins
DCF range from sensitivities on WACC and terminal assumptions
Bridge EV to equity value and per share, then triangulate
items.a: For comps and precedents, I calculate each peer's multiples, look at the range, typically the 25th to 75th percentile, and decide where the target should sit based on its growth, margins and risk. I apply that multiple range to the target's own metric, say NTM EBITDA, which gives an enterprise value range. For the DCF, I build a range by sensitising the WACC and the terminal growth rate or exit multiple. Then I bridge each EV range to equity value by subtracting net debt and other claims, divide by diluted shares for a per-share range, and compare all of them on a football field.
items.t: Applying a single median multiple and presenting one precise value.

items.q: What is a valuation actually used for in banking?
p: M&A pricing: sell-side expectations, buy-side bids
IPO and fundraising: setting a price range
Fairness opinions and board approvals
It produces a range to negotiate around, not a single answer
items.a: Valuation is a tool for decisions, not an answer in itself. In M&A, it helps a seller set realistic price expectations and helps a buyer decide how much it can bid. In an IPO or private placement, it sets the price range. For boards, it supports fairness opinions on whether a deal is fair to shareholders. It is also used in restructurings to decide who gets what, in investment decisions, and in accounting tests like goodwill impairment. In every case the output is a range that frames a negotiation, because the final price depends on competition, synergies and bargaining power.
items.t: Describing valuation as finding the 'true' price rather than framing a negotiable range.
items.in: Indian valuations are often legally required: registered valuer reports for merger schemes, FEMA pricing for cross-border issues, and SEBI-mandated fairness opinions for listed company schemes.

items.q: Why might a company with similar growth and margins to its peers still trade at a premium?
p: Stronger competitive position or brand, i.e. a moat
Higher ROIC or cash conversion for the same growth
Better management, governance or lower risk
Scarcity value, liquidity, or takeover speculation
items.a: Growth and margins are only part of the picture. A company can earn a premium if the market believes its position is more durable: a stronger brand, market leadership or network effects. It might need less capital to grow, so higher return on capital and better cash conversion. Investors pay up for trusted management, clean governance and lower risk, such as less customer concentration or less cyclicality. Technical factors matter too: higher liquidity, index inclusion, scarcity of listed companies in that theme, or speculation about a takeover. Finally, the market may simply expect future growth or margins to beat peers, even if the historical numbers look similar.
items.t: Saying the premium must mean the market is wrong, without identifying fundamental drivers.
items.in: Governance and promoter quality drive big premia in India: MNC subsidiaries like Hindustan Unilever or Nestle India trade richer than local peers with similar numbers.

items.q: What are the weaknesses of using public company comparables?
p: No truly identical peers; differences in mix, size and growth
Reflects market sentiment, which can be irrational
Prices minority stakes, no control premium
Accounting differences and thin or illiquid peer sets
items.a: First, no two companies are truly alike: product mix, geography, scale and growth stage always differ, so the peer set is an approximation. Second, comps reflect market sentiment at a point in time, which can be euphoric or panicked, so you inherit any mispricing. Third, trading prices reflect small minority stakes with no control, so they understate what a buyer of the whole company would pay. Fourth, accounting policies and one-offs differ, so metrics need cleaning before multiples are comparable. And for niche sectors, the set may be tiny or illiquid, making the multiples unreliable.
items.t: Listing flaws without noting that comps remain useful as a market-based check.
items.in: Indian comps face low free float, promoter-dominated stocks and thin trading in small caps, which can make quoted multiples unrepresentative.

items.q: How do you reflect a company's competitive advantage in its valuation?
p: DCF: higher margins and ROIC sustained for longer
Longer forecast period before returns fade to WACC
Comps: position toward the upper end of the multiple range
Avoid double counting with an arbitrary premium
items.a: A moat shows up in how long the company can earn returns above its cost of capital. In a DCF, I reflect it through higher margins, higher return on reinvested capital and a longer period before those returns fade toward the industry average, which may mean a longer explicit forecast. It can also support a higher terminal value, but I would keep terminal growth realistic. In comps or precedents, I would justify placing the company toward the upper end of the peer range. What I avoid is layering a separate arbitrary premium on top, because that double counts something already in the cash flows.
items.t: Lowering the discount rate to reflect a moat; risk and competitive advantage are separate inputs.

items.q: Do you always use the median multiple from a set of comparable companies or precedent transactions?
p: No; use a range, often 25th to 75th percentile
Position target by relative growth, margins and risk
Median limits outlier impact but is not automatically right
Exclude clear outliers and explain the choice
items.a: No. The median is a useful reference because it limits the effect of outliers, but it assumes the target is an average member of the group. I usually look at a range, often the 25th to 75th percentile, and then position the target within it. If it grows faster, has better margins or lower risk than most peers, it belongs toward the top; if it is smaller or weaker, toward the bottom. I also strip out obvious outliers, like a company distorted by a takeover rumour. The point is to justify where the target sits, not apply a statistic mechanically.
items.t: Mechanically applying the median or mean without positioning the target relative to peers.

items.q: Precedent transactions usually give higher values than trading comps. When might that not be the case?
p: Markets have risen sharply since the precedent deals
Precedents were distressed sales or forced sellers
Precedents were minority stakes without control premium
Listed peers trading at bubble valuations
items.a: Several situations reverse the usual order. If public markets have rallied strongly since the deals were done, today's trading multiples can exceed what acquirers paid a few years ago. If the precedent set is full of distressed sales, forced sellers or buyers with little competition, the prices paid will be depressed. If the deals were minority stakes rather than control acquisitions, there is no control premium. And if a sector is in a valuation bubble, listed peers can trade far above any price a disciplined acquirer would pay for a whole company, especially one requiring full cash consideration.
items.t: Saying it can never happen because of the control premium.
items.in: Common in India, where precedents are often minority PE stakes or distressed IBC acquisitions, which carry no control premium or come at deep discounts.

items.q: What are the main weaknesses of precedent transactions analysis?
p: Few truly comparable deals; data often incomplete
Market conditions at deal time may differ from today
Deal-specific factors: synergies, competition, distress, consideration type
Private targets disclose little financial information
items.a: The biggest issue is data: there are rarely many truly comparable deals, and private targets often disclose little, so you may not even know the EBITDA paid for. Second, deals happen in different market environments, and a multiple paid in a boom or a crisis may say little about today. Third, each price reflects deal-specific factors: synergies the buyer expected, how competitive the auction was, whether the seller was distressed, whether it was paid in cash or overvalued stock, and how big a stake was bought. All of that makes precedents noisy, which is why I use them as a range and sanity check, not a precise answer.
items.t: Treating precedent multiples as directly applicable without adjusting for deal context.
items.in: Indian private deal disclosures are thin; bankers piece together data from exchange filings, MCA filings and press, and often lack target EBITDA.

items.q: The same acquirer buys two companies with identical financial profiles, but pays twice the EBITDA multiple in one deal. How could that happen?
p: Competitive auction versus bilateral negotiation
Different synergies or strategic urgency
Different market conditions or timing
Seller pressure, consideration type, or stake size differs
items.a: Identical numbers do not mean identical deals. One target might have been sold through a competitive auction with several bidders, while the other was negotiated one-on-one. The acquirer may have expected far larger synergies from one, perhaps because of geographic overlap or a key technology, or felt strategic urgency to block a competitor. Timing matters: one deal may have happened in a buoyant market and the other in a downturn. The seller's position also matters: a distressed or forced seller accepts less. Finally, structure: paying in highly valued stock, buying 100% versus a smaller stake, or earnouts can all change the headline multiple.
items.t: Assuming one deal was a mistake rather than identifying structural or situational drivers.

items.q: Why might a seasoned investor prefer EBIT multiples over EBITDA multiples?
p: Depreciation reflects a real cost: assets must be replaced
EBITDA overstates cash earnings for capital-intensive businesses
EBIT approximates earnings after maintenance capex
EBITDA can flatter heavily leveraged or asset-heavy companies
items.a: Because depreciation is a real economic cost, even if it is not a cash charge in the year. Machines, stores and networks wear out and must be replaced, so a business that ignores that spend is overstating what it really earns. EBITDA adds depreciation back, which flatters capital-intensive businesses and can make two companies look equally profitable when one needs far more reinvestment. EBIT, by deducting depreciation, is a rough proxy for earnings after maintenance capex, so it better reflects sustainable earning power. That is the logic behind the well-known criticism of EBITDA by investors like Warren Buffett.
items.t: Saying D&A is ignored because it is non-cash, missing that capex is the real cash cost.

items.q: EV/EBIT, EV/EBITDA and P/E all measure valuation relative to profit. How do they differ, and when would you use each?
p: EV/EBITDA: capital structure and D&A neutral; capital-intensive peers, LBOs
EV/EBIT: captures capital intensity via D&A
P/E: after interest and tax, affected by leverage and one-offs
P/E for mature companies and financials with similar leverage
items.a: EV/EBITDA is the most neutral: it ignores capital structure, tax and depreciation policy, so it compares companies with different leverage and accounting choices, and it is the standard in LBOs and capital-intensive sectors. Its weakness is ignoring reinvestment needs. EV/EBIT deducts depreciation, so it rewards businesses that need less capital and suits comparing firms whose D&A genuinely reflects asset wear. P/E is after interest and tax, so it is driven by leverage, tax rates and one-off items. It is the multiple equity investors quote most and works best for mature, stable companies with similar capital structures, and for banks, where EV-based metrics do not apply.
items.t: Mixing pre- and post-lease EBITDA across peers without adjusting EV for lease liabilities.
items.in: Ind AS 116 moved lease rent below EBITDA, inflating EBITDA for retailers and airlines; compare on a consistent basis and add lease liabilities to EV.

items.q: You are buying a vending machine business. In one version you own and depreciate the machines; in another you lease them at the same annual cost. Would you pay a higher EBITDA multiple for either?
p: EBIT is identical; EBITDA is higher for the owned business
Lease rent sits above EBITDA under old operating lease rules
Same underlying value means a higher EV/EBITDA for leased business
Notes Ind AS 116 or IFRS 16 removes the difference
items.a: Under traditional operating lease accounting, both businesses have the same EBIT, but EBITDA differs. The owner adds back depreciation, so its EBITDA is higher; the lessee's rent is an operating expense, so its EBITDA is lower. If cash costs are similar, because the owner must spend roughly its depreciation on replacement capex, the businesses are worth about the same. Dividing the same value by a lower EBITDA means the leased business commands a higher EV/EBITDA multiple. So yes, I would pay a higher multiple for the leased one, but not a higher absolute price. On EV/EBIT, the two would trade at the same multiple.
items.t: Paying the same EBITDA multiple for both, which overvalues the owned business by ignoring replacement capex.
items.in: Under Ind AS 116, lease cost splits into right-of-use depreciation and interest, so both show the same EBITDA and the lease liability is added to EV as debt.

items.q: How would you value a private company?
p: Same three methods, with adjustments
Discount for lack of marketability on public comps
DCF: beta from listed peers, relevered; add size or specific risk premium
Normalise financials: owner pay, related-party items, one-offs
items.a: I use the same core methods with adjustments. First, clean up the financials: private companies often have owner compensation that is above or below market, related-party transactions and personal expenses that need normalising. For trading comps, I apply a discount for lack of marketability, since a private stake cannot be sold easily. Precedent transactions work well because many targets are private. For the DCF, there is no observable beta, so I take peers' betas, unlever them and relever at a target or industry capital structure, and often add a size or company-specific risk premium. There is no market cap, so the output is an implied equity value.
items.t: Applying public trading multiples directly without any illiquidity discount or normalisation.
items.in: Indian family businesses need heavy normalisation: related-party dealings, promoter pay, group cross-subsidies; tax valuations follow Rule 11UA and cross-border issues FEMA pricing.

items.q: When valuing a private company, why might you discount public comparable multiples but not precedent transaction multiples?
p: Public multiples price liquid minority stakes
Private shares are illiquid, so apply a marketability discount
Precedents price control of whole companies, often private
Acquisition itself is the liquidity event; discount already reflected
items.a: Public trading multiples reflect the price of small, freely tradable stakes in listed companies. A private company's shares cannot be sold on an exchange, so an investor would pay less for the same cash flows, which is why we apply a discount for lack of marketability, often in the range of 10 to 30%. Precedent transactions are different: they price the purchase of entire companies, many of which were private themselves, and the buyer gets control. The acquisition is the liquidity event, and any illiquidity is already embedded in what was paid. So discounting precedents would double count.
items.t: Saying precedents are not discounted only because they include a control premium, missing the illiquidity point.

items.q: Can private companies be used in your valuation analysis?
p: Not as trading comps: no market price, limited disclosure
Yes as targets in precedent transactions
Recent funding rounds as reference points
Headline round valuations inflated by liquidation preferences
items.a: Not as trading comparables, because they have no market price and usually limited public financials, so you cannot calculate a current trading multiple. But they are very useful in precedent transactions: many acquisition targets are private, and if the deal terms and financials are disclosed, their multiples are valid data points. Recent funding rounds can also serve as reference points, especially in startup sectors. I would be careful, though: headline round valuations often reflect a small stake with liquidation preferences and other investor protections, so they can overstate the value of common equity.
items.t: Treating a headline funding-round valuation as equivalent to a market capitalisation.
items.in: Indian private companies file financials with the MCA, accessible through databases like Tracxn, Venture Intelligence and Tofler, so private peer data is often obtainable.

items.q: How does valuing a bank or NBFC differ from valuing a normal operating company?
p: Debt is raw material for a bank, so EV and EBITDA are meaningless
Uses P/B, P/TBV and P/E, linked to ROE versus cost of equity
Values equity directly with a DDM or excess capital model, not UFCF
Names bank drivers: NIM, credit cost, asset quality, capital adequacy
items.a: For a bank, deposits and borrowings are not financing; they are the raw material the business lends out, so interest is an operating cost. That makes Enterprise Value, EBITDA and unlevered free cash flow meaningless, so we value equity directly. On multiples, we use P/B or price to tangible book and P/E, and the key link is that a bank deserves a premium to book only if its ROE beats its cost of equity: justified P/B equals ROE minus g, divided by cost of equity minus g. For intrinsic value we use a dividend discount or excess capital model, where regulatory capital requirements cap what can be paid out. Peers are compared on NIM, credit costs, asset quality, CASA and capital ratios rather than margins.
items.t: Calculating EV/EBITDA for a bank, or subtracting deposits as debt in an equity bridge.
items.in: Indian banks and NBFCs are often valued on P/ABV (book adjusted for net NPAs); insurers on P/EV using embedded value; RBI capital adequacy rules cap payouts.

items.q: A company is preparing to list on NSE and BSE. Walk me through how you would value it for the IPO.
p: Listed peer forward P/E or EV/EBITDA is the primary method
DCF used as a cross-check, not the pricing anchor
Applies an IPO discount to peers so new investors see upside
Separates pre-money vs post-money value and fresh issue vs offer for sale
items.a: IPO pricing is relative valuation first. I would pick listed peers and apply their forward multiples, usually one-year-forward P/E or EV/EBITDA, to the company's forecasts, then cross-check with a DCF and recent private rounds. That gives a fair value range. Then I apply an IPO discount, often 10 to 20%, so new investors have a reason to buy and the stock trades well on listing. Next I adjust for structure: fresh issue proceeds add cash, so post-money equity value equals pre-money value plus the primary raise, and the per-share price uses the post-issue share count. Offer for sale shares just change hands and add no cash. Finally, roadshow feedback and the book-build narrow the price band.
items.t: Pricing at the DCF value with no IPO discount, or dividing by pre-issue shares when there is a fresh issue.
items.in: SEBI ICDR book-building: price band in the RHP, anchor allocation a day before opening, KPIs disclosed and benchmarked against peers; many Indian IPOs are largely offer for sale.

items.q: It is April and you are building comps. How would you compute a peer's last twelve months numbers instead of just using its last full fiscal year?
p: LTM = last fiscal year + current YTD minus prior-year YTD
Uses the latest reported period, not the calendar date
Strips one-offs from the stub periods
Distinguishes LTM from calendarisation of different year ends
items.a: LTM uses the most recent reported numbers. Take the last full fiscal year, add the year-to-date period just reported, and subtract the same period of the prior year. Say the fiscal year ends December and Q1 is out: FY revenue Rs. 1,000 crore, Q1 this year Rs. 280 crore, Q1 last year Rs. 250 crore. LTM is 1,000 plus 280 minus 250, or Rs. 1,030 crore. If Q1 results are not yet published in April, the last annual is the LTM. Repeat for every line you need and strip non-recurring items. Calendarisation is separate: it aligns peers with different year ends. For a March year-end company, calendar 2025 is roughly 25% of FY25 plus 75% of FY26.
items.t: Adding the latest quarter to the annual figure without subtracting the prior-year quarter, which double counts a quarter.
items.in: Most Indian companies use an April to March fiscal year; SEBI LODR requires quarterly results within 45 days and annual results within 60 days of period end.

items.q: Walk me through an M&A premiums analysis.
p: Uses only deals with listed targets, so an unaffected price exists
Premium = offer price over unaffected price at 1 day, 1 week, 4 weeks
Applies median and quartile premiums to target's unaffected price
Output is an implied per-share range for the football field
items.a: A premiums analysis shows how much above market price buyers have paid for listed targets. First, select completed deals where the target was public, ideally similar in size, sector, period and consideration type. For each, compute the premium of the offer price over the unaffected share price, typically one day, one week and four weeks before announcement, or before leaks moved the stock. Take the median and the quartiles. Then apply that range to our target's unaffected price. If the target trades at Rs. 400 and the median four-week premium is 30%, the implied value is Rs. 520 per share, with the quartiles giving the range. It sits in the football field as a control value bar.
items.t: Measuring the premium against a price already inflated by deal rumours rather than the unaffected price.
items.in: In India, SAST open offer floors, including the 60-trading-day volume-weighted average price, set a minimum price, so observed premiums partly reflect regulation, not just negotiation.

items.q: Walk me through a future share price analysis.
p: Projects EPS a few years forward
Applies a peer or historical P/E to get a future price
Discounts back at cost of equity, not WACC
Adds PV of dividends received in between
items.a: It asks what the stock is worth today based on where it could trade in a few years. Project the metric, usually EPS, two or three years out. Apply a multiple, from peers or the company's own historical range, to get a future share price. Then discount that price back at the cost of equity, because it is a per-share equity value, and add the present value of any dividends paid along the way. Example: Year 2 EPS of Rs. 50 at a 20x P/E gives Rs. 1,000 at the end of Year 2. At a 12% cost of equity, 1,000 divided by 1.2544 is about Rs. 797 today. Show it across a range of multiples and discount rates.
items.t: Discounting at WACC instead of cost of equity, or ignoring dividends paid during the period.

items.q: Premiums analysis and precedent transactions both use past deals. How does the way you select those deals differ?
p: Premiums analysis needs listed targets only, to measure premium to market
Precedents can include private targets if financials are available
Premiums set can span sectors; precedents need business similarity
Both screen on time period, size and deal type
items.a: Precedents are about what buyers paid relative to fundamentals, so selection is driven by business similarity: same sector, similar size, growth and margins. Private targets are fine as long as you can find revenue or EBITDA. Premiums analysis is about the premium paid over the market price, so every target must have been listed, otherwise there is no unaffected share price. Because control premiums depend more on deal dynamics than on sector, the premiums set is often broader and can cut across sectors, but it is screened on size, geography, time period, cash versus stock consideration and whether control changed hands. So the two sets overlap but are rarely identical.
items.t: Including private company deals in a premiums analysis, where no unaffected share price exists.

items.q: Walk me through a sum-of-the-parts valuation, for example for an Indian conglomerate.
p: Values each segment separately with its own peers or DCF
Deducts capitalised corporate costs and net debt
Adds listed stakes at market value less a holding company discount
Used when segments differ sharply in growth, margins or risk
items.a: SOTP is used when divisions are so different that one multiple would mislead. Value each segment on its own peers or DCF, add them up, subtract unallocated corporate costs, then bridge to equity. Example: Segment A EBITDA of Rs. 200 crore at 10x is 2,000; Segment B Rs. 100 crore at 6x is 600. Head-office costs of Rs. 20 crore at 8x take off 160, giving Enterprise Value of 2,440. Less net debt of 500 gives 1,940. A listed subsidiary stake worth 500 at market, after a 20% holding company discount, adds 400, so equity value is Rs. 2,340 crore. Compare that with the market cap to see whether a conglomerate discount exists.
items.t: Adding the listed subsidiary's whole EV instead of the parent's share of its equity value, or ignoring head-office costs.
items.in: Indian brokers commonly apply holding company discounts of 20 to 50% to listed stakes in groups; tax leakage on any eventual stake sale is one justification.

items.q: How do you value accumulated tax losses carried forward, and how do you reflect them in a valuation?
p: Value is the PV of future tax savings, not the gross loss
Either lower taxes in projections or add PV separately, never both
Usage limited by future taxable profit and expiry
Ownership change rules can restrict use after an acquisition
items.a: A tax loss is worth the taxes it saves, discounted for when it saves them. In a DCF the cleanest way is to set the losses against taxable income in the projections, so cash taxes stay low until the pool runs out. Alternatively, value them separately: Rs. 400 crore of losses at 25% tax is Rs. 100 crore of potential saving; if profits let you use it over four years, discount each year's Rs. 25 crore saving and add that present value. Do one or the other, not both. Haircut for expiry risk and uncertain profits, and check change-of-control rules: in the US, Section 382 caps the losses usable each year after an acquisition.
items.t: Adding the full gross loss to value instead of the PV of tax savings, or counting it in both projections and a separate add-on.
items.in: Indian business losses carry forward 8 years (unabsorbed depreciation indefinitely); Section 79 forfeits a closely held company's losses on over 49% voting change, except under IBC resolution plans.

items.q: You need forward estimates for your comps from broker research. How do you decide which report or estimates to use?
p: Prefers consensus median from a database over a single broker
Uses reports published after the latest results
Checks definitions match: fiscal year, adjusted EBITDA, lease treatment
Avoids outlier estimates and applies one approach across all comps
items.a: Ideally I would not rely on one broker; I would take consensus estimates from Bloomberg, Capital IQ or FactSet and use the median. If I must pick a single report, I would choose one published after the latest quarterly results, from a broker with a long coverage record and a full model rather than a short note. I would check that its numbers sit near consensus rather than at an extreme, and that definitions match the rest of the comps set: same fiscal year, EBITDA before or after lease costs, adjusted or reported, and consistent treatment of one-offs. Then I would apply the same approach to every company in the set.
items.t: Using an old report that predates the latest results, or mixing EBITDA definitions across peers.
items.in: Indian brokers forecast on the April to March year; check whether EBITDA is post Ind AS 116 (lease rent excluded), which matters for retail, aviation and hospitals.

items.q: Many targets in your precedent transactions are private and EBITDA is not public. How would you track it down?
p: Checks acquirer's announcement, investor deck, call transcript and filings
Uses deal databases, financial press and target's statutory filings
Estimates from revenue times peer margin only as a last resort
Flags estimates clearly or drops the deal
items.a: Start with the acquirer: its press release, analyst call transcript and investor presentation often cite the revenue or EBITDA multiple, and its annual report or stock exchange disclosures may give the target's revenue, profit or purchase price allocation. If the target had listed debt or was carved out of a listed parent, check those filings too. Then go to deal databases and the financial press. In India, private companies file audited financial statements with the Registrar of Companies, so you can usually pull revenue and EBITDA from MCA filings for the relevant year. As a last resort, estimate EBITDA from revenue and peer margins and flag it clearly, or exclude the deal.
items.t: Treating a rumoured or estimated EBITDA as hard data without flagging it.
items.in: MCA21 filings give audited statements for Indian private companies; Venture Intelligence and VCCEdge cover Indian deals, and SEBI LODR disclosures often state acquisition consideration.

items.q: How many years back and forward do you usually look for trading comps and precedent transaction multiples?
p: Comps: LTM plus current and next year forward multiples
Precedents: roughly the last 3 to 5 years
Widens window if few deals, or full cycle for cyclicals
Drops deals done in very different market conditions
items.a: For trading comps, you usually show LTM plus the current and next fiscal year forward, sometimes two years out for high-growth names. Beyond that, research estimates thin out and become unreliable. Historical multiples over three to five years are useful context, for example to see where the sector has traded through a cycle. For precedents, the usual window is the last three to five years, because valuations move with interest rates and market sentiment. You go wider if the sector has few deals, or cover a full cycle for cyclical sectors, but you drop deals struck in very different conditions, such as bubble peaks. Precedent multiples are usually on LTM numbers at announcement.
items.t: Including decade-old deals without adjusting for different rate and market conditions.

items.q: Company A has a 40% EBITDA margin and trades at 8x EBITDA; Company B has a 10% margin and trades at 16x. Why can't you compare these valuations directly?
p: A is 3.2x revenue; B is 1.6x revenue, the opposite conclusion
Multiple gaps reflect growth, risk and margin trajectory
B's EBITDA may be depressed, inflating its multiple
Benchmark multiples against growth and returns of true peers
items.a: On EBITDA, B looks twice as expensive. Convert to revenue, though: A is 8 times 40%, so 3.2x revenue, while B is 16 times 10%, so 1.6x revenue. On sales, A is the expensive one. Neither view alone settles it, because the businesses have different economics. B's 16x may reflect faster growth, room for margin expansion, or a temporarily depressed EBITDA that inflates the multiple. A's 8x may reflect slow growth or peak margins. The real point is that they are probably poor comparables: you should judge multiples against growth, margins and returns, using peers with similar profiles, before concluding that either is cheap.
items.t: Concluding A is cheaper simply because its EBITDA multiple is lower.

items.q: How would you value an upstream oil and gas company, and how does that differ from valuing a standard company?
p: NAV: field-by-field DCF to end of life, no perpetual terminal value
Driven by price deck, production profile, lifting costs and fiscal terms
Uses EV/EBITDAX, EV per barrel of reserves, EV per daily production
Values proved reserves fully, risks probable and possible
items.a: An upstream company is a set of depleting assets, so the main method is a net asset value model. For each field, project production from reserves, apply a commodity price deck, deduct lifting costs, royalties, taxes and capex, and discount to the end of field life. There is no perpetual terminal value. Proved reserves are valued in full; probable and possible ones are risked. Add exploration upside, subtract net debt and abandonment costs to reach equity NAV. Multiples are sector specific: EV/EBITDAX, which adds back exploration expense to neutralise accounting choices, EV per barrel of proved reserves, and EV per barrel per day of production. Refiners are valued more like industrials, on through-cycle EV/EBITDA.
items.t: Applying a perpetuity growth terminal value to a depleting reserve base.
items.in: Indian upstream cash flows hinge on government take: royalty, cess and profit petroleum under PSC or revenue-sharing contracts, plus occasional windfall levies; model contract terms field by field.

items.q: How would you value a REIT, and how is that different from valuing a normal company?
p: Uses FFO and AFFO instead of net income or EBITDA
FFO adds back property depreciation and removes property sale gains
NAV: NOI divided by cap rate, less net debt
Distribution yield matters given mandatory high payouts
items.a: A REIT owns income-producing property and must pay out most of its cash, so valuation focuses on distributable cash and asset value. Net income is distorted by depreciation on buildings that often hold their value, so we use FFO: net income plus real estate depreciation, minus gains on property sales. AFFO then subtracts maintenance capex and adjusts for straight-lined rent. Trading metrics are P/FFO, P/AFFO and distribution yield. The second method is NAV: capitalise net operating income at a market cap rate. Rs. 800 crore of NOI at an 8% cap rate gives Rs. 10,000 crore of property value; less net debt of 3,000, NAV is Rs. 7,000 crore, which you compare with market cap.
items.t: Using P/E, or adding back depreciation without removing gains on property sales.
items.in: SEBI REIT rules require at least 90% of net distributable cash flows to be paid out; distributions mix interest, dividend and debt repayment, each taxed differently.

items.q: Walk me through a DCF.
p: Projects unlevered FCF for 5 to 10 years
Discounts at WACC; terminal value by perpetuity growth or exit multiple
Sum of present values is Enterprise Value
Bridges to equity value and divides by diluted shares
items.a: A DCF values a business as the present value of the cash it will generate. First, project unlevered free cash flow for five to ten years: EBIT less taxes, plus D&A, less capex and less the increase in working capital. Second, estimate the discount rate, WACC, which blends the cost of equity from CAPM and the after-tax cost of debt at target weights. Third, calculate terminal value at the end of the forecast, using either perpetuity growth on final-year cash flow or an exit multiple on final-year EBITDA. Discount the cash flows and terminal value at WACC and add them up to get Enterprise Value. Finally, subtract net debt and other claims for equity value and divide by diluted shares.
items.t: Discounting unlevered cash flows at cost of equity, or calling the DCF output equity value.

items.q: In a DCF, how do you get from projected revenue to unlevered free cash flow?
p: Revenue less operating costs gives EBIT; tax on EBIT gives NOPAT
Adds back D&A and other non-cash charges
Subtracts capex and the increase in net working capital
No interest expense anywhere in unlevered FCF
items.a: Start with revenue and subtract COGS and operating expenses to get EBITDA, then subtract D&A for EBIT. Apply the tax rate to EBIT, not to pre-tax profit, because we want cash flow before any financing; that gives NOPAT. Add back D&A and other non-cash charges, subtract capex, and subtract the increase in net working capital. Example: revenue of Rs. 1,000 crore at a 20% EBITDA margin gives 200; D&A of 40 leaves EBIT of 160; tax at 25% is 40, so NOPAT is 120. Add back 40 of D&A to get 160, deduct capex of 60 and a working capital build of 20, and unlevered free cash flow is Rs. 80 crore.
items.t: Deducting interest or starting from net income, which turns it into a levered cash flow.
items.in: Under Ind AS 116 lease rent sits below EBITDA; either treat lease liabilities as debt or deduct lease payments in FCF, consistently with the equity bridge.

items.q: Besides net income plus D&A, minus working capital changes and capex, how else can you calculate free cash flow?
p: Cash flow from operations minus capex
Unlevered: EBIT x (1 - t) + D&A - capex - increase in NWC
EBITDA minus taxes on EBIT, capex and NWC build gives same answer
Notes a net income start gives a levered figure
items.a: The simplest alternative is cash flow from operations minus capex, since the cash flow statement already captures non-cash items and working capital movements. For a DCF I would build it from EBIT instead: EBIT times one minus the tax rate, plus D&A, minus capex, minus the increase in working capital. That is unlevered free cash flow, which you discount at WACC. A third route is EBITDA minus taxes on EBIT, minus capex, minus the working capital build, which gives exactly the same number. Note that the net income route gives a levered figure, because interest has already been deducted.
items.t: Forgetting that a net income starting point includes interest, so it is not unlevered FCF.
items.in: Under Ind AS 7, non-financial companies show interest paid in financing, so Indian CFO minus capex is pre-interest, closer to unlevered (though taxes still reflect the interest shield).

items.q: Why do DCF projections usually run for 5 or 10 years?
p: Long enough to reach steady-state growth, margins and reinvestment
Beyond that, forecasts become guesswork
Ten years for high-growth or long-gestation businesses
Terminal value formula assumes the final year is normalised
items.a: The forecast should run until the business reaches a steady state, because the terminal value formula assumes stable growth, margins and reinvestment from then on. For most mature companies, five years gets you there, and visibility beyond that is poor anyway. You stretch to ten years when the company is still growing fast, margins are still ramping, or the asset has a long gestation, such as an infrastructure project or a young tech platform, so that the terminal year is genuinely normal.
