Going much longer adds false precision. If the final year still looks abnormal, extend the forecast rather than forcing a terminal value onto it.
items.t: Ending the forecast while growth is still far above long-run levels, which inflates terminal value.
items.in: Indian toll roads, renewable projects and other concession assets are often valued over the concession or PPA life, with no perpetuity terminal value.

items.q: What discount rate do you normally use in a DCF?
p: WACC for unlevered FCF, giving Enterprise Value
Cost of equity for levered FCF, giving equity value
Rate must match whose cash flow is being discounted
Same currency and inflation basis as the cash flows
items.a: The discount rate has to match the cash flow. In a standard unlevered DCF, the cash flows belong to all capital providers, so we discount at WACC, the weighted average of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, and the result is Enterprise Value. If we project levered free cash flow, which is after interest and debt repayments, it belongs only to shareholders, so we use the cost of equity and get equity value directly. It must also be consistent in currency and inflation: rupee cash flows need a rupee discount rate built off Indian rates, not a dollar WACC.
items.t: Discounting levered cash flows at WACC, or mixing rupee cash flows with a dollar discount rate.
items.in: For INR cash flows, build WACC off the Indian 10-year G-sec yield; a USD WACC needs USD cash flows, converted using the inflation differential.

items.q: How do you calculate WACC?
p: WACC = E/V x Ke + D/V x Kd x (1 - t)
Uses market value or target weights, not book values
Cost of debt is after tax because interest is deductible
Includes preference capital at its own cost if present
items.a: WACC is the blended return all capital providers require. It is the equity weight times the cost of equity, plus the debt weight times the pre-tax cost of debt times one minus the tax rate, plus preference capital at its cost if there is any. Weights use market values or a target capital structure, not book values. Cost of equity comes from CAPM; cost of debt from current yields on the company's debt or what it would pay to borrow today. Example: cost of equity 14%, cost of debt 9%, tax 25% and 30% debt. Equity contributes 0.7 times 14, or 9.8%; debt contributes 0.3 times 6.75, about 2.0%; so WACC is about 11.8%.
items.t: Using book value weights, or the coupon on old debt instead of today's cost of borrowing.
items.in: Use the tax rate the company actually pays; many Indian companies are on the concessional regime, about 25.17% including surcharge and cess.

items.q: How do you calculate the cost of equity?
p: CAPM: Ke = Rf + beta x equity risk premium
Rf is a long-term government bond yield in the cash flow currency
Beta relevered to the target capital structure
Any size or specific premium is explicitly justified
items.a: Usually with CAPM: cost of equity equals the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium. The risk-free rate is the yield on a long-dated government bond in the same currency as the cash flows. The equity risk premium is the extra return investors demand for holding equities over that bond, taken from historical data or implied from current market levels. Beta measures the stock's sensitivity to the market, ideally derived from peers and relevered. With an illustrative risk-free rate of 7%, a beta of 1.1 and an equity risk premium of 6%, cost of equity is 7 plus 6.6, or 13.6%. For small or riskier companies, practitioners sometimes add a size or specific-risk premium.
items.t: Using a US Treasury yield with rupee cash flows, or double counting country risk.
items.in: Indian practice uses the 10-year G-sec yield as Rf with an India ERP; adding a separate country risk premium double counts unless Rf excludes the sovereign default spread.

items.q: Where does the beta in your cost of equity calculation come from?
p: Takes observed levered betas of comparable listed companies
Unlevers: Bu = BL / (1 + (1 - t) x D/E)
Takes median unlevered beta, relevers at target D/E
Gets the example right: 1.2 unlevers to 0.87, relevers to 1.07
items.a: You can use the company's own regression beta if it is listed and liquid, but the standard approach uses peers. Take each comparable's observed levered beta and unlever it to remove its capital structure: unlevered beta equals levered beta divided by one plus one minus tax times debt to equity. Take the median unlevered beta, then relever it at the target's own debt to equity. Example: a peer with levered beta 1.2, D/E of 50% and 25% tax has unlevered beta of 1.2 divided by 1.375, about 0.87. Relevered at our company's 30% D/E, that is 0.87 times 1.225, about 1.07.
items.t: Relevering at the peers' D/E instead of the target's, or using book rather than market D/E.
items.in: Many Indian stocks are thinly traded, making regression betas unreliable; prefer peer-based betas, measured against Nifty 50 or Sensex using weekly returns over two to five years.

items.q: Why do you need to unlever and then relever beta?
p: Observed beta mixes business risk and financial risk from leverage
Unlevering isolates business risk, comparable across peers
Relevering applies the target's own capital structure
More leverage means a higher levered beta
items.a: A stock's observed beta reflects two things: the risk of the business itself and the extra risk from its debt, because more leverage makes equity returns swing harder. Peers carry different amounts of debt, so their raw betas are not comparable. Unlevering strips out each peer's financial risk and leaves the business risk, which should be similar across companies in the same industry. We take the median of those, then relever at our company's own target capital structure, so the final beta reflects the industry's business risk plus our company's financial risk. That relevered beta is what goes into CAPM.
items.t: Saying unlevering removes company-specific risk; diversifiable risk is never in beta in the first place.

items.q: Would you expect a manufacturing company or a technology company to have the higher beta?
p: Tech usually higher unlevered beta: discretionary demand, long-dated cash flows
Manufacturer's heavier debt can push its levered beta up
Sub-sector matters, e.g. IT services vs capital goods
Compares unlevered betas to make the call
items.a: Usually the technology company, at least on an unlevered basis. Tech revenue depends on discretionary corporate and consumer spending, growth expectations make up much of the value, and cash flows sit further in the future, so the stock moves more with the market. But it is not automatic. Manufacturers tend to carry more debt, and leverage raises levered beta, so a heavily indebted capital goods or auto company can show a higher levered beta than a cash-rich software firm. Sub-sector matters too: a mature IT services company with steady contracts can have a lower beta than a cyclical metals producer. So I would compare unlevered betas.
items.t: Answering tech automatically without considering leverage and sub-sector.
items.in: Indian IT services firms are largely debt-free with contracted, recurring revenue, so do not assume tech means high beta in India; check peer betas.

items.q: What happens if you use levered free cash flow instead of unlevered free cash flow in your DCF?
p: Levered FCF is after interest and net debt repayments
Output is equity value, not Enterprise Value
Must be discounted at cost of equity
Results rarely match in practice because leverage changes
items.a: Levered free cash flow is what is left for shareholders after interest and net debt repayments, so the DCF output is equity value rather than Enterprise Value, and it must be discounted at the cost of equity. In theory, with consistent assumptions, equity value from a levered DCF equals Enterprise Value from the unlevered DCF minus net debt. In practice the two rarely match, because the levered version depends on the debt schedule, and if leverage changes over time the cost of equity should change too. Levered DCFs are mainly used for banks and other financial companies, where debt is part of operations.
items.t: Subtracting net debt again from a levered DCF result, which double counts debt.

items.q: If you use levered free cash flow, what discount rate should you use?
p: Cost of equity, not WACC
Levered FCF belongs only to equity holders
Output is equity value directly
Cost of equity uses beta at the company's actual leverage
items.a: The cost of equity. Levered free cash flow is after interest and debt repayments, so it belongs only to shareholders, and the discount rate must be their required return. WACC would be wrong because it blends in the cheaper after-tax cost of debt, which belongs to lenders whose cash flows have already been taken out; it would understate the required return and overstate value. The cost of equity should reflect the company's actual leverage through its levered beta. The result is equity value, which you divide by diluted shares for a per-share value.
items.t: Using WACC, which understates the required return and overvalues the equity.

items.q: How do you calculate terminal value?
p: Perpetuity growth: FCF in year N x (1 + g) / (WACC - g)
Exit multiple: final-year EBITDA x chosen EV/EBITDA
Discounts terminal value back N years at WACC
Cross-checks implied multiple against implied growth
items.a: Two ways. Perpetuity growth: take final-year free cash flow, grow it by one year, and divide by WACC minus the long-term growth rate. Exit multiple: apply an EV/EBITDA multiple from peers or precedents to final-year EBITDA. Either way, the result is a value at the end of the forecast, so you discount it back N years. Example: Year 5 free cash flow of Rs. 100 crore, 5% growth and 12% WACC gives 105 divided by 7%, which is Rs. 1,500 crore. Discounting five years at 12% means dividing by 1.762, so about Rs. 851 crore today. I always cross-check by backing out the multiple implied by the growth method and the growth implied by the multiple.
items.t: Forgetting to discount terminal value, or using year N cash flow without growing it one year.

items.q: When would you prefer the perpetuity growth method over the exit multiple method for terminal value?
p: Perpetuity growth stays intrinsic; exit multiple imports market pricing
Prefer growth method when comps are few or distorted
Prefer multiple when the sector trades and exits on multiples
Always cross-check one against the other
items.a: The perpetuity growth method keeps the DCF intrinsic: value comes from the company's own cash flows, growth and cost of capital. So I prefer it when there are few good comparables, when sector multiples look distorted by a boom or slump, or when the business is mature and stable enough that a long-run growth rate is easy to defend. The exit multiple method fits better when buyers in the sector genuinely price on multiples, for example a private equity fund planning an exit, or when long-run growth is hard to pin down. In practice bankers show both and check that each one's implied figure is sensible.
items.t: Claiming the exit multiple is more accurate; it turns the DCF partly into a relative valuation.

items.q: What growth rate is appropriate for the terminal value?
p: At or below long-run nominal GDP growth
Same currency and inflation basis as cash flows and WACC
Well below WACC
Consistent with reinvestment: g = reinvestment rate x ROIC
items.a: The terminal growth rate is the rate the company can sustain forever, so it cannot exceed the long-run nominal growth of the economy it operates in; otherwise it would eventually become the economy. In practice it is set around long-term inflation plus modest real growth, in the same currency as the cash flows and the WACC. It should sit well below WACC, because as g approaches WACC the value explodes. Also check reinvestment: growth has to be funded, so terminal-year capex and working capital should be consistent with g equal to reinvestment rate times ROIC. A mature company gets a lower rate than its forecast-period growth.
items.t: Using a high near-term growth rate in perpetuity, or a dollar growth rate with a rupee WACC.
items.in: INR terminal growth is usually higher than USD rates because Indian inflation and nominal GDP growth are higher; keep it consistent with the INR WACC built off G-sec yields.

items.q: How do you choose the exit multiple for the terminal value?
p: Starts from trading comps and precedent multiples
Uses historical through-cycle ranges, not just today's level
Adjusts down for the company's maturity in the terminal year
Checks the implied perpetuity growth rate is sensible
items.a: Start with the EV/EBITDA multiples of trading comps and, where relevant, precedents, and look at the sector's historical range rather than just today's level. Then adjust for where the company will be in the terminal year: by then it should be more mature and growing more slowly, so its multiple should usually be at or below today's peer median, not at the top. Use a range, for example one turn either side, in a sensitivity table. Finally, back out the perpetuity growth rate the multiple implies; if your exit multiple implies the business growing faster than the economy forever, it is too rich.
items.t: Using today's peak-cycle peer multiple for a company that will be mature by the terminal year.

items.q: Which terminal value method gives a higher valuation: perpetuity growth or exit multiple?
p: Neither by construction; depends on the inputs
Exit multiples from current trading often embed optimism
Reconciles implied growth rate and implied multiple
A big gap signals inconsistent assumptions
items.a: Neither method is higher by construction; it depends entirely on the inputs. In practice, exit multiples taken from current peer trading often give the higher number, because market multiples embed growth and sentiment that a conservative perpetual growth rate does not. The right response is to reconcile them: calculate the growth rate implied by your exit multiple and the multiple implied by your growth rate. If the exit multiple implies growth above the economy forever, or the growth rate implies 4x EBITDA in a sector trading at 12x, one assumption is wrong. Consistent assumptions should land in a similar range.
items.t: Claiming one method is always higher instead of tying the answer to the assumptions.

items.q: What is the problem with basing the terminal exit multiple on where comparable companies trade today?
p: Today's multiples reflect current rates and sentiment, not Year 5
Company will be more mature, deserving a lower multiple
Imports relative valuation into an intrinsic DCF
Cyclical peaks or troughs distort terminal value
items.a: Three problems. First, timing: the multiple is applied to Year 5 or Year 10 EBITDA, but today's multiples reflect today's interest rates, sentiment and point in the cycle. If peers are at a cyclical peak, terminal value is inflated. Second, maturity: today's peers may be growing fast, while by the terminal year our company should be slower and more mature, which deserves a lower multiple. Third, it undermines the method: terminal value is often more than half the total, so using market multiples makes the DCF largely a relative valuation. Mitigate by using through-cycle multiples and checking the implied perpetuity growth rate.
items.t: Saying there is no issue because comps reflect the market view.

items.q: How can you tell if your DCF depends too heavily on assumptions about the distant future?
p: Checks terminal value as a share of Enterprise Value
Flags concern when terminal value exceeds roughly 75 to 80%
Runs sensitivities on terminal growth and WACC
Fixes by extending forecast or normalising the terminal year
items.a: Look at how much of Enterprise Value comes from terminal value. For a mature business, something like 50 to 75% is common; at 85 or 90%, almost all the value depends on what happens after the forecast ends. Then look at the sensitivity tables: if a half-point change in terminal growth or WACC moves the value by 20% or more, the model is fragile. The fixes are to extend the forecast until the company genuinely reaches a steady state, to check that the terminal year has normalised margins and reinvestment, and to cross-check the answer against comps and precedents.
items.t: Treating a high terminal value share as automatically wrong; for high-growth companies it is expected but needs scrutiny.

items.q: All else equal, should a Rs. 5,000 crore market cap company or a Rs. 500 crore one have the higher cost of equity?
p: The smaller company has the higher cost of equity
Reasons: less diversified, less liquid, weaker access to capital
Captured via a size premium or higher beta
Notes exceptions, such as a volatile large company
items.a: The smaller company, in most cases. Smaller businesses tend to be less diversified, more dependent on a few customers or on the promoter, have weaker access to capital and less liquid shares, so investors demand a higher return. Regression betas do not always capture this, which is why practitioners often add a size premium on top of CAPM for small caps. It is not a law: a large company in a volatile, high-growth sector can have a higher cost of equity than a small, stable utility. But with all else equal, the smaller company is riskier and its cost of equity is higher.
items.t: Relying only on regression beta, which is often understated for illiquid small caps.
items.in: Indian small caps are often thinly traded and promoter-controlled; practitioners add a size or illiquidity premium, but it should be justified, not used as a plug.

items.q: And WACC: would it be higher for the Rs. 5,000 crore company or the Rs. 500 crore company?
p: Smaller company usually has the higher WACC
Both its cost of equity and cost of debt are higher
Larger company can carry more cheap debt
Notes a heavier debt mix could narrow the gap
items.a: Usually the smaller company. Its cost of equity is higher for the reasons we just covered, and its cost of debt is also higher, because lenders charge a wider spread to smaller borrowers with weaker ratings or no rating at all. The one offset is capital structure: if the small company used much more debt, cheaper after-tax debt could pull its WACC down. In practice, though, larger companies have more debt capacity and can borrow more cheaply, which lowers their WACC further. So both components, and usually the mix, point to a higher WACC for the smaller company.
items.t: Assuming more debt always lowers the small company's WACC, ignoring rising costs of debt and equity.

items.q: What is the relationship between debt and the cost of equity?
p: More debt raises the cost of equity
Shareholders bear more financial risk, so levered beta rises
Example: unlevered beta 0.8 relevers to 1.4 at D/E of 1
WACC falls at first, then rises with distress costs
items.a: More debt raises the cost of equity. Lenders are paid first, so as leverage rises, equity returns become more volatile and shareholders face more risk of being wiped out. In CAPM this shows up through levered beta, which equals unlevered beta times one plus one minus tax times D/E. For example, an unlevered beta of 0.8 with 25% tax and D/E of 1.0 becomes 0.8 times 1.75, which is 1.4. WACC falls at first as cheaper debt replaces equity, but beyond some point the rising costs of equity and debt, plus distress risk, push it back up.
items.t: Saying the cost of equity falls with more debt because debt is cheaper.

items.q: Cost of equity is the return an equity investor expects. Shouldn't we add the dividend yield to the CAPM figure?
p: No: CAPM already gives total return, dividends plus price gains
Adding the yield double counts
Dividends split the return; they do not add to it
Yield appears explicitly only in Ke = D1 / P0 + g
items.a: No. CAPM gives the total return equity investors require, which already includes both dividends and capital gains. A company paying a bigger dividend does not give investors a higher total return; it splits the same expected return into more income and less price appreciation, because paying out cash lowers the share price and retained earnings. Adding the dividend yield on top of CAPM would double count. Where dividend yield does appear explicitly is the dividend growth model: cost of equity equals next year's dividend divided by the current share price, plus the long-term dividend growth rate.
items.t: Adding the dividend yield on top of CAPM, which overstates the cost of equity.

items.q: How could you estimate cost of equity without using CAPM?
p: Dividend growth model: Ke = D1 / P0 + g
Bond yield plus a risk premium
Implied cost of equity from price and consensus forecasts
Multi-factor models such as Fama-French
items.a: A few ways. The dividend growth model: cost of equity equals next year's dividend over the current price, plus long-term dividend growth. If a share trades at Rs. 500, next year's dividend is Rs. 15 and dividends grow 8% a year, that gives 3% plus 8%, or 11%. It only works for stable dividend payers. Second, bond yield plus premium: take the company's own pre-tax cost of debt and add a few percentage points, since its equity is riskier than its debt. Third, an implied cost of equity: solve for the discount rate that equates today's share price with consensus cash flows. Finally, multi-factor models add size and value factors to market risk.
items.t: Using the dividend model for a company with low or irregular payouts.

items.q: Two companies are identical except that one has debt and the other has none. Which has the higher WACC?
p: The no-debt company usually has the higher WACC
Debt is cheaper than equity and interest is tax deductible
Cost of equity rises with debt, only partly offsetting
At high leverage, distress costs can reverse the answer
items.a: Usually the company with no debt. Debt is cheaper than equity because lenders rank ahead of shareholders and have contractual claims, and interest is tax deductible, which lowers its after-tax cost further. Adding debt does raise the cost of equity, but at moderate levels the tax shield means the blended rate still falls. That only holds up to a point. If the levered company has too much debt, both its cost of debt and cost of equity rise sharply as distress risk grows, and its WACC can end up higher than the debt-free company's.
items.t: Saying the levered company has the higher WACC because it is riskier, ignoring the tax shield at moderate leverage.

items.q: Which has a bigger impact on a DCF valuation: a 10% change in revenue or a 1 percentage point change in the discount rate?
p: 10% revenue moves value about 10%, more with operating leverage
Exit multiple method: one point of WACC moves value about 4 to 5%
Perpetuity growth, 10% WACC, 3% g: 11% WACC cuts value 12.5%
Answer depends on terminal value method and WACC minus g
items.a: It depends on the terminal value method, so I would work it through. If margins hold, a 10% revenue change moves free cash flow and value by about 10%, more with operating leverage. With an exit multiple, terminal value does not depend on the discount rate, so a one-point change only alters discounting over about five years, roughly 4 to 5% of value; revenue wins. With perpetuity growth it can flip: at 10% WACC and 3% growth, value is cash flow divided by 7%; at 11% it is divided by 8%, a 12.5% fall, and at 9% a 17% rise. So with a narrow WACC minus g spread, the discount rate can matter more.
items.t: Giving a flat answer without considering the terminal value method and the WACC minus g spread.

items.q: What about a 1% change in revenue versus a 1 percentage point change in the discount rate?
p: 1% revenue change moves value about 1%
One-point discount rate change moves value several percent or more
Discount rate wins in almost every case
Clarifies percentage point versus relative change in the rate
items.a: Here the discount rate almost always wins. A 1% revenue change, with stable margins, moves cash flows and value by about 1%, a bit more with operating leverage. A one percentage point change in WACC, say 12% to 13%, typically moves value by several percent even with an exit multiple, and by 10% or more with a perpetuity growth terminal value. One caveat worth stating: if the interviewer means a 1% relative change in the rate, 12% to 12.12%, the effect is tiny and comparable to the revenue change, so I would clarify which they mean.
items.t: Not clarifying whether 1% means a percentage point or a relative change in the discount rate.

items.q: How would you calculate WACC for a private company with no traded shares?
p: Beta from listed peers, unlevered and relevered
Target or peer capital structure instead of market weights
Cost of debt from actual borrowing rate or synthetic rating
Adds a size or illiquidity premium where justified
items.a: The formula is the same; the inputs come from proxies. There is no share price, so no observed beta and no market value of equity. Take listed peers' betas, unlever them, and relever at a target capital structure, usually the peer median D/E or management's target, because book values are misleading and using the DCF's own equity value is circular. Cost of debt comes from the company's current borrowing rate, or a synthetic rating based on interest coverage and the matching spread. Many practitioners then add a size or illiquidity premium to the cost of equity, since a private stake is harder to sell and the business is usually smaller.
items.t: Using book value of equity for the capital structure weights.
items.in: For Indian private companies, current bank loan rates (MCLR or external benchmark linked) give the cost of debt; CRISIL, ICRA or CARE ratings help where available.

items.q: What would you do if you did not believe management's projections for the DCF?
p: Benchmarks against track record, peers, market size and consensus
Adjusts specific drivers rather than haircutting the output
Builds management, base and downside cases
Shows sensitivities so the gap is visible
items.a: I would not throw them away, because management knows the business, but I would build my own view alongside. First, diagnose what looks wrong by comparing growth and margins with the company's track record, peer performance, market size and, if it is listed, consensus. Then adjust the specific drivers, such as slowing revenue growth or capping margin expansion at peer levels, rather than applying an arbitrary haircut to the final value. Present a management case, a base case and a downside case, with sensitivity tables, so the client sees how much value depends on management's optimism. On a sell-side, buyers will apply their own haircuts anyway.
items.t: Cutting the final value by an arbitrary percentage instead of fixing the underlying drivers.

items.q: Why is a standard DCF not used for banks and other financial institutions?
p: Debt is an operating input, so unlevered FCF is meaningless
Interest income and expense are core revenue and cost
Capex and working capital are not meaningful; capital is the constraint
Uses DDM or FCFE at cost of equity, plus P/B and P/E
items.a: Because for a bank, debt is not financing; it is the raw material. Deposits and borrowings are lent out, and interest is the main revenue and the main cost, so you cannot separate operating cash flow from financing cash flow, which unlevered free cash flow requires. Working capital and capex are not meaningful either: the balance sheet is mostly loans and deposits, and the real constraint is regulatory capital. So we value the equity directly with a dividend discount model, where distributable dividends are the earnings left after holding enough capital to support loan growth, discounted at the cost of equity, alongside P/B and P/E.
items.t: Subtracting deposits as debt to bridge from Enterprise Value to equity for a bank.
items.in: RBI capital adequacy norms under Basel III set how much capital Indian banks must retain, which drives distributable dividends in a DDM.

items.q: What sensitivity analyses would you typically show alongside a DCF?
p: WACC vs terminal growth rate table
WACC vs exit multiple table
Operating drivers: revenue growth vs EBITDA margin
Scenario cases flexing several assumptions together
items.a: The standard two-way tables are WACC against terminal growth and WACC against exit multiple, because those drive most of the value. Then operating sensitivities: revenue growth against EBITDA margin, and sometimes capex or working capital as a percentage of revenue. I would show outputs as both Enterprise Value and value per share, and alongside them the implied multiple or implied growth rate, so the reader can judge whether a cell is plausible. Beyond tables, scenario cases, base, upside and downside, flex several assumptions together consistently, which single-variable tables cannot do. These ranges then feed the DCF bar on the football field.
items.t: Using unrealistic ranges, like terminal growth close to WACC, which produce meaningless outputs.

items.q: A company has heavy debt and repays a large part of the principal each year. How do you account for this in a DCF?
p: Unlevered FCF does not deduct principal repayments
Debt captured by subtracting net debt at the valuation date
Falling leverage reflected in WACC or an APV approach
Levered DCF deducts repayments from free cash flow to equity
items.a: In a standard unlevered DCF you do not deduct principal repayments, because unlevered free cash flow is before all financing flows. The debt is captured when you bridge from Enterprise Value to equity value by subtracting net debt at the valuation date. Repaying debt does not change Enterprise Value; it shifts value from lenders to shareholders over time. What you should reflect is the changing capital structure: if leverage falls sharply, WACC should move towards the long-term target, or you can use an adjusted present value approach. In a levered DCF, by contrast, principal repayments are deducted from free cash flow to equity.
items.t: Deducting repayments from unlevered FCF and then subtracting net debt again, which double counts.

items.q: Why would you use the mid-year convention in a DCF?
p: Cash flows arrive through the year, not on the last day
Discount periods become 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 instead of 1, 2, 3
Raises value modestly versus year-end discounting
Example: Rs. 100 at 12% is 94.5 versus 89.3
items.a: A standard DCF implicitly assumes each year's cash flow arrives on the last day of the year, which is unrealistic for businesses that collect cash continuously. The mid-year convention assumes cash arrives, on average, in the middle of the year, so you discount Year 1 by 0.5 periods, Year 2 by 1.5, and so on. That brings cash flows forward and raises the valuation slightly. For example, Rs. 100 of Year 1 cash flow at 12% is worth 100 divided by 1.12, about 89.3, with year-end discounting, but 100 divided by the square root of 1.12, about 94.5, with mid-year. It suits highly seasonal businesses less well.
items.t: Applying mid-year discounting to an exit multiple terminal value as well.

items.q: Using the mid-year convention, what discount periods would you use if the first projection period is a stub, say only Q4 of Year 1?
p: Stub length is 0.25 years
Stub discount period is 0.125, half the stub
Stub cash flow covers only the remaining quarter
items.a: First, the stub cash flow should only be the cash generated in the remaining quarter, not the full year. The stub is 0.25 years long, so under the mid-year convention its cash flow arrives halfway through it, at 0.125. The first full year then starts at 0.25 and its midpoint is 0.25 plus 0.5, or 0.75. Each later year adds one: 1.75, 2.75 and so on. Without the convention, the periods would be 0.25, 1.25, 2.25. For terminal value, a perpetuity growth value uses the final year's mid-year period, while an exit multiple uses the end of the final year.
items.t: Discounting the stub at 0.5, or including a full year's cash flow in the stub period.

items.q: How does the terminal value calculation change when you use the mid-year convention?
p: Exit multiple terminal value still discounted N full years
Perpetuity growth terminal value discounted N minus 0.5 years
Reason: a multiple values the business at a point in time
Example: Rs. 1,500 crore is about 901 versus 851
items.a: It depends on the method. With an exit multiple, terminal value is what the business would sell for at the end of Year N, a point-in-time value, so you still discount it by the full N years. With perpetuity growth, the formula values a stream of cash flows that, under the convention, also arrive mid-year, so you discount it by N minus 0.5, matching the final year's cash flow. Example: a perpetuity growth terminal value of Rs. 1,500 crore at the end of Year 5, at 12% WACC, is 1,500 divided by 1.12 to the power 4.5, about Rs. 901 crore, rather than 851 discounted over five full years.
items.t: Using N minus 0.5 for an exit multiple terminal value, which overstates it.

items.q: Your DCF is for a listed company. How do you get from the DCF output to a value per share?
p: EV less debt, preference, minorities; plus cash, associates, non-core assets
Divides equity value by diluted shares
Treasury stock method on ESOPs; in-the-money convertibles as shares
Iterates because dilution depends on the implied price
items.a: The DCF gives Enterprise Value, so bridge to equity value: subtract debt, including lease liabilities if lease costs were kept out of cash flow, plus preference capital and minority interest; add cash, investments in associates and other non-operating assets. Then divide by diluted shares. Dilution depends on the share price, because ESOPs and convertibles only dilute when in the money, so it is circular: use the implied price, apply the treasury stock method and iterate until it converges. Example: EV of Rs. 10,000 crore, debt 2,000, cash 500, minority interest 300 and associates 200 give equity of Rs. 8,400 crore; on 100 crore diluted shares, that is Rs. 84 per share.
items.t: Calculating dilution at the current market price instead of the DCF-implied price.

items.q: Walk me through a dividend discount model you would use instead of a standard DCF to value a bank.
p: Projects balance sheet and earnings: loan growth, NIM, fees, credit costs
Dividends = earnings minus capital needed to hold the target ratio
Discounts dividends and terminal value at cost of equity
Justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(Ke - g), e.g. 1.6x book
items.a: Start by projecting the balance sheet, loan and deposit growth, then the income statement from net interest margin, fee income, operating costs and credit costs to reach net income. Next, work out risk-weighted assets and the equity needed to keep the capital ratio at target; dividends are net income minus that capital build, so faster growth means lower payouts. Discount those dividends at the cost of equity. For terminal value, use Gordon growth on final-year dividends or a P/B multiple. Justified P/B is ROE minus g over cost of equity minus g, so 16% ROE, 8% growth and 13% cost of equity gives 8 over 5, or 1.6x book. The sum is equity value directly.
items.t: Using a historical payout ratio without checking that capital ratios can support the projected loan growth.
items.in: Model RBI capital adequacy and CET1 requirements under Basel III; many Indian banks retain most earnings to fund growth, so dividends are small and terminal value dominates.

items.q: When calculating WACC and relevering beta, do you treat a company's convertible bonds as debt?
p: Depends on whether conversion is in the money
In the money: treat as equity and add shares to diluted count
Out of the money: count as debt in D/E, WACC and bridge
Same treatment across beta, WACC weights and share count
items.a: It depends on whether the convertible is likely to convert. If the share price is above the conversion price, holders would convert, so treat it as equity: leave it out of debt in the D/E used to relever beta and in the WACC weights, and include the new shares in the diluted share count. If it is out of the money, it behaves like debt, so include it as debt for beta and WACC and subtract it in the equity bridge. The key is consistency: the same instrument must not be debt in the beta calculation and dilutive equity in the share count. Strictly, a convertible is a hybrid of both.
items.t: Counting the convertible as debt in the bridge and also adding its conversion shares to the diluted count.
items.in: Indian companies also issue compulsorily convertible debentures; since CCDs must convert, they are usually treated as equity regardless of the share price.

items.q: A DCF gives a company a present Enterprise Value of Rs. 200. It will buy a factory for Rs. 100 in cash in Year 4. How do you adjust the DCF, and what is the new value?
p: Adds Rs. 100 of capex in Year 4, cutting that year's FCF
PV of the outflow at an assumed 10% is about 68.3
Capex-only effect: Enterprise Value falls to about Rs. 131.7
Then adds depreciation tax shield and the factory's cash flows
items.a: Treat it as Rs. 100 of extra capex in Year 4, which cuts that year's unlevered free cash flow by 100. How it is funded does not matter here, since the DCF is unlevered. In isolation, value falls by the present value of that outflow. At an assumed 10% discount rate, 100 divided by 1.1 to the fourth, which is 1.4641, is about 68.3, so Enterprise Value falls to about Rs. 131.7. But that is incomplete. From then on the factory adds depreciation, which creates a tax shield, and it should generate revenue and EBITDA, offset by maintenance capex and working capital. If it is a good investment, those inflows are worth more than 68.3 today and Enterprise Value rises.
items.t: Subtracting the full Rs. 100 from today's value, or ignoring the factory's future cash flows and depreciation.

items.q: Walk me through a basic merger model.
p: Projects buyer and target income statements separately first
Sets purchase price, funding mix, and sources and uses
Adjusts for foregone interest, new interest, amortisation, synergies, then tax
Divides by new share count and compares to standalone EPS
items.a: A merger model tells the buyer whether the deal raises or lowers its EPS. First, I project both companies' income statements. Second, I set the offer price, usually the target's share price plus a premium, and decide the mix of cash, new debt and stock. Third, I do the purchase price allocation: write up assets, create new intangibles and a deferred tax liability, and plug goodwill. Fourth, I combine pre-tax income and adjust for interest lost on cash used, interest on new debt, amortisation of new intangibles and any synergies, then tax it. Finally, I divide combined net income by the buyer's shares plus new shares issued and compare that with standalone EPS. Then I sensitise price, funding mix and synergies.
items.t: Forgetting to tax-effect the adjustments, or using the target's share count instead of the new shares the buyer issues.

items.q: Is there any real difference between a merger and an acquisition, and does it change how you model the deal?
p: Acquisition: larger buyer takes control; merger: similar-sized firms combine
Mergers of equals usually stock-funded; acquisitions often cash or debt
Accounting still identifies one acquirer; modelling mechanics are identical
items.a: In practice the labels describe size and tone more than mechanics. An acquisition is when a clearly larger company buys a smaller one and takes control; the target's shareholders are usually paid in cash or a mix, and the target becomes a subsidiary or is absorbed. A merger is closer to a combination of roughly similar-sized companies, typically paid in stock, so both shareholder groups own meaningful stakes in the combined entity. For the model it makes no difference: accounting standards require you to identify one acquirer, fair-value the other company's assets and liabilities, and book goodwill. So the merger model, the purchase price allocation and the accretion or dilution analysis are built exactly the same way.
items.t: Claiming a merger avoids goodwill or purchase accounting; pooling is no longer allowed for unrelated companies.
items.in: Indian mergers are usually NCLT-sanctioned amalgamations (Companies Act sections 230 to 232); buying 25% or more of a listed company instead triggers a SEBI open offer.

items.q: Why would a company choose to buy another company rather than grow on its own?
p: Faster growth than organic: new customers, geographies, products
Synergies: cost savings and revenue upside worth more than the premium
Capabilities, technology, talent or market share it cannot build quickly
Valuation: target undervalued, or buyer's stock is an expensive currency
items.a: The core reason is that buying is faster or cheaper than building. A buyer may want growth it cannot get organically: entry into a new geography, a new product line or a new customer base. It may want capabilities such as technology, a licence, a brand or a team. Consolidation gives market share and pricing power, and combining overlapping operations creates cost synergies. Vertical deals secure supply or distribution. Sometimes the logic is financial: the target looks cheap, or the buyer's shares trade at a rich multiple and are an attractive currency. Sometimes it is defensive: buying a competitor before a rival does. The test is always whether the value created exceeds the premium paid.
items.t: Listing motives without the test: a deal only creates value if synergies and strategic gains exceed the premium.

items.q: What makes an acquisition dilutive to the buyer's EPS?
p: Target's earnings added are less than the after-tax cost of funding
Costs: foregone interest on cash, new debt interest, new shares issued
Amortisation of new intangibles and write-up depreciation reduce EPS
All-stock deal: purchase P/E above buyer's P/E means dilution
items.a: A deal is dilutive when combined EPS falls below the buyer's standalone EPS. That happens when the target's net income, plus any after-tax synergies, is smaller than what it costs to fund the purchase. The costs are the interest income the buyer gives up on cash spent, the after-tax interest on new debt, and the extra shares issued in a stock deal, which spread earnings over a bigger base. Purchase accounting adds more drag through amortisation of newly identified intangibles and extra depreciation on written-up assets. So if you pay a high multiple for a low-earning target, fund it with expensive stock or debt, and create large amortisable intangibles, EPS goes down.
items.t: Assuming dilutive means bad; a dilutive deal can still create value if long-term returns exceed the cost of capital.

items.q: Is there a quick way to tell whether a deal will be accretive or dilutive without building the full model?
p: Compares weighted after-tax cost of funding with target's earnings yield
Target yield = net income / purchase price, the inverse of purchase P/E
Cost of stock = 1/buyer P/E; debt = rate x (1-t)
Cost of cash = foregone interest rate x (1 - t)
items.a: Yes. Compare what the funding costs with what the target earns on the price paid. The target's earnings yield is its net income divided by the purchase price, so 1 divided by the purchase P/E. Each funding source has an after-tax cost: cash costs the interest it was earning times (1 minus tax); new debt costs its interest rate times (1 minus tax); stock costs the buyer's earnings yield, 1 divided by the buyer's P/E. Weight these by the funding mix. If the weighted cost is below the target's yield, the deal is accretive; if above, dilutive. Example: cash earning 6% costs 4.5% after 25% tax, so buying a target at 15 times earnings, a 6.7% yield, with cash is accretive.
items.t: Comparing the pre-tax interest rate with the target's after-tax yield; also forgetting the shortcut ignores synergies, amortisation and fees.

items.q: A buyer trading at a higher P/E acquires a target trading at a lower P/E. Is the deal accretive or dilutive?
p: All-stock deal: accretive if buyer P/E exceeds purchase P/E
Uses purchase P/E including premium, not target's trading P/E
Says the P/E test does not apply to cash or debt deals
Notes it ignores synergies, intangible amortisation and fees
items.a: If it is an all-stock deal, accretive, as long as the P/E paid including the premium is still below the buyer's P/E. The buyer issues shares that cost it its earnings yield and buys earnings at a higher yield. Example: the buyer earns Rs. 100 crore with 5 crore shares at Rs. 500, so EPS is Rs. 20 and P/E is 25. It buys a target earning Rs. 20 crore for Rs. 360 crore, 18 times, issuing 0.72 crore shares. Combined EPS is 120 divided by 5.72, about Rs. 20.98, roughly 5% accretive. For cash or debt deals the P/E comparison does not apply; you compare the after-tax cost of funding with the target's earnings yield.
items.t: Using the target's undisturbed P/E; a 30% to 40% premium can push the purchase P/E above the buyer's and flip the answer.

items.q: Apply the rule of thumb: buyer P/E 20, target bought at 16 times earnings, funded half with new stock and half with new debt at 9%. Accretive or dilutive at 25% tax?
p: Cost of stock = 1/20 = 5%
After-tax cost of debt = 9% x 0.75 = 6.75%
Weighted cost 5.875% is below target yield of 1/16 = 6.25%
Concludes accretive, about 1.4%, before synergies and amortisation
items.a: I compare the weighted after-tax cost of funding with the target's earnings yield. Stock costs the buyer's earnings yield, 1 divided by 20, or 5%. Debt costs 9% times 0.75, or 6.75%. Half and half gives 5.875%. The target's yield is 1 divided by 16, or 6.25%. Funding is cheaper than the earnings we are buying, so it is accretive. Checking in numbers: the buyer earns Rs. 100 crore on a Rs. 2,000 crore market cap. The target earns Rs. 25 crore and costs Rs. 400 crore. Issuing Rs. 200 crore of stock adds 10% more shares, and Rs. 200 crore of debt costs Rs. 13.5 crore after tax. Combined earnings of Rs. 111.5 crore over 1.1 times the shares is about 1.4% accretive.
items.t: Using the 9% pre-tax rate, which gives a 7% weighted cost and wrongly flips the answer to dilutive.

items.q: Walk me through every effect an acquisition has on the buyer's financial statements.
p: Income statement: target earnings in, less foregone interest, new interest, amortisation
Share count rises for stock issued; EPS recalculated
Balance sheet: cash down or debt up, target equity eliminated
Goodwill, new intangibles, asset write-ups and DTL recorded
items.a: On the income statement, the target's revenue and expenses are added. Then you subtract interest income lost on cash used, add interest expense on new debt, add depreciation and amortisation on written-up assets and new intangibles, add synergies, and tax the net change. If stock is issued, the share count rises and EPS is recalculated. On the balance sheet, the buyer's cash falls or debt rises, new shares raise equity, the target's equity is eliminated, its assets and liabilities come in at fair value, new intangibles and a deferred tax liability are created, and goodwill plugs the gap. Transaction fees reduce cash and retained earnings. On the cash flow statement, the purchase is an investing outflow, net of the target's cash.
items.t: Adding the target's shareholders' equity to the combined balance sheet; it is always eliminated and replaced by goodwill and write-ups.

items.q: If a company has enough cash to buy a target outright, why might it still use stock or debt?
p: Preserves liquidity for capex, downturns and other deals
Stock is a cheap currency when the buyer trades at a high P/E
Stock shares risk with sellers when target value is uncertain
Sellers may want stock for tax deferral and upside
items.a: Cash is usually the cheapest source on paper, but there are good reasons not to use all of it. The buyer may want a liquidity buffer for working capital, capex or a downturn, and rating agencies watch cash levels. Some cash may be trapped in overseas subsidiaries or ring-fenced. If the buyer's shares trade at a rich multiple, issuing stock can be less dilutive than giving up interest on cash. Stock also makes sellers share the risk: if synergies disappoint, the value they received falls too. Sellers may prefer stock to defer tax and participate in upside. Finally, cheap debt may be available, giving a tax shield while keeping cash in hand.
items.t: Saying cash is the most expensive option; it is usually the cheapest because foregone interest after tax is low.
items.in: In India, a share-swap amalgamation through an NCLT scheme is generally tax-neutral for shareholders if Income Tax Act conditions are met, so promoters often prefer stock.

items.q: Why can a strategic buyer usually pay more for a company than a private equity fund?
p: Strategic can capture synergies; PE usually cannot, except on add-ons
PE price backed out from a 20% to 25% target IRR and exit multiple
PE price capped by debt capacity and equity cheque
Strategic has longer horizon and lower cost of capital
items.a: Two reasons: synergies and return hurdles. A strategic buyer can cut overlapping costs and cross-sell, so the target is worth more inside it than standalone, and it can share part of that value through a higher premium. A PE fund typically buys the business standalone, so its price is set by working backwards from a target IRR, often 20% to 25%, an assumed exit multiple, and how much debt lenders will provide. A strategic also has a longer or indefinite holding period and usually a lower cost of capital than PE's required return. The exception: a PE fund with a platform company can claim synergies on add-on deals, and cheap credit can let a sponsor outbid.
items.t: Saying PE always pays less; in buoyant credit markets or platform add-ons, sponsors often win auctions.

items.q: Why do goodwill and other intangible assets appear on the balance sheet after an acquisition?
p: Price paid exceeds the target's book value of net assets
Identifiable intangibles written up to fair value first
Goodwill is the residual after fair values and deferred tax
items.a: Because buyers almost always pay more than the target's book value, and the balance sheet must balance. The target's books record assets at historical cost and ignore most internally built value, like brands, customer relationships and technology. In purchase accounting, the buyer first identifies those intangibles and writes them up to fair value, along with any PP&E write-ups, and books a deferred tax liability on the write-ups. Whatever premium is still unexplained is goodwill. Example: pay Rs. 1,000 crore for a target with Rs. 600 crore book value and identify Rs. 150 crore of intangibles; the DTL at 25% is Rs. 37.5 crore. Fair value of net assets is Rs. 712.5 crore, so goodwill is Rs. 287.5 crore.
items.t: Calling goodwill simply price minus book value; it is the residual after fair-value write-ups and deferred tax.

items.q: How is goodwill different from the other intangible assets created in a deal?
p: Other intangibles are identifiable: separable or from contract or law
Finite-life intangibles are amortised, reducing EPS
Goodwill is the residual, never amortised, impairment-tested at least annually
Indefinite-life intangibles, like some brands, are also only impairment-tested
items.a: Other intangibles are specific, identifiable assets you can value and point to: customer relationships, brands, patents, software, licences, order backlog. They are either separable or arise from contractual or legal rights. Most have a finite life, so they are amortised, which reduces reported EPS in the merger model. Goodwill is the residual: the part of the price you cannot attach to any identifiable asset, reflecting synergies, the assembled workforce and going-concern value. Under Ind AS, IFRS and US GAAP for public companies, goodwill is not amortised; it is tested for impairment at least annually and written down if the business underperforms. Indefinite-life intangibles, such as some brands, are treated like goodwill: impairment only.
items.t: Saying goodwill is amortised; that was old Indian GAAP and is a US private company option, not Ind AS.
items.in: For Indian tax, goodwill no longer qualifies for tax depreciation after Finance Act 2021, so acquired goodwill gives no tax shield in Indian deals.

items.q: Apart from goodwill and identified intangibles, what other less visible items can change the combined company after a deal?
p: PP&E and inventory write-ups raise future depreciation and cost of goods
New DTL on write-ups; possible write-down of target's DTA
Contingent liabilities and earnouts recorded at fair value
Soft factors: culture, key talent, customer retention
items.a: Several. On the accounting side, tangible assets get written up too: higher PP&E means more depreciation, and an inventory step-up flows through cost of goods sold in the first few months, hitting margins. Write-ups create a deferred tax liability, and the target's deferred tax asset may be written down if its losses cannot all be used. Contingent liabilities, such as litigation, and contingent consideration like earnouts are recorded at fair value. Beyond accounting, the biggest unmodelled items are people and culture: retention of key employees, integration friction and customer churn. These never appear as assets, but they often decide whether the deal works.
items.t: Forgetting the inventory step-up, which temporarily depresses gross margin after closing and distorts early EPS comparisons.

items.q: What are synergies? Give a few concrete examples.
p: Combined value exceeds the sum of standalone values
Cost synergies: headcount, procurement, facilities, overlapping branches
Revenue synergies: cross-selling, distribution reach, pricing power
Mentions financial synergies (funding cost, tax losses) cautiously
items.a: Synergies are the extra value created because the two companies are together: combined profit or cash flow above what each would earn alone. Cost synergies come from removing duplication: one head office instead of two, closing overlapping branches or plants, merging IT and finance teams, and buying raw materials at better prices on larger volumes. Revenue synergies come from selling more: cross-selling the buyer's products to the target's customers, pushing the target's products through the buyer's distribution network, or better pricing in a more consolidated market. In a cement deal, for instance, serving each market from the nearest plant cuts freight costs. There are also financial synergies, like a lower cost of debt or using tax losses.
items.t: Treating revenue synergies as pure profit; you must apply a margin and a realistic phase-in.

items.q: How do synergies enter a merger model?
p: Cost synergies cut opex; revenue synergies add revenue at a margin
Phased in over two to three years, then taxed
One-time integration costs modelled, usually excluded from adjusted EPS
Used for break-even synergies and to justify the premium
items.a: Synergies are added to combined pre-tax income after the target is consolidated. Cost synergies lower operating expenses directly. Revenue synergies are added as extra revenue, but only the profit on them counts, so you apply the relevant margin. Both are phased in, for example 25%, 75% and then 100% of run rate over three years, and then taxed. If Rs. 40 crore of pre-tax cost synergies are achieved, net income rises by Rs. 30 crore at 25% tax. You also include the one-time costs to achieve them, like severance and IT integration. The model then shows accretion with and without synergies, and the break-even synergies needed to make the deal EPS-neutral.
items.t: Adding synergies below the tax line, or ignoring the one-time integration costs needed to achieve them.

items.q: Which matter more in a deal, revenue synergies or cost synergies?
p: Cost synergies more credible: within management's control
Revenue synergies depend on customers and competitors; slower, uncertain
Revenue synergies count only at the margin; cost savings flow fully
Premium usually justified on cost synergies; revenue treated as upside
items.a: Cost synergies usually carry more weight because they are more certain. Closing a duplicate office or cutting overlapping headcount is within management's control, and every rupee saved flows straight to profit. Revenue synergies depend on customers buying more and competitors not reacting, so they are slower, harder to measure and often never fully delivered. They also add profit only at the margin on the incremental revenue, not the whole amount. That is why bankers and boards typically justify the premium mainly on cost synergies, treat revenue synergies as upside, and investors discount them heavily. In some strategic deals, such as distribution or cross-selling plays, revenue synergies can be larger, but they still get a haircut.
items.t: Saying revenue synergies are worthless; they matter, but are valued with a margin, slower phase-in and a haircut.

items.q: All else equal, would a buyer rather pay with cash, new debt or stock?
p: Cash usually cheapest: only foregone interest, after tax
Debt next: interest rate x (1 - t), plus leverage risk
Stock usually most expensive: higher cost of equity, ownership dilution
Exception: a high-P/E buyer may find stock cheapest on EPS
items.a: Usually cash first, then debt, then stock. Cash costs only the interest it was earning, which is low, and lower still after tax: 6% becomes 4.5% at 25% tax. Debt costs more because borrowing rates exceed deposit rates, though interest is tax-deductible, and it adds leverage risk. Stock is generally the most expensive: the cost of equity is higher than the after-tax cost of debt, and existing shareholders give up ownership and future upside. That said, in an EPS sense the cost of stock is the buyer's earnings yield, so a buyer trading at 40 times earnings has a 2.5% stock cost, cheaper than most debt. In practice, availability, ratings and seller preference drive the mix.
items.t: Ranking only by EPS impact and ignoring that stock gives away permanent ownership and future upside.

items.q: How would you estimate how much debt a buyer can raise to fund an acquisition?
p: Applies leverage multiples: total debt to combined EBITDA, sector norms
Cross-checks interest coverage, EBITDA to interest
Considers target rating, covenants and existing debt
Example: 3x Rs. 1,000 crore EBITDA less Rs. 1,200 crore existing debt
items.a: I look at what the combined company can support, not the target alone. Start with combined EBITDA, including only synergies lenders will credit. Then apply leverage multiples seen in comparable deals and the sector: say lenders accept 3 times debt to EBITDA. On combined EBITDA of Rs. 1,000 crore that is Rs. 3,000 crore of total debt; if the buyer already has Rs. 1,200 crore, new capacity is about Rs. 1,800 crore. I cross-check with interest coverage, perhaps 4 times EBITDA to interest or better, with covenant headroom, and with the credit rating the buyer wants to keep, since a downgrade raises funding costs. Cyclical or asset-light businesses support lower multiples.
items.t: Sizing debt on the target's EBITDA alone, or forgetting the buyer's existing debt.
items.in: RBI's 2026 acquisition finance rules let banks fund eligible Indian non-financial acquirers, up to 75% of deal value; otherwise acquisition debt comes via NCDs, NBFCs or private credit.

items.q: How do you arrive at the purchase price for a target?
p: Listed target: undisturbed share price plus 20% to 40% control premium
Cross-checks DCF, trading comps and precedent transactions
Considers synergies shared and the buyer's ability to pay
Private target: valuation range and negotiation, no market anchor
items.a: For a listed target, the starting point is the undisturbed share price plus a control premium, often 20% to 40%, benchmarked against premiums in precedent deals. I then check that price against an intrinsic range from a DCF, trading comparables and precedent multiples, usually on a football field. For a private target there is no market price, so price comes from those valuation methods and negotiation, often through an auction. On top of that, the buyer looks at what it can afford: how much synergy value it is willing to pay away, the EPS impact, and whether the return on the investment beats its cost of capital. The final number is negotiated within that range.
items.t: Applying the premium to a share price already inflated by deal rumours; use the undisturbed price.
items.in: For listed Indian targets, SEBI takeover rules set a floor open-offer price: the highest of the negotiated price, the acquirer's recent purchase prices and the 60-day volume-weighted market price.

items.q: What typically happens after a company overpays for an acquisition? Can you cite real examples?
p: Buyer's share price falls, reflecting value transferred to sellers
Goodwill impairment later; leverage, management change or divestment follow
Cites real cases, e.g. Kraft Heinz 2019, Bayer and Monsanto
Indian example: Tata Steel and Corus
items.a: Usually the market reacts first: the buyer's share price drops on announcement, reflecting value transferred to the seller's shareholders. Over time, as synergies fall short, the buyer records a goodwill or intangible impairment, a non-cash charge but an admission of overpayment. It may also face higher leverage, rating pressure, activist investors and management changes, and may eventually sell the business at a loss. Examples: Kraft Heinz wrote down about $15 billion of goodwill and brand value in 2019. Bayer's purchase of Monsanto was followed by heavy impairments and litigation, and Bayer's market value fell below what it had paid. In India, Tata Steel's 2007 Corus deal led to years of write-downs and European restructuring.
items.t: Saying impairment reduces cash; it is non-cash, though it signals destroyed value and can pressure covenants.

items.q: A buyer pays Rs. 100 crore in stock for a target, and the next day the market decides the target is worth only Rs. 50 crore. What happens?
p: Buyer's market cap falls by roughly Rs. 50 crore
Target holders now own buyer stock, so share the loss pro rata
Goodwill stays based on consideration; impairment only later if justified
No immediate cash or balance sheet impact
items.a: The market is saying the buyer overpaid by about Rs. 50 crore, so the buyer's market capitalisation falls by roughly that amount, all else equal. Because it is an all-stock deal, the target's shareholders received buyer shares, so they now own part of the combined company and absorb a share of that drop in proportion to their stake. Accounting does not react to the market overnight: goodwill is recorded based on the consideration measured at closing, and nothing changes on the balance sheet the next day. If the underperformance persists, the buyer will eventually impair goodwill. And with a fixed exchange ratio, a falling buyer price before closing reduces the value sellers actually receive.
items.t: Saying the buyer immediately writes down goodwill; impairment follows testing, not daily share price moves.

items.q: Why do so many acquisitions fail to create value?
p: Overpayment: premium exceeds achievable synergies
Integration failure: systems, processes, culture clash
Synergies overestimated, especially revenue synergies
Weak diligence, key talent loss, excess leverage
items.a: Most failures trace back to paying too much for synergies that never arrive. Competitive auctions and management ambition push premiums up, while synergy cases, especially on revenue, are optimistic. Integration is the second big reason: merging IT systems, sales teams, processes and cultures is slow and distracts management, and key people or customers leave. Diligence gaps, such as hidden liabilities or weaker earnings quality than reported, surface after closing. Heavy acquisition debt then leaves no room for error if the cycle turns. Finally, some deals lack a clear strategic logic and are driven by size or empire-building. A good answer ties all of this back to price paid versus value delivered.
items.t: Blaming only culture; the most common root cause is overpaying relative to realistic synergies.

items.q: How does a merger model actually get used during deal negotiations?
p: Sets the maximum price within EPS or return hurdles
Tests consideration mix and resulting ownership split
Shows break-even synergies needed to justify the premium
Sell-side uses it to estimate buyer's ability to pay
items.a: It frames how far each side can go. For the buyer, it shows the price at which the deal stops being accretive or misses the board's return hurdle, and how that changes with different mixes of cash, debt and stock. It shows the synergies needed to break even, which tests whether the premium is defensible to shareholders, plus the post-deal ownership split and leverage, which matter for control and ratings. On the sell side, bankers rebuild the buyer's model to estimate its ability to pay and push for a higher price. It is a guide, not the decision: strategic value and intrinsic valuation matter more than year-one EPS.
items.t: Treating accretion as the deal decision; EPS accretion does not mean value creation.

items.q: Which sensitivities would you run in a merger model, and on which variables?
p: Premium or price against percentage stock versus cash or debt
Synergy level and phasing against premium
Cost of new debt and buyer share price
Outputs: EPS accretion, ownership, leverage, break-even synergies
items.a: The key output is EPS accretion or dilution for the first two or three years, plus post-deal ownership, leverage and break-even synergies. The usual two-way tables are: purchase premium against funding mix, such as percentage of stock versus debt; premium against synergies; cost of new debt against percentage debt; and buyer share price against the exchange ratio, since that sets how many shares are issued. I would also flex the target's growth and margins, synergy phasing, interest earned on cash, and the size of amortisable intangibles. Beyond EPS, I would show combined debt to EBITDA and return on invested capital against the cost of capital.
items.t: Flexing one variable at a time; interviewers expect two-way tables, for example premium against funding mix.

items.q: What is the difference between purchase (acquisition) accounting and pooling of interests?
p: Pooling: combines book values, no write-ups, no goodwill
Purchase: target at fair value, intangibles and goodwill recognised
Pooling abolished for unrelated deals: US 2001, IFRS 2004
Pooling flattered earnings: no extra amortisation or impairment risk
items.a: Under pooling of interests, the two companies simply added their balance sheets at book value, as if they had always been one. No asset write-ups, no new intangibles, no goodwill, so no extra depreciation or amortisation later. Under purchase accounting, now called the acquisition method, one company is identified as the acquirer, the target's assets and liabilities come in at fair value, identifiable intangibles are recognised, and the excess of the price is goodwill. Pooling flattered earnings and invited abuse, so the US abolished it in 2001 and IFRS in 2004. Today every acquisition of an unrelated company uses the acquisition method, which is why merger models always include a purchase price allocation.
items.t: Saying pooling is extinct; it survives for common-control combinations, such as merging two subsidiaries of one group.
items.in: Ind AS 103 requires the acquisition method, but common-control combinations, like group restructurings through NCLT schemes, use pooling of interests at book values.

items.q: Walk me through a concrete example of calculating revenue synergies.
p: Builds from drivers: customers, cross-sell rate, revenue per customer
Applies contribution margin, not full revenue
Taxes the profit and phases it in
Rs. 10 crore revenue becomes Rs. 4 crore EBIT, Rs. 3 crore net
items.a: I build it bottom-up from drivers. Say an insurer buys a distribution company with 10 lakh customers and expects to cross-sell its policy to 5% of them, which is 50,000 customers, each paying Rs. 2,000 a year. That is Rs. 10 crore of incremental revenue at run rate. Only the profit counts, so I apply a contribution margin, say 40%, giving Rs. 4 crore of incremental operating profit. After 25% tax that adds Rs. 3 crore to net income. Then I phase it in, perhaps 30% in year one, 70% in year two and full in year three, and net off one-time costs to achieve it, like marketing and sales force training.
items.t: Adding the Rs. 10 crore of revenue straight to profit instead of applying the margin and tax.

items.q: Walk me through how you would calculate cost synergies in a deal.
p: Identifies specific overlaps: roles, facilities, procurement
Run rate: 200 roles x Rs. 15 lakh = Rs. 30 crore
Separates one-time costs (severance) from recurring savings
Rs. 42 crore pre-tax becomes Rs. 31.5 crore after tax
items.a: I list specific overlaps and cost each one. Suppose two IT services firms merge. Headcount: 200 duplicate corporate and support roles at an average loaded cost of Rs. 15 lakh each saves Rs. 30 crore a year. Facilities: closing 10 overlapping offices at Rs. 1.2 crore annual rent each saves Rs. 12 crore. Total run-rate savings are Rs. 42 crore pre-tax, or Rs. 31.5 crore after 25% tax. These are phased in, say half in year one and all from year two. Separately I model one-time costs to achieve them, such as severance of about six months' pay, Rs. 15 crore, plus lease exit costs. Those are excluded from adjusted EPS but hit cash.
items.t: Ignoring one-time costs to achieve, or assuming the full run rate from day one.

items.q: How do you factor a target's tax losses (NOLs) into an M&A model?
p: Usable losses reduce the combined company's cash taxes
US Section 382: annual cap = equity price x long-term tax-exempt rate
Example: 1,000 x 3% = 30 a year, saving 7.5 at 25%
Unusable losses written off the DTA, increasing goodwill
items.a: Tax losses are valuable because they shelter future taxable income, but a change of ownership restricts their use. In the US, Section 382 caps how much of the target's losses can be used each year at the equity purchase price times the long-term tax-exempt rate. If the equity price is 1,000 and the rate is 3%, only 30 of losses can be used per year, saving 7.5 of tax annually at 25%. In the model I reduce the combined company's cash taxes by that amount each year. I compare the total usable before expiry with the target's loss balance; the unusable part is written off the deferred tax asset, which increases goodwill.
items.t: Assuming the buyer can use all the target's losses immediately, which overstates accretion and value.
items.in: India: business losses carry forward eight years; an over 49% shareholding change in a closely held company lapses them, though qualifying amalgamations can preserve them.

items.q: Why do deferred tax liabilities and deferred tax assets get created in M&A deals?
p: Stock deal: book basis stepped up, tax basis unchanged
Extra book D&A not tax-deductible: DTL = write-up x tax rate
DTA arises when assets are written down or liabilities written up
Rs. 100 crore write-up at 25% gives Rs. 25 crore DTL
items.a: They come from differences between book value and tax value. In a stock purchase, the buyer writes the target's assets up to fair value for book purposes, but the tax authorities still use the old tax basis. So in future, book depreciation and amortisation will be higher than what is deductible for tax, and book tax expense will be lower than cash tax actually paid. That future extra cash tax is a liability today, equal to the write-up times the tax rate. A Rs. 100 crore intangible write-up at 25% creates a Rs. 25 crore DTL. The reverse creates a DTA: writing down assets or writing up liabilities, so future tax deductions exceed book expense. Tax losses also sit as DTAs.
items.t: Saying a standard asset purchase creates a DTL on write-ups; there the tax basis is stepped up too.

items.q: How do DTLs and DTAs flow through the balance sheet adjustments in a merger model?
p: New DTL is a liability; raises goodwill one for one
Writing down the target's DTA reduces assets, raising goodwill
Example: 1,000 - 600 - 200 + 50 = 250 goodwill
Goodwill is the plug; balance sheet still balances
items.a: Goodwill is the plug, so anything that reduces the fair value of net identifiable assets increases goodwill. A new DTL from write-ups is a new liability: it lowers net assets and raises goodwill by the same amount. Writing down the target's existing DTA, for example because its losses cannot all be used, reduces assets and also raises goodwill. Example: price Rs. 1,000 crore, target book value Rs. 600 crore, intangible write-up Rs. 200 crore, so a DTL of Rs. 50 crore at 25%. Goodwill is 1,000 minus 600 minus 200 plus 50, which is Rs. 250 crore. Versus the target's book figures, assets rise by 450 and liabilities by 50: exactly the Rs. 400 crore premium.
items.t: Subtracting the DTL in the goodwill formula; a new liability increases goodwill, it does not reduce it.

items.q: Can you get DTLs or DTAs in an asset purchase?
p: Write-ups usually create no DTL: tax basis also stepped up
US: tax goodwill amortised over 15 years, book goodwill not; DTL builds
Book versus tax depreciation differences still create deferred taxes
Target's tax losses stay with the seller
items.a: Generally the write-ups do not create a DTL in an asset purchase, because the buyer gets a new tax basis equal to the price allocated to each asset, so book and tax bases start equal. But deferred taxes can still appear afterwards. In the US, goodwill and intangibles bought in an asset deal are amortised for tax over 15 years while book goodwill is never amortised, so tax deductions exceed book expense and a DTL builds up over time. Different depreciation methods or lives for book and tax do the same. Provisions deductible only when paid can create DTAs. And since the legal entity is not acquired, the target's tax losses stay with the seller.
items.t: Answering a flat no; timing differences after closing still create deferred taxes.
items.in: In India, goodwill gets no tax depreciation after Finance Act 2021, so the US asset-deal benefit of deducting goodwill does not exist here.

items.q: How do you project a deal-created DTL in the years after closing?
p: DTL unwinds as written-up assets are depreciated or amortised
Annual reduction = extra book D&A x tax rate
Cash taxes exceed book taxes; decrease shown as cash outflow
Rs. 100 crore over 5 years: DTL of 25 falls 5 a year
items.a: The DTL reverses as the written-up assets are depreciated or amortised. Each year the extra book D&A from the write-up is not deductible for tax, so cash taxes exceed book tax expense by that D&A times the tax rate, and the DTL falls by the same amount. Example: a Rs. 100 crore write-up amortised over five years gives Rs. 20 crore of extra book amortisation a year. The opening DTL is Rs. 25 crore at 25%. Book tax falls by Rs. 5 crore a year but cash tax does not, so the DTL drops Rs. 5 crore a year to zero by year five. On the cash flow statement that decrease is an operating outflow. Write-ups on land or indefinite-lived intangibles do not unwind.
items.t: Holding the DTL constant, or showing its decline as a cash inflow.

items.q: Give the full formula for calculating goodwill in an acquisition.
p: Equity purchase price less target's book equity
Adds back target's existing goodwill, which is written off
Less asset write-ups; plus new DTL, DTA write-downs, liability write-ups
items.a: Goodwill equals the equity purchase price, minus the target's book value of equity, plus the target's existing goodwill, which is written off, minus write-ups of PP&E, intangibles and other assets, plus write-ups of liabilities, plus the new DTL on the write-ups, plus any write-down of the target's existing DTA. If less than 100% is bought, add the fair value of the non-controlling interest. Example: price Rs. 1,000 crore, book equity Rs. 500 crore including Rs. 100 crore of old goodwill, so Rs. 400 crore excluding it. Write-ups of Rs. 200 crore create a Rs. 50 crore DTL at 25%. Goodwill is 1,000 minus 400 minus 200 plus 50, which is Rs. 450 crore.
items.t: Forgetting to write off the target's existing goodwill, which double counts it in net assets.

items.q: Why would you write down the target's existing deferred tax asset in an acquisition?
p: DTA mostly from tax losses; ownership change limits annual use
Losses expiring unused are not recoverable, so DTA is cut
Write-down reduces assets and increases goodwill
Example: losses 200, DTA 50; only 120 usable, cut 20
items.a: Most of a target's DTA usually comes from tax losses. After a change of ownership, rules like Section 382 in the US cap how much of those losses can be used each year. If some losses will expire before they can be used, the related DTA is no longer recoverable and must be written down to what will realistically be used. Example: losses of Rs. 200 crore give a DTA of Rs. 50 crore at 25%. If only Rs. 120 crore can be used before expiry, the DTA should be Rs. 30 crore, so it is cut by Rs. 20 crore. That lower asset reduces net identifiable assets and increases goodwill by Rs. 20 crore.
items.t: Writing off the entire DTA by default; only the portion that cannot be used is written down.
items.in: In India, a closely held company's losses lapse on a change of over 49% in shareholding (subject to exceptions), so the related DTA may be fully written down.

items.q: What is a US Section 338(h)(10) election, and why might buyer and seller agree to it?
p: Legally a stock purchase, treated as an asset purchase for tax
Buyer gets tax step-up: deductible write-ups, goodwill over 15 years
No DTL on write-ups; target's tax attributes do not carry over
Seller taxed as on asset sale, so buyer usually pays more
items.a: It is a US tax election that lets a deal be a stock purchase legally but an asset purchase for tax. It is available when the target is an S corporation or a subsidiary sold by a corporate parent. The buyer gets the legal simplicity of a stock deal, with contracts and licences staying in the entity, plus a step-up in tax basis, so write-ups become tax-deductible and goodwill is amortised for tax over 15 years. That creates real cash tax savings and no DTL on write-ups. The seller is taxed as if it sold assets, which can mean a higher tax bill, so the buyer usually pays a higher price to compensate. It works when the buyer's tax savings exceed the seller's extra tax.
items.t: Saying any target qualifies; it needs an S corporation or a subsidiary sold out of a corporate group.
items.in: India has no equivalent election; a tax basis step-up needs an actual asset transfer, and goodwill no longer earns tax depreciation, so the benefit is much smaller.

items.q: What is an exchange ratio, and when do companies use one?
p: Buyer shares issued per target share in a stock deal
Ratio = offer price per target share / buyer share price
Fixed ratio: sellers bear price risk; fixed price: share count floats
Collars limit movement between signing and closing
items.a: The exchange ratio is the number of buyer shares each target shareholder receives per target share, used whenever stock is part of the consideration.
