It equals the offer price per target share divided by the buyer's share price. If the offer is Rs. 300 and the buyer trades at Rs. 600, the ratio is 0.5. In a fixed exchange ratio deal, the share count is locked, so if the buyer's price falls before closing, sellers receive less value, but the ownership split is certain. In a fixed price deal, the value per target share is locked and the number of shares issued floats, so the buyer bears the risk. Collars cap how far either can move between signing and closing.
items.t: Mixing up who bears risk: under a fixed ratio, sellers bear the buyer's share price risk.
items.in: Indian share-swap mergers fix a swap ratio in the NCLT scheme, backed by a registered valuer's report and, for listed companies, a merchant banker's fairness opinion.

items.q: Walk me through the most important terms in an acquisition agreement.
p: Price, consideration form, and net debt and working capital adjustments
Reps, warranties and indemnities with caps, baskets and escrow
Conditions precedent: regulatory and shareholder approvals, MAC clause
Interim covenants, non-compete, termination rights and break fees
items.a: First, price and consideration: cash, stock or earnout, and the adjustment mechanism, usually cash-free, debt-free with a normalised working capital peg, or a locked box. Second, representations and warranties from the seller about the business, backed by indemnities with a cap, a basket or deductible, a survival period, and often an escrow or holdback; warranty and indemnity insurance is increasingly used. Third, conditions precedent to closing: competition, regulatory and shareholder approvals, and a material adverse change clause. Fourth, covenants on how the seller runs the business between signing and closing, plus non-compete and non-solicit clauses. Finally, termination rights, long-stop dates and break fees.
items.t: Listing clauses without saying whom each protects: reps and indemnities protect the buyer, caps and baskets protect the seller.
items.in: Deals crossing CCI thresholds, including the Rs. 2,000 crore deal value test, need Competition Commission approval before closing; listed targets also follow SEBI takeover timelines.

items.q: What is an earnout, and why would a buyer offer one to a seller?
p: Contingent payment tied to future revenue or EBITDA targets
Bridges the valuation gap between buyer and seller
Shifts performance risk to seller and retains founders
Fair value included in price at closing; later changes hit P&L
items.a: An earnout is part of the price paid later, only if the business hits agreed targets, usually revenue or EBITDA, over one to three years. Buyers use it when the seller's price assumes growth the buyer doubts. For example: Rs. 400 crore upfront plus up to Rs. 100 crore if FY28 EBITDA reaches Rs. 60 crore. The buyer pays the full price only if the growth arrives, the seller gets a shot at its asking price, and founder-managers stay motivated. Downsides are disputes over how EBITDA is measured and incentives to boost short-term profit. In accounting, the earnout's fair value is included in the purchase price at closing, and later changes go through profit and loss.
items.t: Saying later earnout revaluations adjust goodwill; under Ind AS 103 and US GAAP they go through profit and loss.
items.in: With non-resident parties, FEMA rules allow deferred, escrowed or earnout consideration up to 25% of the total, payable within 18 months, which limits long earnouts.

items.q: How would an accretion/dilution model differ if the seller is a private company?
p: No share price: price from valuation and negotiation, not a premium
Normalises earnings: owner pay, related-party items, tax status
Few dilutive securities; asset deals and earnouts more common
Combination and EPS mechanics unchanged
items.a: The mechanics stay the same: add the target's earnings, adjust for funding costs and purchase accounting, and divide by the new share count. What changes is the inputs. There is no share price, so the purchase price comes from valuation and negotiation rather than a premium to market, and you work with an agreed equity value instead of offer price times diluted shares. The target's earnings need normalising for owner salaries, related-party transactions, one-off items and sometimes a different tax status. There are usually few options or convertibles. Private deals more often use asset structures, earnouts and seller notes, and any stock consideration is issued directly to the owners.
items.t: Looking for the target's P/E; for a private target, use the purchase multiple implied by the agreed price.
items.in: If a listed Indian buyer pays private sellers in its own shares, it is a preferential allotment under SEBI ICDR, with a pricing floor, shareholder approval and lock-in.

items.q: How do you calculate break-even synergies, and what does the number tell you?
p: Pre-tax synergies that make pro forma EPS equal standalone EPS
(Standalone EPS x pro forma shares - pro forma NI) / (1 - t)
Example: (20 x 12 - 230) / 0.75 = about Rs. 13.3 crore
Compared with management's credible synergy estimate
items.a: Break-even synergies are the pre-tax synergies needed for the deal to be neither accretive nor dilutive. Take the buyer's standalone EPS, multiply by the pro forma share count to get the net income needed, subtract pro forma net income without synergies, and gross up for tax. Example: buyer EPS Rs. 20 on 10 crore shares, issuing 2 crore new shares. Pro forma net income before synergies is Rs. 230 crore, so EPS is about Rs. 19.17, dilutive. Needed net income is 20 times 12, or Rs. 240 crore. The gap is Rs. 10 crore after tax, about Rs. 13.3 crore pre-tax at 25%. If realistic synergies comfortably exceed that, the deal is defensible on EPS.
items.t: Forgetting to gross up the after-tax shortfall for tax, which understates the synergies required.

items.q: Merger models usually combine only income statements. How would you combine all three statements?
p: Adds both balance sheets, then cash, debt and new share adjustments
Eliminates target equity; adds write-ups, intangibles, goodwill, DTL
Fees: advisory expensed, financing fees capitalised
Projects forward and checks the balance sheet balances
items.a: Start with the balance sheet at closing. Add the buyer's and target's balance sheets line by line, then post adjustments: subtract cash used, add new debt and new shares issued, eliminate the target's shareholders' equity and existing goodwill, write up assets and add new intangibles, record the DTL and any DTA write-down, then plug goodwill. Expense advisory fees against cash and retained earnings, and capitalise financing fees. Then project forward: the combined income statement includes new interest, amortisation and synergies; the cash flow statement adds back the new non-cash amortisation, reflects the DTL unwind and debt repayment; and the balance sheet rolls forward from those. Finally, check that assets equal liabilities plus equity every year.
items.t: Adding the target's shareholders' equity to the combined balance sheet instead of eliminating it.

items.q: How do you handle the target's options, convertibles and other dilutive securities in a merger model?
p: Diluted share count measured at the offer price
Options via treasury stock method; in-the-money convertibles as shares
Example: 10 crore + 0.4 crore net = 10.4 crore shares
Out-of-the-money convertibles stay debt, often repaid at change of control
items.a: The purchase price is the offer price times the target's fully diluted shares, calculated at the offer price, because that decides which securities are in the money. Options use the treasury stock method. Example: 10 crore basic shares, offer Rs. 500, 1 crore options at a Rs. 300 strike. Exercise brings in Rs. 300 crore, which buys back 0.6 crore shares at Rs. 500, so 0.4 crore net new shares. Diluted shares are 10.4 crore and equity value is Rs. 5,200 crore. Convertibles in the money at the offer price are treated as converted: add the shares, remove the debt. Out-of-the-money ones stay as debt and are often repaid on change of control. Check unvested options for acceleration.
items.t: Using the target's current share price instead of the offer price, understating dilution and the equity purchase price.

items.q: What are the three main transaction structures for acquiring a company?
p: Stock purchase: whole entity, all liabilities; DTL, no tax step-up
Asset purchase: chosen assets and liabilities; tax basis stepped up
US 338(h)(10): stock purchase legally, asset purchase for tax
Contrasts tax, liability and DTL effects for each
items.a: In a stock purchase, the buyer acquires the target's shares, so it gets the whole legal entity, including all assets, liabilities and contracts. Book values are written up but the tax basis does not change, so a DTL is created and goodwill is not tax-deductible. In an asset purchase, the buyer buys chosen assets and assumes chosen liabilities, gets a stepped-up tax basis so write-ups and goodwill are deductible in the US, and no DTL arises, but contracts and licences may need consent to transfer. The third, in the US, is a Section 338(h)(10) election: legally a stock purchase but treated as an asset purchase for tax, combining legal simplicity with the tax step-up.
items.t: Saying goodwill is tax-deductible in a plain stock purchase; without a tax basis step-up it is not.
items.in: Indian equivalents: share purchase (with a SEBI open offer if listed), business transfer by slump sale or itemised asset sale, and merger or demerger through an NCLT scheme.

items.q: Would a seller prefer a stock sale or an asset sale? What about the buyer?
p: Seller prefers stock sale: one level of tax, liabilities leave
Corporate asset sale taxed twice: company gain, then distribution
Buyer prefers asset deal: tax step-up, avoids unwanted liabilities
Price adjusts to split tax effects; 338(h)(10) a middle route
items.a: The seller usually prefers a stock sale. Shareholders sell their shares, pay capital gains tax once, and every liability, known or hidden, goes with the company. In an asset sale by a corporation, the company is taxed on the gain on its assets and shareholders are taxed again when proceeds are distributed, and the seller keeps any liabilities not transferred. The buyer usually prefers an asset purchase: it picks the assets it wants, leaves behind unwanted liabilities, and gets a stepped-up tax basis, so write-ups and goodwill create tax deductions. In negotiation, a buyer pushing for an asset deal often pays a higher price to cover the seller's extra tax, and 338(h)(10) is one middle route.
items.t: Ignoring execution: asset deals are slower because contracts, licences and permits may need consent to transfer.
items.in: In India, asset transfers attract state stamp duty on property and GST on itemised sales, while share transfers carry only 0.015% stamp duty; slump sales are taxed as capital gains.

items.q: What is a contribution analysis, and why would you look at it in a merger model?
p: Each side's share of combined revenue, EBITDA, net income
Compared with ownership each shareholder group receives
Used mainly in stock deals and mergers of equals to test exchange ratio
Adjusts EBITDA contribution for differing net debt
items.a: A contribution analysis shows what percentage of the combined company's revenue, EBITDA, net income and sometimes market value each side brings, and compares that with the ownership each shareholder group ends up with. It matters most in stock deals and mergers of equals, because it is a quick fairness check on the exchange ratio. If the target contributes 40% of combined EBITDA but its shareholders receive only 30% of the shares, the seller will argue for a higher ratio. One caution: metrics before interest, like EBITDA, ignore leverage, so if one company carries much more debt you should convert to an equity basis before comparing with ownership. It is a negotiation tool, not a valuation.
items.t: Comparing EBITDA contribution directly with equity ownership without adjusting for each company's net debt.

items.q: How do you treat advisory fees, financing fees and other transaction costs in a merger model?
p: Advisory and legal fees expensed: cash and retained earnings fall
Not added to goodwill under Ind AS 103 or US GAAP
Financing fees capitalised, amortised over debt life, tax-deductible
One-time costs excluded from adjusted EPS; equity issue costs reduce equity
items.a: Advisory, legal and due diligence fees are expensed when incurred under the acquisition method, not capitalised into goodwill. In the model they reduce cash and retained earnings at closing and are treated as one-time, so excluded from adjusted EPS. Debt financing fees are capitalised against the debt and amortised over its life as part of interest cost. Example: Rs. 20 crore of fees on a five-year loan gives Rs. 4 crore of non-cash amortisation a year, Rs. 3 crore after 25% tax, which does hit EPS and is added back on the cash flow statement. Equity issuance costs reduce the equity raised. Integration and restructuring costs are modelled as one-time cash costs, phased with synergies.
items.t: Adding advisory fees to goodwill; that was allowed under old rules but not under Ind AS 103 or current US GAAP.
items.in: Under the Companies Act, share issue expenses can be written off against the securities premium account (section 52), so equity issuance costs often bypass profit and loss.

items.q: Walk me through how a basic leveraged buyout model works, from entry to exit.
p: Entry: purchase price, sources and uses, debt plus sponsor equity
Projects FCF and uses it to pay down debt
Exit value minus net debt gives exit equity
Quotes MOIC and IRR: 2x in 5 years is about 15%
items.a: First, set the entry price, usually a multiple of EBITDA, and build sources and uses: the price plus fees is funded by debt tranches and sponsor equity. Second, project the operating case and free cash flow after interest, tax, capex and working capital. Third, run the debt schedule, using that cash for mandatory repayments and a sweep. Fourth, assume an exit after about five years at an exit multiple, subtract remaining net debt to get exit equity, and compute MOIC and IRR. Example: buy at Rs.1,000 crore, 10x EBITDA of 100, with 600 debt and 400 equity. Exit at 10x EBITDA of 150, Rs.1,500 crore, with debt down to 300: equity of 1,200 is 3x, roughly 25% IRR over five years.
items.t: Forgetting transaction and financing fees in uses, or ignoring remaining debt when computing exit equity.

items.q: Why would a buyer use borrowed money to acquire a company instead of paying entirely with equity?
p: Smaller equity cheque amplifies returns on the same exit value
Debt is cheaper than the fund's equity, which targets 20%+
Interest is tax deductible, creating a tax shield
Leverage cuts both ways: magnifies losses too
items.a: Leverage lets the sponsor put in less equity for the same asset, so any gain in value accrues to a smaller base. Say you buy a business for Rs.1,000 crore and sell it for Rs.1,500 crore in five years, ignoring interim cash flows. All equity, you make 1.5x, about 8% IRR. With Rs.600 crore of debt still outstanding at exit, you put in 400 and take out 900: 2.25x, roughly 18% IRR. Debt also costs less than the fund's equity, interest is tax deductible, and the repayment obligation forces cost discipline. The flip side is that a fall in value hits the thin equity layer first.
items.t: Saying leverage always raises returns; it only helps if the business earns more than the after-tax cost of debt.

items.q: Which assumptions move the returns in an LBO model the most?
p: Entry and exit multiples are usually the biggest drivers
EBITDA growth and margin expansion
Amount and cost of leverage, and FCF for paydown
Hold period: IRR falls as time lengthens for same MOIC
items.a: The purchase and exit multiples dominate: a one-turn change on a 10x deal moves value by 10% of EV, and much more as a share of equity. Next is operating performance, meaning revenue growth and margins, which set exit EBITDA and the cash available to repay debt. Then leverage: how much debt, at what rate, and how fast free cash flow pays it down. Finally the holding period, because the same 2x return is about 26% IRR over three years but only about 15% over five. In practice I would show sensitivity tables of IRR against entry and exit multiples and against leverage.
items.t: Listing every input without ranking them; the interviewer wants entry and exit multiples named first.

items.q: How would you decide the entry multiple and the exit multiple to use in an LBO?
p: Entry from comps, precedents and what wins the auction
Exit usually set equal to or below entry multiple
Avoid relying on multiple expansion for returns
Sensitise IRR across a range of entry and exit multiples
items.a: Entry is anchored on trading comps and precedent transactions for similar businesses, adjusted for what it takes to win the process, since the seller and competing bidders set the clearing price. Often you also back-solve: what price still gives the fund its target IRR at a sensible leverage level. For exit, the conservative convention is to assume the same multiple as entry or slightly lower, because the business may be bigger but slower growing, and you do not want the return to depend on markets re-rating. Then I would show a sensitivity table of IRR across, say, plus or minus two turns on both.
items.t: Assuming a higher exit multiple than entry without justification; returns should come from EBITDA growth and paydown.

items.q: What does an ideal leveraged buyout target look like?
p: Stable, predictable free cash flow to service debt
Low capex and working capital needs
Strong market position, capable management, low existing debt
Clear operational upside and a credible exit route
items.a: The core requirement is stable, predictable cash flow that can service and repay debt, so recurring revenue and a defensible market position matter. Low capex and working capital needs mean more cash goes to debt paydown. Low existing leverage and tangible assets help raise financing. You also want a strong management team, room to improve margins or sell non-core assets, and a reasonable entry price, ideally a business the market undervalues. Finally, there must be a clear exit: a strategic buyer, a secondary sale to another fund, or an IPO.
items.t: Saying high growth is the main criterion; cash flow stability matters more than growth for an LBO.
items.in: Full control buyouts are rarer in India since promoters seldom cede control; targets are often MNC carve-outs, IT services firms or businesses facing promoter succession gaps.

items.q: How can an LBO model be used to value a business, and why is it often described as setting a floor valuation?
p: Back-solve price for target IRR, e.g. 20% to 25%
Example: exit equity / (1+IRR)^n plus debt gives max EV
Financial buyer has no synergies, so pays less
Floor: shows minimum a credible financial buyer would pay
items.a: You fix the target IRR, say 20% over five years, and solve for the maximum price the sponsor can pay. If exit equity is Rs.1,200 crore, the equity cheque can be at most 1,200 divided by 1.2 to the power five, about Rs.482 crore. Add the Rs.600 crore of debt and the maximum EV is about Rs.1,080 crore, roughly 10.8x EBITDA of 100. It is called a floor because a financial buyer has no synergies and demands high returns, so strategic buyers can usually pay more. For a seller it shows the minimum value a credible financial buyer should support.
items.t: Treating the LBO value as intrinsic value; it is a buyer-specific price constrained by return targets and debt capacity.

items.q: Give me an everyday analogy for a leveraged buyout.
p: Buying a flat with a home loan is the classic analogy
Rent services the loan, like company cash flow
Small down payment amplifies return on sale
Maps each piece to equity, debt, cash flow and exit
items.a: Buying a flat with a home loan. You pay Rs.20 lakh down and borrow Rs.80 lakh to buy a Rs.1 crore flat. The rent covers the EMI, just as the company's cash flow covers interest and principal in an LBO. After five years the loan has come down to Rs.70 lakh and you sell for Rs.1.3 crore. You receive Rs.60 lakh on a Rs.20 lakh investment: 3x, about 25% a year, even though the flat itself rose only 30%. The down payment is the sponsor equity, the home loan is the acquisition debt, and the sale is the exit.
items.t: Picking an analogy without explaining how cash flow repays debt and how leverage magnifies the equity gain.
items.in: Well-known Indian control buyouts include Blackstone's purchase of Mphasis from HPE (2016) and Carlyle's acquisition of Hexaware from Baring (2021).

items.q: How does the target's balance sheet change at the close of a leveraged buyout?
p: Old equity and old goodwill eliminated; sponsor equity added
New debt added; existing debt usually refinanced
New goodwill = price minus fair value of net assets
Advisory fees expensed; financing fees netted against debt
items.a: On the liabilities side, the target's old shareholders' equity is wiped out and replaced with the sponsor's new equity, existing debt is typically repaid, and the new acquisition debt is added. On the assets side, cash may fall if it is used in the funding, any old goodwill is written off, identifiable assets are revalued to fair value, and new goodwill is created as the purchase equity price minus the fair value of net identifiable assets. Advisory and legal fees are expensed, reducing equity, while financing fees are capitalised by netting them against the debt and amortised. Both sides must balance after these adjustments.
items.t: Leaving the target's old equity and goodwill on the balance sheet, or adding the purchase price as an asset.

items.q: Why does an LBO create new goodwill and other intangibles on the balance sheet?
p: Purchase price usually exceeds book value of net assets
Identifiable intangibles (brand, customers) recorded at fair value
Goodwill is the residual after all fair value step-ups
Goodwill is not amortised; tested for impairment
items.a: Under acquisition accounting the buyer records the target's assets and liabilities at fair value. A sponsor almost always pays more than book value, for the earning power, brand, customer base and workforce. First you identify intangibles that can be valued separately, such as brands, customer relationships, licences or technology, and record them at fair value; these are amortised. Whatever premium is left over after all fair value step-ups and any deferred tax adjustments becomes goodwill. Goodwill is not amortised but is tested annually for impairment.
items.t: Saying goodwill is price minus book value; identifiable intangibles and fair value write-ups come first.

items.q: A corporate buyer usually prefers paying cash for an acquisition. Why then does a private equity fund rely heavily on debt?
p: Corporate uses idle cash with low opportunity cost
PE fund has no surplus cash; its equity is costly
LPs expect 20%+ returns, so debt is cheaper capital
Debt reduces equity cheque and magnifies IRR
items.a: For a corporate, surplus cash is the cheapest funding: the cost is only the foregone after-tax interest income, which is lower than the cost of new debt or issuing shares. A PE fund is different. It has no surplus balance sheet cash; its capital is LP money that expects returns of 20% or more, so equity is the most expensive source it has. Borrowing at, say, 9% to 12% before tax is far cheaper, and every rupee of debt reduces the equity cheque and magnifies the IRR. The fund's goal is equity returns over a fixed horizon, not long-term ownership, so leverage fits its model.
items.t: Answering only 'debt is cheaper' without explaining why the cost-of-funding ranking differs for a corporate and a fund.

items.q: Do you need full three-statement projections in an LBO model, or can you take shortcuts?
p: Must project income statement items through to cash flow
Balance sheet can be simplified to cash, debt, working capital
Shortcut: EBITDA less interest, tax, capex, NWC change = FCF
Paper LBO for quick back-of-envelope checks
items.a: You need enough to calculate free cash flow, because that drives debt paydown and the exit equity value. So the income statement down to net income, and the cash flow items, are essential. The full balance sheet is optional in a quick model: you really only need to track cash, debt balances and working capital. A common shortcut is to go straight from EBITDA: subtract cash interest, cash taxes, capex and the increase in working capital to get cash available for debt repayment. A full model is used for the final bid and lender materials; a paper LBO with rounded numbers is enough for screening.
items.t: Claiming you can skip interest or taxes; both are needed because they directly reduce cash for paydown.

items.q: How would you work out how much debt a buyout can support and how to split it into tranches?
p: Debt/EBITDA multiples from recent comparable financings
Coverage ratios and ability to repay from FCF
Senior secured first, then high yield or mezzanine
Leveraged finance team tests lender appetite
items.a: Start with the market: recent comparable deals tell you what total and senior leverage lenders will accept, expressed as multiples of EBITDA. Then test the target's own capacity: interest coverage, fixed charge coverage, and whether free cash flow can repay a meaningful share within the loan tenor under a downside case. Tranching follows cost and risk: cheapest senior secured bank debt up to what the asset base and cash flows support, often with a revolver for liquidity, then second lien, high yield or mezzanine to fill the gap if the sponsor wants more leverage. In practice the leveraged finance desk sounds out lenders to confirm size, pricing and terms.
items.t: Picking a leverage number without reference to coverage ratios, downside cash flows or comparable deals.
items.in: RBI's 2026 acquisition finance rules cover only non-financial corporate acquirers, not financial sponsors, so Indian buyouts still lean on NBFCs, private credit funds and offshore holdco debt.

items.q: When sizing acquisition debt and setting terms, what leverage and coverage ratios would you consider reasonable?
p: Total debt/EBITDA roughly 4x to 6x in US/European deals
Senior debt/EBITDA roughly 3x to 4x
EBITDA/interest comfortably above 2x
Ratios depend on sector cyclicality and market conditions
items.a: In developed-market sponsor deals, total leverage is typically 4x to 6x EBITDA, with senior secured debt around 3x to 4x. On coverage, lenders want EBITDA to interest of at least 2x, ideally 2.5x to 3x, and EBITDA minus capex to interest of at least about 1.5x. The right level depends on the business: stable, recurring cash flows can carry more, cyclical or capex-heavy businesses less. It also moves with credit markets, rising in loose conditions and falling when rates spike. I would always stress test the coverage ratios under a downside case before settling on a number.
items.t: Quoting a single leverage figure as a rule; it depends on sector, cash flow stability and the credit cycle.
items.in: Indian buyouts usually run lower leverage, often 2x to 4x EBITDA, because bank acquisition finance is restricted and private credit typically costs mid-teens.

items.q: What are the main differences between bank debt and high-yield bonds in a buyout financing?
p: Bank debt: senior secured, floating rate, cheaper
Bank debt amortises and can be prepaid freely
High yield: fixed, higher coupon, bullet, longer tenor
Maintenance vs incurrence covenants; HY has call protection
items.a: Bank debt, meaning revolvers and term loans, is senior and secured, carries a floating rate at a lower spread, and usually has a shorter tenor of five to seven years. It often amortises, can be prepaid without penalty, and term loan A style debt carries maintenance covenants tested every quarter. High-yield bonds are typically unsecured or junior, pay a higher fixed coupon, mature in seven to ten years with a bullet repayment, and have only incurrence covenants. In exchange for that flexibility, bondholders get call protection: a non-call period and premiums if the issuer repays early.
items.t: Calling high-yield debt secured or saying it amortises; it is normally junior, bullet and non-call for a period.

items.q: Why might a sponsor choose bank debt over high-yield bonds to fund a buyout?
p: Lower interest cost from senior secured position
Prepayable without penalty, suits fast deleveraging
Quicker, private, viable for smaller deals
Accepts tighter covenants in exchange for cheaper funding
items.a: Mainly cost and flexibility to repay. Bank debt is senior and secured, so it is cheaper than high-yield bonds. It can be prepaid at par without call premiums, which suits a plan to deleverage quickly from strong free cash flow or asset sales, or a short hold before exit. It is arranged privately and faster, with no public offering documents, and it works for smaller deals where a bond issue is not economical. The trade-off is tighter maintenance covenants and amortisation, which the sponsor accepts if the business is stable.
items.t: Ignoring that prepayment flexibility is often the key reason when the plan includes rapid debt paydown.

items.q: Why would a sponsor instead prefer high-yield bonds?
p: Allows more total leverage than banks will provide
No amortisation frees cash for growth or acquisitions
Only incurrence covenants, so more operating flexibility
Fixed rate and longer tenor suit a longer hold
items.a: High yield lets the sponsor push total leverage beyond what banks will lend, reducing the equity cheque. Because bonds have bullet repayments, cash is not tied up in amortisation and can fund growth capex, add-on acquisitions or dividends. Covenants are incurrence-based, so a weak quarter does not trigger a default the way a maintenance covenant would. The fixed coupon removes interest rate risk and the longer maturity fits a longer holding period. The sponsor pays for this with a higher coupon and call protection, so it makes most sense when early repayment is not the plan.
items.t: Forgetting the cost: high coupon and non-call periods make high yield a poor fit for a quick flip.

items.q: Why would a PE fund buy a company in a seemingly risky sector such as technology?
p: Many tech businesses have recurring, sticky revenue
Mature software can be a stable cash cow
Value from undervalued entry, cost cuts, carve-outs
Can use lower leverage or a growth equity structure
items.a: Risky at the sector level does not mean risky cash flows. Many tech businesses, such as enterprise software with subscription revenue, have high switching costs, recurring revenue and high margins, which is exactly what lenders like. A mature software or IT services firm with slowing growth may trade cheaply yet generate steady cash. Funds also see opportunities to cut costs, sell non-core units, consolidate through add-ons, or take private an underperforming listed company. Where cash flows are less certain, the fund simply uses less leverage and relies more on growth, more like a growth equity deal.
items.t: Assuming PE avoids tech entirely; the key is cash flow predictability, not the sector label.
items.in: Indian control buyouts have clustered in IT services (Mphasis, Hexaware) precisely because these businesses produce steady, dollar-linked cash flows.

items.q: What levers can a PE firm pull to increase its returns on a buyout?
p: Pay less at entry; sell at a higher exit multiple
Grow EBITDA through revenue growth and margins
More or cheaper leverage; faster paydown via working capital
Dividend recap or earlier exit to lift IRR
items.a: Returns come from three sources: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and debt paydown. So the levers are: negotiate a lower entry price; grow revenue and improve margins; buy smaller add-ons at lower multiples and get the combined business re-rated; release cash from working capital and cut capex to pay down debt faster; use more or cheaper debt to shrink the equity cheque; and return cash early through a dividend recap or exit sooner, since IRR rewards time. Remember the rule of thumb: 2x over five years is about 15% IRR, 3x over five years about 25%, and 2x over three years about 26%.
items.t: Listing levers without linking them to the three return drivers: EBITDA growth, multiple change, and deleveraging.

items.q: What do people mean by the tax shield in a leveraged buyout?
p: Interest is deductible, so it reduces taxable income
Saving = interest expense x tax rate
Higher after-tax cash flow speeds debt paydown
Reduces effective after-tax cost of debt
items.a: Interest expense is tax deductible, so the large debt load in an LBO lowers taxable income and the company's tax bill. The saving equals interest times the tax rate: Rs.100 crore of interest at a 25% tax rate saves Rs.25 crore of tax, so the after-tax cost of that interest is only Rs.75 crore. That extra cash goes towards repaying debt, which raises equity value at exit. It is one reason debt is cheaper than equity and why returns rise with leverage, up to the point where distress risk outweighs the benefit.
items.t: Saying the tax shield increases net income; net income falls, but cash taxes and the after-tax cost of debt fall.
items.in: India has no group tax consolidation, so holdco acquisition debt cannot shield opco profits unless merged; thin capitalisation rules cap interest to non-resident associated enterprises at 30% of EBITDA.

items.q: What is a dividend recapitalisation?
p: Company raises new debt to pay a special dividend
Sponsor gets cash back without selling
Leverage rises; ownership unchanged
Usually done after deleveraging or in strong credit markets
items.a: A dividend recap is when a portfolio company borrows new debt, or upsizes existing debt, and uses the proceeds to pay a special dividend to its shareholders, mainly the PE owner. The sponsor gets part of its investment back without selling any stake, so ownership and control are unchanged, but the company's leverage goes back up. It typically happens a few years into the hold, after the business has grown EBITDA and paid down acquisition debt, and when credit markets are receptive.
items.t: Confusing it with a recap that changes ownership; here only the capital structure changes, the owner stays.
items.in: Indian companies can pay dividends only out of profits (Companies Act s.123), so recaps often use buybacks or capital reduction; since Budget 2026, buybacks are taxed as capital gains again.

items.q: Why might a PE sponsor decide to do a dividend recap of a portfolio company?
p: Returns cash early, which raises IRR
De-risks the investment; locks in part of the return
Alternative when IPO or sale markets are weak
MOIC may fall slightly due to extra interest
items.a: The main reason is IRR. Getting cash back in year two or three rather than at exit raises the IRR because of the time value of money. It also de-risks the investment by recovering part of the equity early, and lets the fund return money to LPs or show distributions when fundraising. It is useful when exit markets are weak but credit markets are open, so the sponsor monetises value without selling. The cost is higher leverage and interest, which reduces exit equity, so MOIC is usually flat or slightly lower even as IRR rises.
items.t: Claiming a recap raises MOIC; it mainly lifts IRR, while extra interest can trim the total multiple.

items.q: Walk me through how a dividend recap flows through the three financial statements.
p: Balance sheet: debt up, equity down; cash unchanged
Cash flow: debt raised and dividend paid net to zero in CFF
No income statement effect on day one
Later periods: higher interest, net income falls
items.a: Say the company raises Rs.200 crore of new debt and pays it all out as a dividend. On the income statement, nothing changes on day one, since dividends are not an expense. On the cash flow statement, financing activities show plus 200 from debt issued and minus 200 for dividends paid, so net cash is unchanged. On the balance sheet, debt rises by 200 and retained earnings fall by 200, so it balances. In later periods, at 10% interest, interest expense rises by Rs.20 crore, so net income falls by Rs.15 crore after 25% tax, and cash flow falls by the same amount.
items.t: Putting the dividend through the income statement or forgetting the subsequent increase in interest expense.

items.q: Walk me through the types of debt available in an LBO and how they differ.
p: Ranks by seniority: revolver, term loans, second lien, bonds, mezz
Cost rises as seniority and security fall
Compares amortisation, tenor, covenants, prepayment
Mentions PIK, seller notes or holdco debt
items.a: From most to least senior. The revolver is a secured credit line for liquidity, floating rate with a fee on undrawn amounts. Term Loan A is secured, cheap, amortises meaningfully, five or six years, with maintenance covenants. Term Loan B is secured but held by institutional investors, minimal amortisation, about seven years, often covenant-lite, slightly pricier. Second lien loans are secured but junior. High-yield bonds are usually unsecured, fixed rate, bullet, seven to ten years, incurrence covenants and call protection. Mezzanine and subordinated notes are the most junior and expensive, often with PIK interest or warrants. Holdco PIK notes and seller notes can fill remaining gaps. Moving down, cost and flexibility rise while security falls.
items.t: Mixing up the ordering, e.g. putting mezzanine above high yield, or saying term loan B has heavy amortisation.
items.in: In India, buyout debt is usually NBFC term loans or NCDs subscribed by private credit funds, often at an offshore or Indian holdco, rather than leveraged loans or high-yield bonds.

items.q: How do asset write-ups or write-downs affect an LBO model, and how is the balance sheet adjusted?
p: Write-up raises asset values and reduces goodwill
Extra D&A reduces pre-tax income and net income
Stock deal: book-tax difference creates a deferred tax liability
Cash flow unchanged in stock deal; DTL unwinds
items.a: At close you eliminate the target's equity and old goodwill, add the new debt and sponsor equity, and revalue identifiable assets to fair value. A write-up increases those assets and, in a stock deal where tax basis does not change, creates a deferred tax liability; goodwill is the plug and falls accordingly. Example: Rs.100 crore PP&E write-up, depreciated over 10 years, 25% tax. DTL at close is Rs.25 crore. Each year book D&A rises by 10, pre-tax income falls 10, book tax falls 2.5 and net income falls 7.5. Cash taxes are unchanged, so on the cash flow statement you add back 10 of D&A and subtract the 2.5 DTL unwind: cash is unchanged. A write-down does the reverse.
items.t: Assuming the write-up saves cash tax in a stock deal; only an asset deal or tax step-up does that.

items.q: We normally focus on the sponsor's IRR. How would you calculate the IRR earned by the lenders in an LBO?
p: Lender outflow at close, net of upfront fees or OID
Inflows: cash interest, amortisation, final principal repayment
Include call premiums, PIK accruals, warrants if any
Example: 10% coupon bought at 98 yields about 10.5%
items.a: Treat it like the sponsor's IRR but from the lender's cash flows. The outflow at close is the amount lent, net of upfront fees or original issue discount. The inflows each year are cash interest plus any amortisation or sweep repayments, and the final inflow is the remaining principal at maturity or exit, plus any prepayment premium. PIK interest is received only when the debt is repaid, and warrants add equity value at exit. Example: a five-year, Rs.100 crore bullet loan at 10% interest, funded at 98 after a 2% fee. The lender pays 98, receives 10 a year and 100 at the end, an IRR of about 10.5%.
items.t: Using only the coupon rate; fees, OID, timing of repayments and premiums all change the lender's IRR.

items.q: Why would a sponsor set aside part of the new equity as a management option pool, and how does it change the model?
p: Aligns management with sponsor; rewards value creation
Typically around 5% to 15% of equity
Dilutes sponsor share of exit equity, lowers MOIC and IRR
Option value at exit = pool % x gain above strike
items.a: The pool aligns management with the sponsor: they gain only if equity value rises, which motivates them to hit the value creation plan and retains them through exit. Pools are typically around 5% to 15% of equity, often vesting with time and performance hurdles. In the model, it reduces the sponsor's share of exit proceeds. Example: sponsor equity Rs.400 crore, exit equity Rs.1,200 crore, and a 10% pool struck at entry value. Management receives 10% of the gain, 0.10 x 800, or Rs.80 crore. The sponsor keeps 1,120, so MOIC falls from 3.0x to 2.8x and IRR from about 25% to about 23%. Accounting-wise, there is also a non-cash share-based compensation expense.
items.t: Ignoring the pool at exit, which overstates the sponsor's returns.

items.q: Why might a sponsor use PIK debt, and how does it flow through the debt schedule and the statements?
p: Interest accrues to principal instead of being paid in cash
Preserves cash for senior debt paydown; adds leverage
IS: interest expense reduces net income; added back on CFS
Debt balance compounds; higher coupon than cash-pay debt
items.a: PIK debt pays interest by adding it to the principal rather than in cash. Sponsors use it to push leverage higher without straining cash flow, often at a holding company where senior lenders do not allow cash interest, or when cash is earmarked for senior paydown or growth. Example: Rs.100 crore at 12% PIK, 25% tax, assuming deductibility. Year one interest is 12, so net income falls by 9. On the cash flow statement, add back the 12 as non-cash, so cash rises by 3, the tax saving. The debt balance grows to 112, and year two interest is 13.44. The price is a higher coupon and a bigger balance to repay at exit.
items.t: Treating PIK interest as a cash outflow, or forgetting to compound the balance in the debt schedule.
items.in: Indian private credit often achieves a similar effect through zero-coupon or redemption-premium NCDs, where the return accrues and is paid at maturity.

items.q: Give some examples of incurrence covenants and of maintenance covenants.
p: Incurrence: tested only when the company takes an action
Examples: limits on new debt, dividends, liens, asset sales
Maintenance: tested every quarter regardless of action
Examples: max leverage, min interest coverage, capex caps
items.a: Incurrence covenants restrict specific actions and are tested only when the company wants to take them. Examples: it may only raise new debt if pro forma leverage stays below a set multiple; limits on dividends and other restricted payments; limits on new liens, asset sales, acquisitions and transactions with affiliates. They are typical of high-yield bonds and covenant-lite loans. Maintenance covenants must be met every period whether or not the company does anything. Examples: maximum total or senior debt to EBITDA, minimum interest or fixed charge coverage, and maximum capex. They are typical of bank loans, and breaching one can trigger a default even without a missed payment.
items.t: Calling a leverage test only maintenance; the same ratio can be an incurrence test if checked only when raising debt.
items.in: Indian bank, NBFC and NCD financings usually carry maintenance-style covenants such as DSCR, debt to EBITDA and TOL/TNW, tested on periodic financials.

items.q: An LBO can be a stock or an asset purchase. Can a US buyer also use a Section 338(h)(10) election, and what does it do?
p: Stock purchase treated as asset purchase for tax
Buyer gets tax basis step-up; deductible D&A and goodwill
Target must be a corporate subsidiary or S corporation
Sponsor buys via corporate vehicle; seller may want higher price
items.a: Yes, if the conditions are met. A 338(h)(10) election lets a stock acquisition be treated as an asset purchase for tax. Legally the buyer acquires shares, avoiding the hassle of transferring individual assets and contracts, but for tax the assets are stepped up to fair value, so the buyer gets higher tax-deductible depreciation and amortisation, including goodwill. The target must be a subsidiary of a corporate group or an S corporation, and the buyer must be a corporation, so a PE fund buys through a corporate acquisition vehicle. Both sides must elect jointly. Because the seller may face more tax, it often asks for a higher price, so the step-up's value must exceed that.
items.t: Saying PE buyers can never use it; they can, via a corporate acquisition vehicle, if the target qualifies.
items.in: India has no such election; a step-up needs an asset deal or slump sale, and goodwill has not been tax-depreciable since 2021.

items.q: Walk me through how optional debt repayments, or a cash sweep, are calculated in an LBO model.
p: Cash available = opening cash + FCF less minimum cash
Subtract mandatory amortisation first
Repay in priority order using MIN(cash, balance)
Sweep % per credit agreement; circularity from interest
items.a: Start with opening cash plus free cash flow for the year, subtract the minimum cash balance the business needs, and subtract mandatory amortisation. What remains is cash available for optional repayment, sometimes limited to a percentage of excess cash flow under the credit agreement. You then apply it in order of seniority and prepayability: revolver first, then term loans, each step using MIN of cash remaining and the tranche balance. Example: opening cash 20, FCF 80, minimum cash 10, mandatory amortisation 10 leaves 80. Repay the revolver's 30 balance, then 50 of term loan B. Interest on average balances creates a circular reference, so modellers use iteration or a circuit breaker.
items.t: Sweeping cash into high-yield bonds that are non-call, or ignoring minimum cash and mandatory repayments.

items.q: How does a revolving credit facility work in an LBO model?
p: Drawn when cash falls below the minimum balance
Draw = MAX(0, shortfall after FCF and mandatory payments)
Repaid first when excess cash is available
Interest on drawn amount; commitment fee on undrawn
items.a: The revolver is a liquidity backstop. Each period you compute opening cash plus free cash flow, less mandatory debt repayments and the minimum cash balance. If that is negative, the revolver is drawn for the shortfall, so the draw is the MAX of zero and minus that figure, capped at the facility limit. If it is positive, any outstanding revolver is repaid first, before optional term loan repayments. Drawn amounts pay interest at a floating spread, and the unused portion pays a commitment fee, say 0.5%. In most base cases it stays largely undrawn and matters mainly in downside scenarios.
items.t: Leaving revolver draws on indefinitely or forgetting the commitment fee on the undrawn amount.

items.q: What adjustments would you make to the income statement in an LBO model?
p: Replace old interest with interest on each new tranche
Amortise capitalised financing fees as non-cash interest
Add D&A from asset write-ups and new intangibles
Add sponsor monitoring fees, adjust taxes, normalise EBITDA
items.a: Start from a normalised EBITDA, removing one-offs and adding agreed cost savings. Below EBITDA, add depreciation and amortisation on any written-up assets and newly recognised intangibles. Remove the target's old interest and replace it with interest on each new tranche, cash and PIK, computed on average balances, plus commitment fees on the revolver. Amortise capitalised financing fees as a non-cash interest item over the loan's life. Include any sponsor monitoring fees and transaction expenses at close. Finally, recompute taxes on the new pre-tax income, which is lower given the interest burden.
items.t: Keeping the target's historical interest expense, or forgetting the amortisation of financing fees and new intangibles.

items.q: Can lenders in an LBO end up earning a higher return than the PE sponsor? What would that tell you about the deal?
p: Yes, if equity IRR falls below the cost of debt
Debt gets contractual return; equity takes residual risk
Signals underperformance, overpayment or poor exit
Example: 1.25x over five years is about 5% vs 10% debt
items.a: Yes. Lenders get a contracted return as long as the company does not default, while the sponsor gets only what is left over. If the deal goes badly, equity IRR can fall below the interest rate. Example: the sponsor puts in Rs.400 crore and receives Rs.500 crore after five years, 1.25x or about 5% IRR, while senior lenders earned their 10% coupon. That tells you the deal underperformed: EBITDA missed plan, the entry price was too high, the exit multiple contracted, or interest costs ate the cash flow. Equity is supposed to earn more because it bears more risk, so this outcome means the risk did not pay off.
items.t: Saying it is impossible; equity has no guaranteed return, so a weak outcome can fall below debt yields.

items.q: Higher leverage usually raises IRR. How could adding more debt actually reduce it?
p: Incremental debt costs more than the unlevered return
Higher interest absorbs FCF, slowing paydown
Junior tranches like mezzanine are much more expensive
Distress or covenant risk can erode equity value
items.a: Leverage helps only while the business earns more on the incremental capital than the after-tax cost of the debt. The first turns of senior debt are cheap, but each extra turn comes from pricier tranches: second lien, high yield or mezzanine at perhaps 14% or more. If the business earns an unlevered return of, say, 9%, every rupee of that expensive debt dilutes equity returns. Heavy interest also absorbs free cash flow, so little debt is repaid, and it can force cuts to growth capex. At the extreme, covenant breaches or distress hand value to lenders and push equity IRR down sharply.
items.t: Ignoring that each additional turn of debt comes from more expensive, junior tranches.

items.q: You drive 60 km to a city at an average 30 km/h. How fast must you drive the 60 km back to average 60 km/h for the round trip?
p: Average 60 km/h over 120 km requires 2 hours total
Outbound leg already took 2 hours
Return would need zero time: impossible
Avoids averaging the two speeds
items.a: Set it up as distance over time. The round trip is 120 km, so to average 60 km/h you need to finish in 2 hours. The outbound 60 km at 30 km/h has already taken 2 hours. That leaves zero time for the return leg, so it is impossible at any finite speed. The tempting answer of 90 km/h fails because average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the average of the two speeds: at 90 km/h the return takes 40 minutes, giving 120 km in 2 hours 40 minutes, or 45 km/h.
items.t: Answering 90 km/h by simply averaging speeds rather than dividing total distance by total time.

items.q: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 1:45?
p: Minute hand at 270 degrees from 12
Hour hand moves 0.5 degrees per minute: at 52.5 degrees
Difference 217.5 degrees; smaller angle 142.5 degrees
States which angle is being given
items.a: Measure both hands from 12 o'clock. The minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute, so at 45 minutes it is at 270 degrees. The hour hand moves 30 degrees per hour plus 0.5 degrees per minute, so at 1:45 it is at 30 plus 22.5, or 52.5 degrees. The difference is 270 minus 52.5, which is 217.5 degrees. The smaller angle between the hands is 360 minus 217.5, or 142.5 degrees.
items.t: Leaving the hour hand at 1 o'clock (30 degrees) and answering 120 degrees.

items.q: You have unlimited quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies (25, 10, 5 and 1 cents). What is the most money you can hold in these coins without being able to make exact change for a dollar?
p: No nickels: any nickel lets you complete a dollar
Maximum three quarters, four dimes, four pennies
Answer: $1.19
Checks no combination sums exactly to 100 cents
items.a: Build up greedily while checking you cannot hit exactly 100 cents. Four quarters make a dollar, so at most three, worth 75 cents. Pennies: five would let you add a nickel's worth, so at most four. Dimes: with three quarters, two dimes plus a nickel completes a dollar, so you cannot hold any nickels; five dimes plus two quarters make a dollar, so at most four dimes, and 75 plus 20 plus at most 4 pennies never hits 100. So three quarters, four dimes and four pennies: 75 plus 40 plus 4, which is $1.19. One quarter, nine dimes and four pennies also gives $1.19, and no larger total works.
items.t: Including a nickel, which combines with three quarters and two dimes to make exactly a dollar.

items.q: You have a tap, a 3-litre bucket and a 5-litre bucket, with no markings. How do you measure exactly 4 litres?
p: Fill 5, pour into 3, leaving 2 litres
Empty 3, transfer the 2 litres into it
Refill 5, top up the 3 (takes 1 litre)
Leaves exactly 4 litres in the 5-litre bucket
items.a: Fill the 5-litre bucket and pour it into the 3-litre bucket until full; 2 litres remain in the 5. Empty the 3-litre bucket and pour the 2 litres into it. Refill the 5-litre bucket, then pour from it into the 3-litre bucket, which already has 2 litres, so it takes only 1 litre. That leaves exactly 4 litres in the 5-litre bucket. An alternative route fills the 3-litre bucket repeatedly into the 5, but this one takes fewer steps.
items.t: Losing track of which bucket holds what; narrate each step's quantities aloud.
